It took the hyperinflation of the Occupation, which wiped out citizens' deposits and a large part of the banks' portfolio, for the Bank of Greece to become the undisputed champion of the stability of the banking sector. In the first post-war years, the publishing institution undertook the direct financing of all banks, which initially could not even cover the salaries of their employees. This was the first time that the Bank had been called upon to bail out the entire banking system of the country  but not the last, as you surely remember from the recent period of crisis. when the decisions to provide emergency liquidity assistance (EIA) by the Bank of Greece, taken by the Governing Council of the European Central Bank on the recommendation of the Bank of Greece, kept the Greek banking system alive. In any case, to return to the early post-war years, conditions were such that the Monetary Committee had no difficulty in imposing controls, while in 1952 the General Inspectorate of Banks, which was the first specialized supervisory body, began operating . Since then, the Bank has gradually become responsible for both the control and the eventual resolution of those institutions facing sustainability issues. Today, in order to regain the institutional path we have traveled, the Bank now has at its disposal a variety of tools to safeguard financial stability, through the exercise of both so-called macro-prudential supervision, which focuses on the prevention of systemic risks, and micro-prudential supervision, which concerns the adequate shielding of each individual institution. In addition to banks, it currently supervises insurance companies and other financial services institutions. Since 2014, as already mentioned, the Single Supervisory Mechanism (88M) has been established, with the aim, among other things, of avoiding any kind of national bias in the supervision of banks in the euro area. This does not mean that national supervisors have been weakened. Effective cooperation between the ECB's Single Supervisory Mechanism (88M) and local supervisors (the vast majority of whom belong to national central banks), who also have a long institutional memory of national banking systems, is crucial for effective supervision of all banks in the euro area. A third role, which is often overlooked, is that the Bank of Greece is the treasurer and agent of the state, i.e. it keeps the accounts and executes the transactions of the state. This is a role it has acquired since its inception, although it has admittedly had difficulty convincing NBG to release these deposits! I do not think I need to dwell on the importance of this service, which is both neuralgic and invisible. You will allow me just one historical reference, which is illuminating: during the Second World War, when the Greek Government went into exile in London, it had to pay the salaries of the Greek army that had fled to the Middle East, but also the Red Cross ships that transported food to occupied Greece. Have you ever wondered about where the money comes from and how payments are made? These were mainly the Bank's foreign exchange reserves, which were managed by only three of its employees, who had fled Greece and accompanied the government, carrying the necessary documents in their suitcases! Equally inconspicuous and crucial, though perhaps less heroic, is the fourth role I want to mention, which concerns support for payment systems. I am not referring to the banknotes themselves, which the Bank is also responsible for issuing. Because, as you know, more and more transactions - by far most in terms of value - are now executed without cash. Nor am I referring to cheques, although the country's first clearing house was founded in 1928 and operates until today under the Bank of Greece. I am referring mainly to electronic payment systems, of greater or lesser value, such as TAK0ET2 or DIAS, on which all the individual means and systems with which millions of citizens and businesses carry out their transactions on a daily basis. Within the Eurosystem, several of them are managed or supervised by the Bank of Greece, which thus ensures the security of transactions. This is undoubtedly a sector in which developments are rapid, mainly due to the emergence of new means of payment but also to a whole ecosystem of technology companies offering financial services (EU). In response to these developments in financial innovation, the Bank of Greece has created, among other things, the so-called Protected Regulatory Environment for FinTech companies. Finally, the creation of a digital currency by Central Banks (OBDOs) is the new challenge and answer to volatile and dangerous for financial stability cryptocurrencies of the private sector, along of course with the effective supervision of the cryptocurrency ecosystem. The Bank, as a multidimensional institution, does not stop constantly assuming new roles. It strengthens its role in environmental and climate change issues by establishing the Center for Climate Change and Sustainability. It also acts as a custodian and disseminator of Greek culture. Through the activities of the Centre for Culture, Research and Documentation, which is responsible for its Collections, Historical Archive, Library and Museum, it is a body that educates citizens on financial issues and contributes to the fight against financial illiteracy. At the same time, and in order to continue to respond effectively to the challenges of the new era and technological developments, it is also changing itself by proceeding with its overall Management Reorganization, in order to remain an efficient, reliable and innovative central bank that enjoys the trust of society. I could talk to you for some more time, listing additional roles, initiatives and responsibilities of the Bank of Greece. Don't worry  I don't plan to. I would like to close with a role, which I consider particularly important, that of advisor to the State and citizens on issues of the Greek economy. By publishing reports, studies and statistics, the Bank of Greece informs citizens and provides reliable information to the government, political parties, competent authorities and foreign investors on economic policy issues. It may also be worth mentioning that the Bank warned as early as June 2021 in its Monetary Policy Report about the risk of a global inflation surge, even pointing out that there are also structural factors, such as the deinternationalisation of production and climate change, which may lead to higher inflation in the long run. It is said that institutions are distinguished by constant, value-based, repetitive patterns of behavior. Over time, the Bank of Greece, its management and executives have acted as the "alarm bell" for the respective governments, but also the compass to which everyone turned their eyes when things started to go wrong. Attentive readers of the annual Reports of the Governor of the Bank of Greece will, I believe, recognize that, especially in recent years, in addition to the Bank's references to the risks threatening the country's economy and which usually find their way to the headlines more easily, the necessary measures and reforms are proposed, as well as the opportunities the country has to overcome its inherent weaknesses. transform itself into a modern economy and enhance its adaptability and resilience in a highly uncertain international environment. The effective handling of major challenges during the Bank of Greece's long course is certainly due to its strong institutional set-up and operating framework, which harmoniously combines the fundamental imperative of independence with the legitimate demand for accountability and control. It is also due to its commitment to the European orientation of the Greek economy and the duty imposed on it by its participation in the Eurosystem and its Statute. The above constitute its formal institutional framework, that is, the set of written rules, laws on which it bases its operation. To a large extent, however, the effectiveness of the Bank of Greece is due to its high-level human resources and customary institutional framework, codified and unwritten rules of conduct followed over time by the staff who have served in it. A typical example of the above rules is the final sentence of the message of the Board of Directors of the employees on the 25th anniversary of the Bank's operation in 1953, which I singled out in H. Venezis' book "The Chronicle of the Bank of Greece" and with which I would like to close my speech today: "The seniors of officials pass on to our juniors the tradition of virtue and duty. And we all promise that the tradition will continue." And to continue with E. Venezis: "This is how the story of twenty-five years ended An institution that had begun its life in a small building on Panepistimiou Street in order to evolve into a tradition and institution." Thank you!

Title: Speech by Bank of Greece Deputy Governor Ch. Papaconstantinou at the 4th NPL Summit
text: Speech by Bank of Greece Deputy Governor Ch. Papaconstantinou at 41II NPI_ 3yIPii 17/05/2022 - Speeches  Evolution of non-performing loans in 2021 Ladies and gentlemen, It is a fact that we are living through an economic juncture characterised by considerable uncertainty and challenges. After the long period of the pandemic and as the European economy and financial sector began to recover, a new exogenous shock was added, the Russian invasion of Ukraine. Stagflationary pressures and challenges faced by governments and central banks compose the environment in which banks operate, increasing the complexity they face. At the same time, the domestic banking system has managed to strengthen its resilience compared to the past, primarily by improving asset quality. In six years, since March 2016, Non-Performing Loans (NPLs) have decreased by 82.8%, confirming the extraordinary efforts made by all parties involved to resolve the Greek banking sector. Actions in this direction continued during the pandemic and in fact in 2021 there was an acceleration, which is reflected in the ratio of NPLs to total loans, which stood at 13%, the lowest rate observed in more than a decade, compared to 30.1% at the end of 2020. However, we have to acknowledge that the NPL ratio is still very high and a multiple of the European average, which in 2021 was only 2.0%. This rapid decline in NPLs in Greek systemic banks in 2021 was mainly the result of the completion of securitisation transactions and the de-recognition of NPLs from banks' balance sheets. Simultaneously with the implementation of the securitisations, three systemic banks also proceeded with corporate transformation as well as direct loan sales agreements. The securitisation transactions used the Hercules Asset Protection Scheme to provide a guarantee by the Greek State on the senior securities of the securitisation held by the banks. The amount of NPLs securitised amounted to 49.5 billion. 37.7% of this amount was channelled to the Hercules programme, with the total guarantees granted by the Hellenic Republic at the end of 2021 amounting to 18.6 billion. euro. It is noted that in 2021 the extension of this program for an additional 18 months was approved, with the corresponding possibility of granting additional guarantees of up to 12 billion. euro. As a result, today two of the four systemic banks have achieved the operational target of achieving a single-digit NPL ratio with end-2021 data, while NPL resolution and NPL management actions are expected to reach single digits for the entire banking sector by the end of 2022. The ultimate goal is for the Greek banking system to approach the average of European banks [about 2%].  Future challenges for further consolidation Therefore, we have already come a long way from the peak of NPLs, using all available tools used by banks However, as I mentioned above, the stock of NPLs remains high. At the same time, the emergence of new non-performing loans cannot be excluded as a result of the definitive withdrawal in 2022 of borrower support measures to protect against the pandemic. Moreover, Russia's invasion of Ukraine is an additional factor of uncertainty about the future path of NPLs as the global economy faces inflationary pressures, mainly due to rising energy costs. Of course, I should point out at this point that inflationary pressures in the Greek economy were relatively mild in 2021 and smaller than those faced by other European economies, while, for the time being, GDP forecasts can be described as encouraging. We are therefore expected to see the real impact of prices and, hence, the reduction in household disposable income and the increase in business operating costs, on the quality of banks' loan portfolios. It is becoming clear that a new wave of NPLs may emerge, especially if the geopolitical crisis persists for a long time or escalates further. This impact cannot be accurately estimated, but it is a valid cause for concern Some early indications suggest that we have new flows of NPLs and an increase in regulated loans. For this reason, complacency is not allowed and the Bank of Greece is closely monitoring developments. In light of the above challenges, the rapid and complete reflection of new NPLs on banks' balance sheets is an immediate priority for the consolidating and strengthening the resilience of the banking sector. At the same time, efforts to de-escalate the existing stock should be intensified. In addition, the effective implementation of the new bankruptcy legislation will also play an important role in the course of non-performing loans. In particular, in the context of addressing financial weakness and the collective satisfaction of creditors, the new bankruptcy framework (Law 4738/2020) was drastically reformed, through the integration of individual debt settlement tools into a single framework. More specifically, it is imperative to apply the prescribed procedures for bankruptcy and discharge of debtors as well as to use the basic tools at an early/pre-insolvency stage. These tools include: Making use of the new framework should contribute both to preventing over-indebtedness and avoiding the build-up of debts that are difficult to sustain, but also to maintaining the viability of companies whose insolvency can be avoided if they are restructured. It is self-evident that, in case preventive debt restructuring is not achieved, there is the possibility of applying the bankruptcy procedure, through which the liquidation of the bankruptcy estate is now accelerated. Another point is worth noting, which is the decoupling of insolvency capacity from commercial capacity, allowing natural persons who do not have the status of trader to go bankrupt. Another important element is the electronic conduct of auctions using the B-3 solar platform. I would not like to omit the new regulations for vulnerable debtors (Article 3 of Law 4472/2017) and stress the need for the immediate operation of the Acquisition and Leasing Agency, as through it the debtor will be able to continue living in his main residence, avoiding eviction, as well as to become the owner of the property again, if he so wishes. The experience so far with the implementation of the new bankruptcy legislation has been positive, but not satisfactory. Of course, the pandemic has created malfunctions in some mechanisms. From now on, it is of the utmost importance that all parties involved use the tools of the law and support debtors with prospects of viability to become aware in the future, thus contributing both to improving the quality of banks' loan portfolios and to the overall effort to tackle non-performing loans.  Secondary market for NPLs electronic mechanisms for notifying the debtor and advisory services from special centres and bodies, a new out-of-court settlement and Pre-insolvency resolution proceedings I left for the end the most interesting parameter for dealing with non-performing loans, the smooth and effective functioning of the secondary market of non-performing loans. Specifically, there are 23 Loan and Credit Receivables Management Companies operating in the Greek secondary NPL market, which have been authorised by the Bank of Greece. The degree of activity of existing companies varies significantly. In particular, the sector is highly concentrated with only 3 of them holding around 80% of the market share, based on the total value of exposures under management [123 billion end-2021], The majority of these exposures have been assigned to management companies over the last two years as part of the implementation of banks' NPL reduction strategies and relate to exposures resulting from the de-recognition of securitised loans by banks and their transfer to management companies. This highlights the importance of effective management of exposures by these companies in order to effectively utilize collateral and offer restructuring solutions. Based on the estimates of the business plans for the securitized exposures, it is expected that the largest part of the proceeds, almost 60%, will come from settlements and the rest will come mainly from liquidations and finding a consensual solution [36%], while a very small percentage [5.5%] will concern simple collections. At the same time, the implementation of the relevant business plans by the management companies will create opportunities for the banking industry, such as financing viable businesses, real estate markets, as well as purchases of sustainable sound loans. It is recommended that banks exercise caution in the next steps and ensure that conservative rules/credit standards and policies are applied to any new funding. At this point, I would like to focus on the expected further expansion of the secondary market for NPLs, which is expected to occur due to its maturity. Loans that have been resolved or are being resolved by existing companies, as well as loans that are still red but can be regulated on a sustainable basis, provided that new liquidity or, where necessary, capital is provided, I believe that they will attract the buying interest of new investors. As observed at European level, the trend is for smaller investors specialised in certain sectors or asset classes to become active in the market, playing an important role as the market will also create further opportunities to manage smaller portfolios. In addition, expansion is expected in the real estate market with interest turning to loan transactions with residential collateral from specialized companies. In closing, let me point out once again the really significant progress that has been made in cleaning up banks' balance sheets. But we still have a long way to go in terms of consolidating businesses and households. Non-performing loans remain a burden on highly indebted businesses, but also on households. For this reason, vigilance and acceleration of actions are required, taking into account all the above mentioned factors, in order to overcome this problem and so that the banking system can further contribute to the recovery of the economy through, in part, the use of the European resources of the Recovery Fund. Thank you and I wish you every success in today's workshop.

Title: Speech by Bank of Greece Governor Yannis Stournaras at the launch of the book by Spyros Vliamos and Konstantinos Gravas: "Central Banks"
text: Address by the Governor of the Bank of Mr. Yannis Stournaras in Greece presentation of the book by Sparos Vliamos and Konstantinos Gravas: 'Central banks' 30/05/2022 - Speeches It is with great pleasure that I am with you tonight at the presentation of the book entitled "Central Banks", by the excellent scientists and friends Sparos Vliamos and Konstantinos Gravas. In this book, the authors present to readers in a meaningful and concise way the role that central banks have played over time in stabilizing macroeconomic and financial conditions in its largest economies World. They also describe the important milestones and doctrines of monetary systems internationally. Their narrative is short but also complete. The book reads breathlessly -- after all, this is the aim of the "Small Introductions" series: "to provide valid and in-depth information in simple but not simplistic writing, on matters of immediacy of interest"[1]. In this spirit, the authors examine many important historical episodes and the evolution of the institution of central banks. From the reader's perspective, this book offers plenty of food for thought: The institution of central banks has a long history, from at least the 17th century to the present day. During this time, central banks have taken on a variety of roles, which converged on the institutional obligation and responsibility to give early warning and face risks that could disrupt monetary and monetary affairs financial stability. Central banks have often found themselves at the core of intense criticism, fair or unfair, covert or overt, substantiated or arbitrary. And it is precisely this fact that demonstrates not only their importance as institutions of an economically orderly society, but also the extent of their impact on the economic process. Above all, however, central banks are an institution that evolves as prevailing economic conditions and social values change. And on this basis I will agree with the authors - we have not reached "the end of history" even for central banks. From a slightly different perspective, the authors aim to shed light on the question of how a monetary union can evolve and integrate. Remaining a Union of Stability and Growth. In this pursuit, central banks have played a distinct role: they have, I would say, "navigated" between alternative policy objectives and tools to achieve them, while adapting their operating framework and the scope of their mandate. In view of the unprecedented challenges they have faced over time, they have adopted innovative monetary policy measures in an inventive and decisive way. Central banks have been transformed as an institution over their long history. And this is precisely what is at the heart of the book, which, to paraphrase E3poi8 Bbop, "traverses like a ship the vast ocean of time"[2] drawing lessons from the past that can be translated into exhortations for the future. As memory and knowledge underlie responsibility, I would like to address some of these more recent lessons, choosing to focus on our experiences at the Eurosystem and the Bank of Greece: First, the bold and multidimensional response of central banks to the Global Financial Crisis, and the Eurosystem in particular in the subsequent debt crisis in the euro area, and Secondly, the rise and fall of the monetary systems of the last century, which essentially paved the way to the euro. The lessons of recent decades Central banks and "monetary peace" The first part of the book touched me a lot in my role as Governor of the Bank of Greece, from where I was called upon to face the great challenge of the debt crisis for the banking system in our country. The second part of it won me over, as it is at the heart of my interests as an academic. This section describes the successive rise and fall of monetary systems from the late 19th century to the present day, on the way to achieving the "monetary peace" that, as the authors say, describes modern international cooperation in the field of monetary policy. In the aftermath of the famous "Nixon shock", which led to the decoupling of the dollar from gold and the collapse of the BCT system, the preference of economies began to be directed towards free exchange rate fluctuation, which was seen as offering better prospects for stabilizing economies in cases of macroeconomic shocks. At this point, the question posed by the authors, a question that has also piqued my interest as an academic, concerns the conditions for stabilisation in cases of shocks under various exchange rate regimes, and the need for cooperation between the participating countries in order to achieve macroeconomic and financial stability. At the same time, the authors refer to the role of central banks in relation to these issues. The starting point for these answers is the model of the Guidelines and Studies, which makes it possible to study the effectiveness of macroeconomic policy (monetary or fiscal) in relation to exchange rate and capital mobility regimes. The corollary of this model is the "impossible trilemma", i.e. that a group of countries cannot simultaneously 1) maintain a stable exchange rate, 2) pursue autonomous monetary policies, and 3) maintain complete freedom of capital movement: it can pursue any two of these goals, but must necessarily give up the third. This trilemma posed great challenges for European countries trying to strengthen their economic cooperation after the collapse of the UK. Almost the entire history of European monetary cooperation up to the early 1990s was marked by attempts to maintain some form of exchange rate stability. These attempts were undermined by great tensions between national currencies whenever a The country was forced (or tempted) to devalue its currency, or even abandon the common currency rule.[3] The best approach to solving Europe's "impossible trilemma" of reconciling the free movement of capital with fixed exchange rates was for European countries to adopt a single monetary policy and thus a single currency vis-a-vis the rest of the world. In this way, the vision of the euro that has defined the history of our continent became a reality.[4] However, this story also contains an important lesson: the adoption of irreversible exchange rates and the conduct of a single monetary policy should provide the scope for effective adjustment to shocks in euro area Member States. Thus, in order to ensure the economy's return to stability, cooperation, systemic adjustment and coordinated action between institutions and decision-makers are needed, as well as a mechanism to address imbalances. As we have seen during the pandemic, the maintenance of "monetary peace" has been favoured by the coordination of appropriate policies across the EU. levels, including those of fiscal policy, but also of supervisory policy. In this context, the euro area will benefit significantly from further integration steps: advancing the Capital Markets Union and the Banking Union with the launch of the European Deposit Insurance Scheme, as well as strengthening initiatives to consolidate the banking crisis management framework, are fundamental to achieving a comprehensive and more resilient banking and economic union. Challenges ahead for central banks I could refer to other interesting aspects of central bank activity, such as the Sino-American interaction aptly called Kimmer or the power of central bank communication with the wider public, but I would prefer to encourage you to navigate the history of central banks through the pages of this book. According to the nnipeiop Obreii, anyone who does not remember the past is doomed to relive it.[5] Economic history books like this help us learn from the past so that we can better plan for the future. There is no doubt that central banks, as guardians of the currency, should remain committed to price stability over the medium term. In this way, they contribute to a healthy and stable economy, and thus to the well-being of citizens and countries. However, this does not mean that the institution of central banking will remain unchanged. The authors already demonstrate very significant changes compared to the past at all levels. Developments such as climate change, globalisation, digitalisation, the possible introduction of digital currencies affect the functioning of markets and the economy and price formation, and pose new challenges for central banks that need to be addressed in a relatively short period of time. Thus, central banks will continue to evolve in an ever-changing environment. Because as Nelson Mandela says in his autobiography, "I discovered a secret: after climbing a mountain, you discover that there are many more mountains to climb."[6] The very interesting first part of the book briefly describes the course of the world's largest central banks over time, and their institutional evolution from their birth until today. The main objective of modern central banks is to contribute to the economic well-being of society by maintaining price stability over the medium term. As the macroeconomic environment rarely remains unchanged for long periods of time, there are often unforeseen disruptions in the functioning of the economy and financial markets, sometimes leading to severe economic crises. In these circumstances, central banks need to intervene to ensure the stability of the currency's value, the smooth functioning of the financial system and, ultimately, economic growth. At the beginning of the 21st century, it was believed that monetary policy had reached a "perfect" stage as the economic environment was characterized by low and relatively stable inflation and robust growth. However, in 2008 the "unexpected" happened with the outbreak of the World financial crisis. In an economic environment with strong deflationary pressures and interest rates close to the minimum possible level, central banks have taken drastic, unconventional, measures to support economic activity and proper functioning of the financial system. The main tool used by central banks to create favourable financial conditions and ensure the uninterrupted flow of funding to the real economy in this period has a long tradition in central banking. This is quantitative easing or, as is often said, eavesdropping. In the euro area, the ECB has made large-scale purchases of both public and private sector bonds, which continue to this day. With the asset purchase programme, together with the one-off long-term refinancing operations, inflation converged to a level consistent with price stability and economic growth strengthened, compared with the very low (even negative) levels prevailing during the twin crises. More recently, during the pandemic, central banks have again resorted to extraordinary measures to ease the climate of high uncertainty and contain the economic downturn. In particular, the ECB immediately activated an emergency asset purchase programme, the well-known PEPP, which, thanks to its flexibility, managed to ensure smooth financial conditions in all economies, reducing the risk of financial market fragmentation and contributing to the smooth transmission of monetary policy in every corner of the euro area. In practice, this flexibility has been applied by allowing the allocation of purchases of public sector securities to temporarily deviate from each national central bank's key for holding the ECB's share capital. In fact, in this emergency programme, Greek government securities were granted a derogation from the minimum credit quality requirements applicable to the regular government bond purchase programme (P8PP), which contributed to limiting the impact of the pandemic on financial conditions in the Greek economy. This flexibility shall also be maintained in the period of reinvestments of maturing securities purchased under the PEPP. According to the recent review of the ECB's monetary policy strategy, these highly effective monetary policy tools can, where circumstances warrant, be used flexibly when the economy is operating close to the lower bound of nominal interest rates. Thus, these measures, although unconventional, remain in the toolbox of central banks, and the Eurosystem in particular, significantly enriching it. However, the ingenuity and flexibility of central banks does not end here. It was also evident in the way they faced malfunctions in the provision and distribution of liquidity to the banking system during the twin crises. In this context, the ECB opted for the provision of liquidity through fixed-rate operations without quantitative limitation, against collateral (i.e . whether it will be correct), providing a safety net for the euro area banking system to ensure its smooth functioning and the protection of citizens and businesses. The function of central banks as lenders of last resort for the banking system is based on the doctrine of the Treasury, formulated in 1873 in England and significantly influenced economic thinking. Correctly diagnosing its importance, the authors refer extensively to this topic. In this context, central banks worldwide used another long-standing monetary policy tool during crises  the emergency liquidity assistance to healthy banks (at a higher price also against collateral), known in the case of the Eurosystem as the "EIA" facility. At this point, I would like to refer specifically to the Bank of Greece, which, having a positive assessment by the Governing Council of the ECB, managed, through the provision of liquidity to Greek banks through the EIA_A mechanism, to ensure the flow of funding to all sectors of the economy. The successful activation of this mechanism contributed significantly to the proper functioning of the financial system in conditions of acute crisis and, ultimately, to the improvement of the economic climate. Another example of central banking developments is the stagflation experience of the 1970s, when central banks were faced with economic conditions that included both weak economic growth and high inflation. Central banks' commitments at the time to control inflation lacked the necessary credibility, so expectations of even higher inflation became entrenched across the economy. Thus, in order to tame inflation, central banks had to tighten monetary policy strongly with a negative impact on economic aggregates. Since then, central banks have managed to consolidate their independence and gain the trust of markets and the general public, enabling them to address inflationary risks much more promptly and effectively. [This is also largely due to the continuous effort made by central banks in the area of communication, in which much progress has been made.] In the current period, inflationary pressures have intensified globally. As the effects of the pandemic began to fade, there was a rapid restart of the economy, causing supply-demand imbalances until the affected supply chains could be restored. At the same time, energy and other commodity prices rose significantly, which accelerated with the start of the war in Ukraine. In the euro area in particular, inflation is at its highest level in decades, well above the ECB's target. However, the rise in inflation is largely due to supply-side shocks, while output remains below potential and uncertainty remains high. This is why, in the euro area, we are gradually moving towards monetary policy normalisation by carefully assessing the outlook and risks for inflation over the medium term. Although net asset purchases are expected to be completed in the coming months, we continue to reinvest maturing securities amounts, maintaining favourable financing conditions. As regards policy rates, their increase should be gradual in order to avoid negative effects on economic activity and possible fragmentation in financial markets. As credibility and confidence in the central bank (ECB) have been established, we aim to slow down price growth through a mild and gradual normalisation of the monetary policy stance so as not to interrupt the recovery of the euro area economy. Title: Speech by Bank of Greece Governor Yannis Stournaras at the Economist conference "Sustainable Finance in Uncertain Times: Solid Foundations in volatile economies" on "Contemporary challenges for sustainability"
text: Speech by Bank of Greece Governor Yannis Stournaras at the Conference of the European Union "8l8l3a3a1e P r o c t i on o f the "Modern challenges for sustainability" 26/09/2022 - Speeches The world and economies became much more complex after the pandemic and Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Achieving the 17 sustainability goals set by the United Nations (including eradicating pandemics, hunger, inequalities and, of course, environmental sustainability) has become more difficult. It requires cooperation and coordination across the globe in the scientific field (public health is a striking example) but also in the sphere of economics Policy. Viruses, greenhouse gases and economic crises cross borders and cannot be tackled in isolation. A joint approach is needed. The current geopolitical crisis and the associated impact on societies, economies and the environment mark a step backwards in addressing humanity's problems. If it is perpetuated it will cause a significant reduction in prosperity in most countries of the world (certainly in European countries mainly through very high energy prices imported), through lower product and higher prices, characteristics of stagflationary pressures manifested. Inflation today in Europe comes from the supply side, not the demand side. A very high percentage is due to imported natural gas from Russia, which has been instrumentalized. This means that it cannot be countered by the normalisation of monetary policy alone, but requires complementary action by energy policy and fiscal policy at European level. The so-called normalisation of monetary policy (i.e. the return of intervention rates to a neutral level and/or higher) cannot effectively address current inflation  which, as mentioned above, is supply-side inflation  but only inflation expectations and the wage-price spiral. In my view, the ECB should maintain the basic principles of graduality (C&au&1ii) and flexibility (C&au&1ii) since the problem it faces is different from that faced by Gea in the US. The combination of rising interest rates and the very large increase in energy prices pose risks to corporate balance sheets and to households' disposable income, which, in turn, pose risks to banks' balance sheets. Banks benefit from rising interest rates, but face risks from a possible deterioration in their asset quality for the reason mentioned above and from inflation remaining high. This combination has increased supervisors' preparedness. 2022 is progressing better than expected for the economy (GDP) of the European Union and especially for the member-states of the European South and especially for Greece. This is mainly due to two factors: better-than-expected travel receipts (tourism) and, more generally, the increase in so-called "suppressed" demand (reir) - suppressed by its confinement pandemic). Especially for Greece, the GDP growth currently expected for the whole of 2022 is much higher than initially expected, hovering around 6%. Together with high inflation, nominal GDP growth is expected to be well above the weighted average government borrowing rate, thereby supporting a significant decline in the government debt-to-GDP ratio. For the euro area, GDP growth in 2022 is expected at 3.1%. But these developments do not allow complacency. For 2023, euro area GDP growth is expected to be slightly positive in the baseline scenario (0.9%) but negative in the worst-case scenario (-0.9%). For Greece, GDP growth for 2023 is currently expected at 2.8%. For 2023 the combination of (i) rising interest rates, (ii) very high gas prices, (iii) a gradual, further withdrawal of government aid for fiscal reasons, and (iv) the exhaustion of Suppressed5 demand, may bring economic developments in the euro area closer to the worst-case scenario than to the baseline. This will also affect developments in Greece. However, the proportionately large inflow of funds from the CPY (Recovery and Resilience Fund) and the EU Structural Funds, combined with the lower energy burden of the Greek economy compared to the EU average and the characteristics of its public debt structure, create the conditions for the eventual implementation of the worst-case scenario for the EU not to have a corresponding impact on the Greek economy. A prerequisite for this is the respect of the fiscal targets for 2022 and 2023 (primary deficit close to 2% of GDP for 2022 and surplus close to 1% of GDP for 2023) and the implementation of the reforms agreed with the European Commission. The goal of obtaining investment grade status becomes even more urgent under these more adverse international economic and financial conditions. The transition to a climate-neutral growth model is now more necessary than ever and requires the mobilisation of significant resources from the private and public sectors. In particular, the financial system can make a significant contribution in this direction, through its practices and the role it can play in financing the economy and managing risks. Financing sustainable growth and addressing climate change and transition risks can increasingly be integrated into a financial institution's strategy, governance, risk management framework and disclosures. It is now clear that climate-related risks are a source of instability for the economy and vulnerability for the financial system. Natural risks, such as more frequent occurrence and increased severity of extreme weather events, as well as transition risks, e.g. from a delayed and abrupt transition to a low greenhouse gas emissions economy, can affect the transmission of monetary policy and jeopardise price, financial and economic stability. Proper assessment and supervision of financial risks stemming from the transition to a climate-neutral economy is an important factor in promoting sustainable growth and safeguarding the smooth functioning of the financial system. Central banks' task is therefore to prevent risks to price stability and, in cooperation with supervisors, to ensure that the financial system is resilient to these risks. This task must be translated into concrete measures, both in the area of monetary policy and supervision. While the main responsibility remains with governments (for example through carbon taxation, subsidies for alternative energy sources and investment programmes), central banks can and should take an active role in tackling climate change. Central banks are already considering ways to include climate change impacts, whether physical or linked to the transition to a low-carbon economy, in macroeconomic projections and financial stability monitoring. They are also actively involved in integrating climate-related risks into the prudential institutional framework and practice, while in constant dialogue with rating agencies and financial sector companies to ensure that these agencies understand climate risks, disclose them appropriately and take them into account in their overall risk assessment and credit decisions. Until recently, most central banks focused primarily on raising awareness of the risks of climate change and how these issues affect their own operations. However, central banks are committed and are already doing more. The Governing Council of the European Central Bank (ECB) launched in 2021 a comprehensive action plan to further integrate climate considerations into the monetary policy framework and integrate environmental sustainability criteria more systematically into it. Always within its mandate, the Eurosystem, like other central banks around the world, is exploring the range of tools at its disposal, adapting the monetary policy framework and catalysing change in the financial system, seeking to accelerate the transition to a climate- and environmentally-friendly economy and strengthen society's resilience to climate change risks. The Bank of Greece is one of the first central banks in the world to deal with climate change and sustainability, already in 2009 with the Climate Change Impact Study Committee, while in 2021 it established the Centre for Climate Change and Sustainability to coordinate and implement the Bank's climate actions. On the occasion of the 26th Conference of the Parties to the UN Convention on Climate Change (POP26), the Bank of Greece has planned a series of actions in the coming years and committed to contribute, within its competences, to the achievement of the Goal set out in the Paris Agreement, which foresees that financing flows should be made compatible with a path leading to low greenhouse gas emissions and change-resilient growth Climate. The Bank of Greece's objective is a modern, robust and environmentally sustainable economy, guided by the social well-being of citizens. And in this effort, the central banks, and the Bank of Greece in particular, are contributing, within the framework of their mandate, with all their might.

Title: Speech by Bank of Greece Governor Yannis Stournaras at the presentation of the IOBE study "Adaptation to climate change: Challenges and prospects for the Greek economy"
text: Address by the Governor of the Bank of Greece Yannis Stournaras in presentation of the IOBE study "Adaptation to climate change: Challenges and prospects for the Greek economy" 14/02/2023 - Speeches I would like to welcome you and thank you for attending today's event. The Bank of Greece, continuing its long-standing engagement with climate change adaptation issues, is today hosting the presentation of a new study by the Foundation for Economic & Industrial Research (IOBE) on the challenges and prospects of climate change adaptation for the Greek economy. In the midst of the multiple crises we have been experiencing in recent years, climate change is perhaps the most important threat to the sustainability of our societies and is emerging as one of the dominant challenges worldwide. According to the recent assessment report of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPO), the planet will have to face significant climate risks even within an optimistic reduction scenario greenhouse gas emissions [1], It is therefore imperative to act early beyond the level of climate change mitigation and the level of adaptation to this change. While states are making progress in their mitigation actions [2], efforts remain insufficient and funding for the green transition needs to be significantly increased to achieve the goals of the Paris Agreement. Moreover, it is a common finding, confirmed by a recent UN study [3], that funding is mainly geared towards mitigation and less towards adaptation. As for the role of central banks in tackling the climate crisis, while the main responsibility for action and achieving the targets lies with governments, central banks have an active role, always within the limits of their mandate. In fact, the European Central Bank included climate change and sustainability issues in its latest strategy review and since July 2021 has been implementing a comprehensive action plan, extending inter alia to monetary policy, supervision of the financial system and its operational functions [4]; As far as the Bank of Greece is concerned, we are one of the first, if not the first central bank in the world to deal systematically, since 2009, with issues related to climate and sustainability. The interdisciplinary Committee for the Study of the Impacts of Climate Change (CCISC), with distinguished scientists from various fields, has implemented research projects in a wide range of fields. The Commission's flagship study, "The environmental, economic and social impacts of climate change in Greece" of 2011, formed the basis of the design of the National Strategy for Adaptation to Climate Change in 2015. The National Strategy, which the CCISC drafted in collaboration with the Ministry of Environment and Energy, was the first step of a continuous and dynamic process that continues to this day, through the eight-year Athrinb Ogthoth program, coordinated by the Ministry of Environment and Energy. In addition, the Bank of Greece is the first central bank in the world to subscribe to the Principles for Responsible Banking of the United Nations initiative INER EI. These principles define the criteria for responsible and sustainable banking, through a holistic assessment of the risks and opportunities arising from banks' activities. In 2021, we created the Centre for Climate Change and Sustainability at the Bank of Greece on the occasion of the 26th Conference of the Parties to the UN Convention on Climate Change (OPP26), we published a series of commitments, covering almost the entire range of our activities [5]. At the same time, we continue our contribution to climate change research through the action of the CCISC and the project Athrinth Ogthoth. The study presented today is the work of the Foundation for Economic & Industrial Research (IOBE) and its support is part of our contribution to adaptation issues. In closing, I would like to thank IOBE and the authors of the study for their valuable contribution and I hope that the publication of the study and today's debate will contribute substantially both to the debate on adaptation issues and to the necessary financing of climate action. Thank you.  IROO (2022). FIGURE 2022: PIir3i3. 33  . Title: Speech by Bank of Greece Governor Yannis Stournaras at the German-Hellenic Chamber on "Challenges for the Greek and European economy"
text: Address by the Governor of the Bank of Greece Yannis Stournaras at German-Hellenic Chamber on "Challenges for the Greek and European economy" 16/02/2023-Speeches A. Introduction First of all, I would like to thank the German-Hellenic Chamber for inviting me to refer to the upcoming challenges for the Greek and European economy. The future course of Greece, but also of Germany, is intertwined with European integration and with the progress made in this field. The path towards a united Europe is a political vision, since, according to Ib3 Moppthi, "by creating Europe, Europeans create a true foundation for peace". An important catalyst, the driving force in this process, it is Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) with our common currency, the euro, being the key element of our European identity. But, as we shall see, much remains to be done to complete EMU. Besides, as Ooieth said in free version, the difficulties seem to be grow as we approach the goal[1], B. The Greek economy The Greek economy has admittedly made remarkable progress since the great debt crisis of the previous decade. Especially if we recall that in both 2012 and 2015 the scenario that Greece would not manage to remain in the eurozone was very popular in the markets. Today it outperforms the euro area average. In other words, it achieves strong growth in its economy, real convergence of its prosperity level, constantly implements reforms in many areas, plays a leading role in shaping decisions at European level, has consolidated the value of fiscal responsibility and repays its public debt, the dynamics of which are considered sustainable and resilient to negative shocks. In this way, the country has regained much of its credibility, often even citing as an example of effectiveness, as the experience of absorbing the Recovery and Resilience Fund has shown. Of course, there are still long-standing structural problems that are responsible for the relatively low ranking of the country in international structural competitiveness indicators despite the progress of recent years, such as delays in the administration of justice, the resilience of bureaucracy in some other areas of Public Administration, delays in the creation of a national cadastre, the relatively low participation of women in the workforce, The shortage of labour in important sectors of the economy (along with a high unemployment rate), the resilience of tax evasion, some gaps in the so-called "knowledge triangle" (public education-research-innovation), which coexists with a very high-level academic and research workforce, and the quasi-oligopolistic conditions in specific markets for goods and services. In general, however, most of these challenges are already under way, while most of the reforms of previous years have significantly corrected the imperfections of the Greek economy, in particular fiscal problems, competitiveness problems in terms of relative labour costs and relative prices, problems in the insurance system and problems in the balance sheet of Greek banks. In the current adverse economic environment, as shaped by the energy crisis and Russia's invasion of Ukraine, the Greek economy is estimated to have continued to grow at a high rate in 2022, close to 6%, following the also very high rate in 2021 (8.4%), fuelled by private consumption, investment and the strong rise in tourism and shipping revenues. Support measures to contain the impact of the pandemic and the energy crisis on households and businesses have also contributed to this. However, rising energy prices, rising food prices, as well as the tightening of monetary policy are expected to lead to slower growth in 2023, close to 1.5%. However, the effective use of the resources of the EU's long-term budget 2021-2027 and the European Recovery Instrument NHS can mitigate the negative impact of the energy crisis and monetary policy tightening on the economy, leading to medium-term growth rates close to 3% in 2024 and 2025. In particular, investment is expected to grow at very high rates throughout the period 2023-2025, 10% on average, supported by the maintenance of adequate liquidity in the banking sector and the use of available European resources. In the coming years, Greece will receive 40 billion in support. around 30 billion from the EU's long-term budget 2021-2027 and 30 billion. from the Recovery and Resilience Facility until 2026. These resources are expected to attract additional private capital. At the same time, increased foreign direct and indirect investment is expected to be attracted. Exports of goods have shown resilience during the pandemic. After an increase of 13.8% in 2021, they are estimated to have continued and continue to grow in 2022 and 2023, albeit at a much milder pace, owing to the expected downturn in economic activity and the deteriorating outlook in the euro area and the global economy. Services exports are estimated to have recovered significantly in 2022 and will continue to grow in the coming years. At the same time, however, imports are expected to increase throughout the period 2023-2025, as a result of the stimulation of domestic demand, especially investment. The gradual decline in unemployment and the increase in the number of employed persons are expected to continue in the period 2023-2025, as a result of economic growth, which will be supported by the implementation of the National Recovery and Resilience Plan. Inflation, based on the Harmonized Index of Consumer Prices, stood at a particularly high level in 2022, namely at 9.3%, mainly due to the upward trend in energy commodity prices, but also food prices. For 2023 and 2024, a gradual decline to 5.8% and 3.6% respectively is expected, mainly due to the expected decline in energy prices and the negative base effect. Underlying inflation, i.e. inflation excluding changes in food and energy prices, stood at 4.6% in 2022 and is expected to remain equally high in 2023, owing to the incorporation of strong inflationary pressures from the non-energy industrial goods and services components. General government debt is projected to decline from 169% of GDP in 2022 to 160% of GDP in 2023, mainly owing to estimated nominal GDP growth. As regards public debt sustainability, the observed increase in Greek bond yields due to the tightening of monetary policy does not halt its downward trajectory. The favourable composition of public debt, consisting of approximately 76% of medium to long-term liabilities to the official sector, the highly favourable repayment structure, as established in the context of the agreements with Greece's partners and the interest rate hedging operations, make debt virtually unaffected by increases in financing costs over the medium term. Therefore, according to the Bank of Greece's updated estimates, despite the observed increase in Greek bond yields, risks to public debt sustainability remain contained over the medium term, subject of course to the following conditions: First, the fiscal measures taken in the context of the pandemic and the energy crisis remain targeted and temporary in nature. Second, fiscal policy is returning to permanent and sustainable primary surpluses from 2023 onwards, approaching 2% of GDP, to fully cover interest on public debt. Toiton. All available European resources are effectively utilized, contributing decisively to filling the investment gap and enhancing the potential growth rate of the economy. However, in the long run, uncertainty is increasing as the gradual refinancing of accumulated debt to the official sector on market terms will increase the exposure of the Greek government to interest rate and market risk, which eliminates the scope for easing the required level of primary surpluses. Therefore, the next decade is a unique window of opportunity for the rapid reduction of Greek public debt since, despite increased yields on new issues, only a small share of debt is expected to be refinanced annually on market terms, while a significant share of official sector loans has been hedged against interest rate risk. In this environment and context, the absolute orientation of economic and especially fiscal policy towards the acquisition of investment grade for Greek government bonds should be a non-negotiable national goal, as its achievement will have beneficial effects on all sectors of the Greek economy. The Greek economy is now very close to this goal. Recently, the rating agency "Eiioi K8IIP95" upgraded the country, placing it just one "step" before investment grade. This was the third upgrade of the Greek economy in the last year. Now, three of the four agencies eligible by the European Central Bank have placed the country on the threshold of investment grade. Indeed, given that 2023 is a year of national elections, political forces need to come together and come to an understanding in order to implement the basic commitments of economic policy and preserve what the Greek economy has achieved over the last decade. C. European integration Today I would like to refer to the general framework of economic governance (9thPI3hob) of the Eurozone, and not so much to recent macroeconomic developments. These are more or less known, with the latest data pointing to a visible de-escalation of inflation and a slight strengthening in economic activity, allowing for greater optimism, both in relation to the last official forecasts of the Eurosystem in December, and about the possibility that in the end increases in the key ECB interest rates to a level that might cause a hard landing of the eurozone economy will not be needed in order to tame the inflation. The ECB's next moves will depend mainly on the dynamic path of inflation, as reflected in its March forecast. Already the latest forecasts from the European Commission reflect improved data on inflation and economic growth in the euro area. The prospects of the Greek economy depend, of course, on developments in European integration. The European Union has, despite setbacks and setbacks, made great progress. This progress is mainly attested by the fact that the original six members are now twenty-seven, twenty of which share the same currency, the euro, while a number of European countries also aspire to become members of the European project. The euro was undoubtedly the most important and successful move towards European integration. BTVII was - unfortunately - the exception confirming the rule! Today, the major challenges, in principle, are to find the right balance between collective common European action and the sovereignty of the 27 different member states. The choice between global market domination, national sovereignty and democracy is at the heart of the European Union's political decisions. There is a solution to the deadlocks often caused by the different views of the member states on major issues such as taxation, defence, foreign policy, migration, etc.: It is the replacement of the unanimity rule with qualified majorities and, of course, with the cooperation of willing and capable countries, in which I consider the leading participation of Germany and France to be self-evident. as has been, and continues to be, the case from the beginning of the effort to unify Europe until today. At policy level, major challenges include the search for a common foreign and defence policy, deepening democracy at supranational European level, building inclusive societies, reducing inequalities (which now directly affect political developments, domestic and international), completing the Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), investing more in high technology and transitioning to a green economy. What is at stake is whether the European Union can exercise effective political power in a multipolar, highly asymmetric and increasingly unstable world, while maintaining a functional relationship between global markets and social contracts. This is a high stakes, and not just for Europe. A Europe in decline, a Europe that is marginalised, will not be able to defend fundamental interests and values, such as the freedom and security of its citizens. But the whole world would also stand to gain greatly from the sober influence of a major power operating on the basis of broad consensus and compromise. The way should ultimately be shown by European citizens through their institutions, led by the willing and capable member states of the European Union. One of the greatest challenges facing us is the completion of the EMU edifice. EMU is a full monetary union with a single currency and an issuing authority, the European Central Bank, but, despite its important evolutionary steps, it remains an incomplete economic union, i.e. an incomplete fiscal union, an incomplete banking union and an incomplete capital markets union. These imperfections create serious problems and centrifugal forces in times of crisis, reinforcing North-South asymmetries. Russia's invasion of Ukraine has presented the European and global economy with its biggest challenge since the end of the Cold War. Globalisation is regressing. The result is a slowdown in economic growth and higher prices. Winds of stagflation are blowing everywhere, but particularly in Europe, which is a major net importer of energy, and has been hit hard by the unfavourable change in the terms of trade. In essence, it is as if a tax has been imposed in Europe by another country. The world around us has changed. Concerns about value chain security and energy efficiency dominate, creating the need for regional solutions and counterweights. This is the well-known issue of open strategic autonomy, which is currently being discussed extensively in the euro area. So far, reforms have been carried out mainly in the wake of crises such as the debt and banking crises in Greece, Ireland, Portugal, Spain, Cyprus, as well as the pandemic crisis. The reforms themselves are welcome and necessary, but they come too late and undermine Europe's role on the international stage, weaken social cohesion and incite anti-European sentiment. I am not sure that we can afford either economically, socially or politically to rely on the same mechanisms of post-crisis response. A multipolar world order dictates that Europe must react in advance rather than in retrospect, especially at a time when crises seem likely to be commonplace. On some pressing issues of international competition, Europe seems to react rather reluctantly, and does not address the concerns of less wealthy member states. In response to the announcement of the Viaop administration's announcement of the Viaop Administration spending and subsidy program, which creates incentives for companies to do business in the United States by raising concerns about unfair competition, the European Commission has recently proposed the so-called Industrial Policy (3IP). This plan is based on four pillars: a predictable and simplified regulatory environment, accelerating access to finance, boosting skills and open trade for resilient supply chains. A key element of the plan is the relaxation of state aid rules to support environmentally friendly industrial projects. However, The relaxation of state aid rules due to the pandemic and the energy crisis has mainly benefited wealthier member states, raising concerns among smaller member states about the functioning of the Single Market. However, for the financing of the EOIP, the Commission proposed to make use of existing resources, for example from the KERonthi and the EINH, and to set up a new common European Fund (Euro-Energy) to collectively finance projects in critical and emerging technologies, which would also support less prosperous and less technologically advanced countries. will be examined in the future. This is mainly due to the reaction of some member states to a new initiative that will involve joint borrowing at European Union (EU) level before the available NGA funds are exhausted. There is no doubt that significant changes and reforms have taken place in the construction of EMU since the outbreak of the great financial crisis of 2008 until today, or as a result of the crisis to be precise. Many times I feel that the Greek debt crisis of 2010 acted as the midwife of history for all these necessary changes and reforms. Let me remind you of them: The reform of the Stability and Growth Pact between 2011 and 2013. The creation of two main pillars of the Banking Union (Single Supervisory Mechanism in 2014 and Single Resolution Mechanism in 2016). The creation of the European Financial Stability Facility in 2010 and the successor to the European Stability Mechanism in 2012. The amendment of the European Stability Mechanism Treaty in 2021. The use of new monetary policy measures - conventional or non-conventional - by the ECB (a) to address the consequences for the stability of the euro and (b) to safeguard the smooth transmission of monetary policy, during the debt crisis, but also during the pandemic and the war in Ukraine. But that is no longer enough. They have exhausted their potential. The time has come for bold decisions, both in the area of banking union and in the fiscal area, to be taken now, before the next major, and perhaps fatal, fiscal and/or financial crisis. As I already mentioned, the eurozone is a full monetary union, but it is still an incomplete fiscal and banking union, as well as an incomplete capital markets union. This imperfection in times of crisis and uncertainty, such as the current one due to Russia's invasion of Ukraine and the ongoing war, creates, among other things, obstacles (pp3po3 IL'9GP) to the smooth transmission of monetary policy to all euro area Member States. This makes it necessary to fill in the missing elements of the Banking Union. For example, the EUSKUR has so far been unable to agree either on the creation of a pan-European deposit insurance scheme, the third pillar of the Banking Union, or on completing the banking crisis management framework. The reason why eurozone member states have so far not agreed to complete the banking union has mainly to do with a basic dilemma: should financial risk reduction measures (e.g.r.c.3eu.s.r.s.) precede or follow risk-sharing measures (e.m.e.a.3.p.9.s.a.s.s.)? But why could these measures not be taken at the same time, perhaps allowing enough time before they are implemented? This would be a win-win solution and not a zero-sum game. As regards budgetary initiatives, the time has come to review the fiscal framework embedded in the Stability and Growth Pact. The European Commission has already tabled its proposals and they are, by and large, in the right direction. Several member states have already expressed their views. But others do not. Our objectives here should be to ensure public debt sustainability for all member states, to achieve countercyclicality of fiscal policy, a credible and automatic sanction mechanism in case of non-compliance with new ones fiscal rules and the creation of a central fiscal tool for all euro area member states, activated to address symmetric shocks (e.g. pandemic, effects of wars, etc.). Several, including the current German chancellor, OI3L 8thq, have described the Recovery and Resilience Fund as the "moral moment" for Europe. However, this Fund was made to deal with a temporary crisis, the pandemic. It needs to be transformed into a permanent mechanism linking the conduct of fiscal policy at the centre of the euro area to appropriate rules in order to avoid moral hazard of loosening fiscal stability at national level. At the same time, however, it should be made clear that the creation of a permanent fiscal capacity must necessarily be accompanied by significant changes at the level of economic governance, with member states losing control of fiscal tools in the conduct of national policy. Policy proposals aimed simply at adding a permanent fiscal instrument at EU level, without the necessary accompanying governance reforms, do not address the underlying issue of cooperation and policy coordination (or lack thereof) among monetary union member states. Without the required level of political representation and accountability at EU level, combined  ideally  with stricter limits on the exercise of national discretionary fiscal policy, a central fiscal capacity would remain barren and ultimately fail. D. Improving economic governance in the euro area Two key questions arise about the future of economic governance in the euro area: What economic governance framework can make the euro area more resilient in the face of the acute economic uncertainty it is currently facing. supply-side disruptions and rising public debts; How can we improve the exchange relationship between the need to ensure fiscal sustainability in all Member States and the need to address symmetric shocks (and especially the challenges of the climate crisis) at a time when monetary policy is normalising and interest rates are rising; Our reforms must move in two directions: (a) in the financial field (b) in the area of completing the Banking Union. (a) Financial sector As regards the budgetary area, the objectives of a new framework are as follows: Public debt sustainability at national level. Countercyclicality of fiscal policy at national level to enable national authorities to stabilise GDP in downturns and generate adequate fiscal policy fiscal reserves in times of growth, thus ensuring sound financial management over the economic cycle. A credible sanction mechanism in case of non-compliance with the new fiscal rules, which will be quite automated, leaving little room for political intervention. This enhances the credibility and effectiveness of compliance with the new financial framework. Creation of a central fiscal policy tool, transforming the Recovery and Resilience Fund into a permanent fiscal tool, which will finances investments (it will not make transfers, except in extreme situations, such as the pandemic, it will only give loans to avoid moral hazard easing fiscal measures at national level) mainly in the areas of climate change, energy and digital transformation. As I have already said, the European Commission's proposals are a step in the right direction. This is encouraging. It would be a serious setback if there were no deal and to return to the pre-pandemic Stability and Growth Pact, the which, firstly, contains elements that could create a new crisis, secondly, it is very likely to hinder the necessary new public investment of common European interest, for example, in climate change mitigation and adaptation, and thirdly, it will not contribute to achieving the best possible mix of monetary and fiscal policy. (b) Completing the Banking Union The completion of the Banking Union is key to creating a full economic and monetary union. Otherwise, financial obstacles (Tiethioll IL39GPh1:3ii) will remain active, hampering the smooth transmission of monetary policy, and the euro will not be able to compete on equal terms with other international reserve currencies. The basic idea here is that the supervision of all banks, and not only the systemic ones, their resolution, the framework for managing banking crises and, above all, the creation of a deposit insurance scheme should acquire pan-European status, and not be based on national specificities and regulations. The establishment, in particular, of a pan-European deposit insurance scheme can contribute to the financial stability of the euro area much more broadly than its role as a mere depositor compensation mechanism. In particular, it can also act as a mechanism for minimizing risks and preventing a banking crisis: (a) before a banking institution is deemed non-viable; (b) in the case of resolution of a banking institution; (c) ensuring an orderly exit of a banking institution from the market without consequences for its depositors. E. Epilogue The greatest danger we face collectively in the euro area is that we carry out too few reforms and too late. We need to act early and in advance (i.e. before a new major crisis breaks out), with decisive, balanced and well-planned reforms at the level of the euro area, in a spirit of cooperation and mutual concessions, in line with what has been said before. These changes will make our economies more resilient, give greater acceptance to the euro as a global reserve currency and lay the foundations for sustainable and lasting prosperity for all euro area citizens. The adoption of the euro is a federal form of governance in Europe. Moreover, the European Central Bank and the Eurosystem are the most advanced form of unified governance within the euro area, which can be a guide for addressing the European Union's other major challenges. The road to full European integration is still long and difficult. But anything less than this will lead to the gradual marginalisation of Europe and the loss of prosperity for its citizens. So we need to focus on our goal: a united Europe of freedom, security, prosperity and democracy. In conclusion, I would like to express an optimistic thought. As I described above, the Greek economy is now on a positive, albeit difficult, path. Although it faces several important challenges, it seems to have the potential to overcome obstacles. The assessment of European integration is similar. Here, too, the road will be long, but not impassable. It is up to us, the citizens of a united Europe, to strive to achieve our objectives and to act in advance, not afterwards, as Suppliers and not as Trustees. Title: Speech by Bank of Greece Deputy Governor Christina Papaconstantinou at the 4th Occupational Insurance Conference
text: Speech by Bank of Greece Deputy Governor Christina Papaconstantinou at the 4th Occupational Insurance Conference 23/02/2023 - Speeches Madam President of the European Insurance and Occupational Pensions Authority, Mr. Minister, Madam Chairman of the Hellenic Capital Market Commission, Ladies and gentlemen, Let me begin my speech with a brief account of the current macroeconomic situation. The impact of Russia's ongoing war with Ukraine on energy commodity prices and supply chains, heightened uncertainty, rising inflation to very high levels and tightening financial conditions have shaped an adverse economic environment, leading to a worsening global economic outlook. Therefore, the growth rate of the Greek economy is expected to decelerate this year, as a result of the expected downturn in economic activity in the euro area and the significant decline in private consumption growth. Moreover, both fiscal policy and monetary policy are expected to have a contractionary effect on economic activity. Inflation is expected to decline gradually, although it will remain elevated. However, despite the gloomy initial forecasts, it appears that the impact of the current crisis on Europe has so far been milder than expected. Reflecting these developments, the European Commission has revised upwards its recent forecast [13.02.2023] for GDP growth in the European Union and the euro area in 2023. The better performance of the European economy supports external demand for the Greek economy. In any case, Greece's return to high growth rates from 2024 will largely depend on the de-escalation of the geopolitical crisis and energy commodity prices, as well as on the good course of tourism, investment plans and the eurozone economy. The positive prospects of the Greek economy in the medium term are significantly supported by the European Recovery Instrument . However, the challenges facing the Greek economy are not necessarily linked to the current adverse conjuncture. A major structural challenge facing the Greek economy is the ageing population. This implies a shrinking workforce and therefore negatively affects the potential long-term growth of the Greek economy. At the same time, it has important implications for the social security system, which I will come back to later. Ladies and gentlemen, I would now like to share with you some thoughts regarding the organization and development of occupational insurance in Greece. Occupational Insurance Funds (ISFs) (or institutions for occupational retirement provision - IORPs), which constitute the 2nd pillar of the pension system, were introduced in Greece by Law 3029/2002. Until the adoption of this law, no substantial opportunity was provided to sectors and professional groups to create complementary and self-managed systems except through private insurance companies. The activities and supervision of Occupational Insurance Funds are regulated at European level by Directive 2016/2341, referred to as IOCR II (Ind. Iorp II Article ). This Directive establishes a set of rules for the taking-up and pursuit of the activities of institutions for occupational retirement provision and was incorporated into the Greek legal order in 2020 by Law 4680. The number of Occupational Insurance Funds in Greece, according to data from the European Insurance and Occupational Pensions Authority (EIOPA) and the Hellenic Association of Occupational Insurance Funds (ELETEA), increased from 3 to 28 in the period 2004-2021, most of which have been created in the last 6 years. Compared to other eurozone countries, Greece is among those with the lowest ISF penetration. Indicatively, in 2019, there was one ISF per approximately 250 thousand employees. At the top of the ranking, with the highest penetration, is Luxembourg, where there is one TEA per approximately 25 thousand employees. There are several possible reasons for the relatively limited development and operation of ISFs in Greece. The first possible cause lies in the institutional characteristics of the traditional social security system of our country, which has always included a strong and quite generous first pillar, with a strongly redistributive character, as well as high replacement rates compared to other countries. Moreover, there is generally a low degree of confidence among Greek households in supplementary insurance institutions, beyond the arrangements provided by the public sector. Structural features of the Greek economy also contribute to the limited development of the institution in Greece, in particular, the small size of enterprises and the high rate of self-employment compared to other countries. Specifically, in the In Greece, the average number of employees per company is about 33% lower than in the EU. Also, the percentage of self-employed in the total employed in our country is double that of the EU. In addition, the development of the institution is likely to be hampered by the low level of private savings.
