Finally, the relatively high "tax wedge", as shaped by insurance contributions and compensation taxes, may deter employees from choosing additional deductions from their earnings. However, the benefits of the existence and strengthening of the ISF institution are multiple. In particular, ISFs achieve: diffusion of insurance risk between the pillars of the system, improving the adequacy of pension provision; enhancing productivity and savings; increasing investment and, as a result of all of the above, improving the standard of living of workers. In addition, as I mentioned above, the adverse demographic forecasts for our country are a structural development that makes the development of the institution imperative. The ageing of the population has a negative impact on the pay-as-you-go social security system and places a burden on both workers (higher burden in terms of contributions) and pensioners (greater insecurity in terms of pension benefits). At the same time, international trends towards raising retirement ages and lengthening working lives make it timely to discuss the differentiation not only of insurance risk, but also of the type of benefits or even the retirement period in relation to the first pillar. Obviously, occupational insurance alone could not address all of the above challenges. However, a mixed insurance system, combining pay-as-you-go and capitalisation features in the form of separate pillars, could achieve the diffusion and greater diversification of insurance risk, to the benefit of policyholders, increasing their well-being. Ladies and gentlemen, The existing institutional framework provides a solid basis for the organisation and operation of ISFs. At the same time, it also involves several areas that could be improved in order to make the institution of ISFs more functional within a three-pillar insurance system in Greece. An important area of improvement of the existing institutional framework is related to the fact that the establishment of multi-employer occupational funds ("multi-employer" ISFs) is not foreseen. Law 3029/2002 allows the establishment of a TEA "per enterprise or sector or sectors of employees",[1] thus setting as a prerequisite the common professional bond of the members of the fund on the part of the employers. Therefore, The professional funds that have been established and operate until today by businesses in Greece are basically "closed" and aim at the exclusive coverage of their employees. In addition, a minimum threshold of 100 policyholders applies to the establishment of a TEA. These restrictions exclude smaller employers, who may not have the necessary resources to establish their own, personalized, TEA. The dissemination of the institution is therefore difficult, since the Greek economy consists, as I mentioned earlier, mainly of small and medium-sized enterprises. Restrictions on the establishment of multi-employer funds are not conducive to achieving economies of scale that would make it possible to reduce investment and management costs. In addition, they distort healthy competition between domestic ISFs and ISFs from other EU countries. It is indicative that ISFs based in other Member States, operating cross-border in Greece, have the possibility to insure different domestic employers without a common professional bond, unlike domestic ISFs. In conclusion, the introduction of the possibility of establishing multi-employer TEAs could enable employees of small and medium-sized enterprises, as well as freelancers, to reap the benefits of occupational insurance, remedying the current situation where access to them is excluded for the vast majority of workers. It goes without saying that a reform in this direction must be accompanied by the establishment of minimum conditions and high operating standards that multi-employer funds must meet. I believe that the dialogue on this issue helps to highlight the importance of ISFs and appropriate interventions for the benefit of all stakeholders, especially policyholders, and I welcome your initiative to organise today's conference. Thank you very much! [1] Article 7(3).

Title: Speech by Dimitris Malliaropulos, Chief Economist and Director of economic analysis and research, during the Greece Trek 2023 initiative of The Fletcher School of Law and Diplomacy at Tufts University
text: Speech by Dimitris Malliaropulos, Chief Economist and Director of economic analysis and research, during the Greece Trek 2023 initiative of The Fletcher School of Law and Diplomacy at Tufts University 22/03/2023 - Speeches Global economic outlook and monetary policy challenges in the face of banking stress Good morning and welcome to the Bank of Greece. It is a great pleasure for me to talk to you today. We live through very challenging times. The global economy has been hit by a number of shocks over the past three years - pandemic, energy crisis, inflation, monetary policy tightening, and banking turmoil more recently - and we go through a period of elevated uncertainty. Uncertainty comes in waves and the events are so fast that it is sometimes almost impossible to prepare even a small speech for the next day and sleep over it. In fact, I had to review my speech this morning and to make some changes even ten minutes ago. Having said this, please allow me in the following few minutes to share with you my views on the outlook of the global economy, the euro area and Greece, and to give you some food for thought on the challenges for monetary policy of the recent events in the banking sector. . Economic outlook Global economy High inflation, monetary policy tightening and pandemic-related disruptions in China dampened global growth in 2022. These factors continue to constrain growth in the first months of 2023, except for disruptions in China, which were short-lived and recovery is already under way. Overall, manufacturing output remained weak by historical standards, but there are tentative signs of stabilisation especially in Europe, supported by declining energy prices. Also, the services sector activity across advanced economies seems to benefit from still resilient labour markets. Looking further ahead, the reopening in China is expected to provide support to the global economy. However, global growth will remain relatively subdued. The ECB projects world real GDP growth to decline from 3.3% in 2022 to 3.0% this year, before very gradually increasing to 3.3% in 2025. Global growth forecasts have been revised upwards compared to previous projection rounds in late 2022, on the back of an improved outlook for China and stronger growth in the US. However, rising stress in financial markets following the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank in the US increase the uncertainty about the global economic outlook, as it can potentially lead to a tightening of banks credit standards. Although there are increasing signs that global headline inflation has passed its peak, price pressures in the global economy remain high. While lower energy prices and a weaker dollar support a deceleration of inflation, resilient labour markets and strong wage growth point to still strong underlying inflation pressures. In addition, food price inflation remains stubbornly high. This suggests that the process of disinflation will be gradual. Euro area Euro area economic activity slowed significantly at the turn of the year, with growth stalling. However, with the energy supplies now more secure and energy prices having eased significantly over the past few months, confidence has improved and the short-term outlook has brightened somewhat. Lower energy prices, dissipating global supply chain bottlenecks and robust labour markets are expected to support aggregate demand. Meanwhile higher interest rates, tighter financing conditions and the unwinding of fiscal support measures during the energy crisis are expected to weigh on growth. Overall, annual average real GDP growth is expected to slow down to 1.0% in 2023 (from 3.6% in 2022), before rebounding to 1.6% in 2024 and 2025. Headline inflation is expected to fall below 3.0% only at the end of 2023, stabilise in 2024 and moderate further to reach the inflation target of 2.0% in the third quarter of 2025. The expected decline of headline inflation in the medium-term also reflects the gradual impact of monetary policy normalisation. Greece The growth rate of the Greek economy in 2022 is estimated at 6.1%. The drivers of this good performance are private consumption, investment and exports. Government support measures, improving consumer and investor confidence as well as reviving tourism and other exports supported economic activity. In 2023, the growth rate is projected to slow to somewhere between 2% and 2.5%, due to a slowdown in economic activity in the euro area, affecting export growth, and a significant deceleration of private consumption growth. In addition, both fiscal and monetary policies are expected to have a contractionary impact on economic activity in 2023. In 2024 and 2025, the growth rate is expected to recover, reaching 3.1% and 2.8%, respectively. The main drivers of growth over the projection period 2023-2025 are expected to be investment and exports and, to a lesser extent, private consumption. Investment will be supported by the utilisation of available European Union resources. Greece is expected to receive funding of around 40 billion from the EU long-term budget 2021-2027 and 30 billion from the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) until 2026. These resources are expected to attract additional private funds. Exports will grow in 2023 at a much softer pace compared to 2022, due to weaker economic activity in the euro area and the global economy. HICP inflation is expected to gradually decelerate to 4.4% in 2023, 3.4% in 2024 and 2.4% in 2025, mainly due to lower energy prices and negative base effects. Core inflation will remain high in 2023. It will decline only gradually over the rest of the projection horizon, due to lower indirect effects from easing energy prices. Risks to the outlook The improvement in the outlook is still fragile. The balance of risks to growth remains tilted to the downside and to inflation to the upside. Risks include: (i) an escalation of the war in Ukraine and additional sanctions; (ii) supply-side risks in global commodity markets; (iii) more adverse developments in the residential real estate sector in China; (iv) financial vulnerabilities from high debt and stretched asset valuations, and also in specific financial market segments; and (v) fragmentation of the global trading system. Challenges for monetary policy Most central banks have continued to raise their policy rates in the first two and a half months of 2023 in order to bring inflation under control. Global financial conditions continue to tighten as investors respond in a risk-off fashion, particularly after the collapse of Silicon Valley Bank (SVB) on March 10. Credit spreads widened and stock prices of banks dropped. As a result, composite indices of financial conditions tightened sharply, indicating a greater drag on future output growth. Monetary policy tightening creates interest rate risk in the financial system. Particularly when monetary tightening is fast and synchronised. The current global tightening cycle stands out from a historical perspective. First, it is the most synchronised in the past half-century. By February 2023, more than 90% of economies had hiked their policy rates when, historically, this share has rarely exceeded 50%. Second, central banks have so far raised policy rates at a faster pace than in previous tightening cycles, about twice the historical pace. The collapse of SVB and two other regional US banks highlights the role of interest rate risk in the financial system. When interest rates were low and asset prices high, banks were buying long-term bonds. When the Fed hiked rates to multiyear highs bond prices dropped and the banks were left with large losses. Capital rules in the US do not require small and medium sized banks to account for the losses from the falling price of bonds they plan to hold to maturity. Only large banks are required to report their bond holdings at market prices (mark to market). In fact, unrecognised losses do not matter up to the point they are crystalized, i.e. when the bank is forced to sell (part of) its bond holdings in order to cover its liabilities. This happens when the banks depositors start a run on their deposits. Bank runs wipe out banks equity. To prevent a bank run, authorities provide deposit guarantees. Usually these guarantees cover deposits of up to a specific amount, e.g. USD 250 thousand in the US, EUR 100 thousand in Greece. The purpose of these guarantees is to reassure depositors that their money is safe at the banks. Central banks responded swiftly and effectively to the collapse of SVB to limit contagion. The Fed provided protection for all deposits of two failed banks, independent of size. US Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen said yesterday that guarantees offered to depositors of the two failed banks could be replicated at other institutions. The Fed also initiated the Bank Term Funding Program, which provides emergency liquidity funding against eligible collateral with no haircuts applied. The Swiss National Bank provided liquidity assistance to Credit Swiss of up to CHF 250 bn. Both central banks acted as a lender of last resort to protect their banking system. The recent turbulence in the banking sector has led investors to dramatically revise their expectations for central bank policy rates. Prior to the Silicon Valley Bank collapse, markets were pricing a US terminal rate of more than 5.5% and an ECB terminal rate of 4%. Once the news broke, investors sharply lowered their expectations, with markets pricing multiple rate cuts by the end of the year due to rising worries about financial stability. To some extent, this may be an overreaction since central banks can use other tools than interest rates to address financial stability risks, while still using rate hikes to tame inflation. Let me conclude. Financial market stress has increased recently as the central banks tightening cycle started to bite. Monetary policy faces a challenge: To safeguard financial stability while continuing to fight inflation. When financial stress increases, financial markets start to question the determination of central banks to continue the course of tightening in order to tame inflation. Instead, investors expect central banks to cut rates in order to avoid breaking anything else in the financial system. However, price stability and financial stability are not conflicting targets and there is no trade-off between the two. Central banks and supervisory authorities do have the policy tools to deliver on both. And they will!

Title: Speech by Bank of Greece Deputy Governor Christina Papaconstantinou at the 4th International Conference of the Economic Chamber of Greece entitled: "The Greek economy: Looking to the future"
text: Speech by Bank of Greece Governor Christina Papaconstantinou at 4th International Conference on Economic Hellenic Chamber of Commerce entitled: "The Greek economy: Looking towards the future" 28/03/2023 - Speeches Good morning ladies and gentlemen, It is my pleasure to participate in today's event of the Economic Chamber of Greece and in the discussions on the course of the Greek economy in the future, especially in the current international conjuncture characterized by a lot of uncertainty. It is a fact that the Greek economy is showing significant resilience, despite successive exogenous shocks in recent years  the pandemic (Othin-19) and the energy crisis, as well as the current turbulence in capital markets centred on the banking system. This allows us to look to the future with optimism. In particular, Greece has returned to a strong growth trajectory, and medium-term economic growth prospects remain positive, supported by available European resources and favourable public debt profiles. The resilience of the Greek economy has been helped by progress made since the debt crisis of the previous decade, which laid the foundations for sustainable growth. Undoubtedly, at great economic and social cost, macroeconomic imbalances (the "twin" deficits, general government and current account deficits) were addressed, the competitiveness of the Greek economy was restored and important reforms were implemented in areas such as the insurance system, the labour market, the business environment and tax administration. At the same time, the capital adequacy and liquidity of the Greek banking system improved and the stock of non-performing loans (NPLs) declined significantly. The positive prospects of the Greek economy are reflected in the significant increase in foreign direct investment observed in recent years, the uninterrupted and costly access of the Greek State to international markets, as well as the successive upgrades of the creditworthiness of the Greek economy by credit rating agencies. Greece is just one notch away from regaining investment grade, a target that is achievable during this year, especially after the recent upgrade of the economy's prospects by Mowag'd. Such a development is crucial for the unhindered financing of the Greek economy amid tightening monetary and financial conditions, as well as deteriorating investor sentiment and the search for safer assets. Ladies and gentlemen, The energy crisis, exacerbated by Russia's invasion of Ukraine in early 2022, and the necessary contractionary monetary policy stance due to inflation rising to historically high levels have worsened the economic outlook at European and global levels. Uncertainty about Europe's energy sufficiency has added to volatility in international energy prices, especially natural gas, weighing on economic sentiment, demand and investment. By contrast, fiscal policy measures and the European Instrument for Stimulus, deferred demand and accumulated savings from the pandemic period, as well as a shift in consumption from goods to services, supported economic activity and employment prospects in the euro area. At the same time, the softer tightening of the ECB's monetary policy compared to the Federal Reserve led to more favourable financial conditions in the euro area and to a significant depreciation of the euro against the US dollar, which reinforced the prices of imported goods and inflationary pressures. In this complex economic environment, the Greek economy grew at a rate of 5.9% in 2022, following the also very high pace of 2021 (8.4%). Growth was supported by private consumption, investment and exports of services (tourism and shipping). The most important impact of the ongoing energy crisis is an increase in the general price level, which reduces households' real disposable income and undermines the outlook for the economy. Inflation, as measured by the rate of change in the Harmonized Index of Consumer Prices, increased significantly in 2022 and stood at 9.3% on average, reflecting very high price increases in energy and food. Moreover, the deterioration in international monetary and financial conditions during 2022 had an increasing impact on the borrowing costs of the Greek government and Greek non-financial corporations. Indeed, Greek bond yields showed greater sensitivity to international volatility compared to their counterparts in other European countries, due to their lower credit ratings and the limited market depth of Greek securities. However, there have also been a number of positive developments in recent months. The European benchmark gas price has fallen to pre-Russian Ukraine war levels, helped by falling gas consumption and continued diversification of supply sources. European households and businesses have shown considerable resilience, benefiting from the support measures, while labour market conditions and economic sentiment have continued to improve in recent months. Also, according to the latest data, inflation has been gradually declining since the last months of 2022, in line with the downward path of energy prices, reaching 6.5% in February 2023. Undoubtedly, however, the pass-through of high energy prices to services and non-energy goods will keep core inflation (i.e. the HICP excluding energy and food) high. Core inflation stood at 4.6% per year on average in 2022 and stood at 6.8% in February 2023. Overall, economic developments for the European Union (EU) economy are better than forecast in autumn 2022 by the European Commission, leading to a downward revision of its winter forecast for GDP growth for the EU (0.8%) and euro area (0.9%) in 2023 (from 0.3% for both). However, risks to the growth forecast remain on the downside. The ECB's recent forecasts (March 2023) have been revised along the same lines. Recently, uncertainty has increased again as a result of capital market shocks linked to the collapse of the BPC and other smaller banks in the US, as well as the rescue of OGathai 8y85i with the intervention of the Swiss Central Bank and its acquisition by IIB8. The Greek banking system has low direct exposure to these banks. Its resilience to the current shocks is supported by its high capital adequacy and liquidity, the clean-up of Greek banks' balance sheets by reducing NPLs, the strong supervisory framework, as well as the authorities' readiness to provide the European banking system with additional liquidity if necessary. Nevertheless, deteriorating confidence is contributing to increased risk aversion on the part of investors and to a further deterioration in financial conditions. According to Bank of Greece forecasts, growth is expected to decline in 2023, owing to the expected slowdown in economic activity in the euro area and the fact that both fiscal policy and monetary policy are expected to have a contractionary impact on economic activity in 2023. However, based on the most recent GDP and so far, available precursor indicators of economic activity and expectations, the Greek economy (as well as the EU economy) is growing faster than expected in the previous period. The growth rate of the Greek economy is expected to recover in 2024 and 2025. This performance can be achieved provided that on the one hand the geopolitical crisis has de-escalated and energy prices have fallen and, on the other hand, that the Greek economy continues to be significantly strengthened by international tourism, as well as the good progress of the implementation of investment plans by making effective use of the resources of the EU's long-term budget 2021-2027 and the European Recovery Instrument. Inflation, based on the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices, is expected to gradually decline in 2023 and further in 2024, mainly on account of the expected decline in energy prices and the negative base effect. Looking at fiscal aggregates, the general government primary deficit is estimated to have declined in 2022 to levels better than initially estimated, while a return to a primary surplus of 0.7% of GDP is projected for 2023. At the same time, general government debt is projected to continue its rapid decline in 2023, primarily due to estimated nominal GDP growth and, secondarily, to the restoration of fiscal balance. The forecasts for the course of the economy in the period ahead are subject to uncertainties and risks, mainly related to exogenous factors. In particular, the Risks of a further slowdown in the growth rate of the Greek economy are linked to the possibility of adverse developments related to the war in Ukraine, the inflation and the pandemic. In addition, risks to GDP growth are the low absorption of EU funds and the emergence of a new generation of non-performing loans due to the pandemic and the energy crisis after the end of state support measures. However, medium-term growth prospects for the Greek economy are positive. At least two factors contribute to this. First, Greece will receive 40 billion in support in the coming years. around 30 billion from the EU's long-term budget 2021-2027 and 30 billion. from the Recovery and Resilience Facility until 2026. In particular, according to the National Recovery and Resilience Plan (Greece 2.0), resources from the Facility will be allocated to investments and reforms aimed at, inter alia, the green and digital transitions, enhancing employment, skills and social cohesion, upgrading infrastructure, modernising public administration and improving the efficiency of the justice system. In fact, additional private capital is expected to be mobilised, in particular through the loans of the Mechanism that will be channelled by the Greek banking system on favourable terms. At the same time, upgrading infrastructure and improving the business environment will help attract foreign direct and indirect investment. This gives Greece a unique opportunity to renew and upgrade its capital qualitatively, creating the framework to cover the investment gap. At the same time, the allocation of productive resources will improve, as new investments will focus on high-productivity sectors, and new sustainable jobs will be created. Also, the implementation of the National Plan creates the conditions to address some of the chronic weaknesses of the Greek economy that are holding back growth, such as its low structural competitiveness. More specifically, this weakness is linked to digital lag, inefficiency of public administration and delays in the administration of justice. Therefore, the actions foreseen in the National Recovery and Resilience Plan on these individual issues will be complementary, leading to an improvement in structural competitiveness, with positive effects on productivity, investment and exports of the Greek economy. Second, the positive medium-term prospects of the Greek economy are supported by favourable public debt characteristics. In particular, public debt has not only a favourable composition, consisting of approximately 76% of medium to long-term liabilities to the official sector, but also an extremely favourable repayment structure, as established in the context of debt relief measures. It is also worth noting that almost all public debt is in fixed-rate liabilities, with the PDMA having carried out interest rate hedging operations on time in previous years. As a result, there are no significant risks from rising financing costs in the medium term. However, in the longer term, there is heightened uncertainty, as the gradual refinancing of the accumulated debt to the official sector on market terms will increase the exposure of the Greek government to interest rate and market risks, which eliminates the scope for easing the required level of primary surpluses and, by extension, the contribution of the budget balance to the sustained downward path of public debt. Moreover, it cannot be overlooked that high public debt limits the ability of fiscal policy to implement public investment and support the economy whenever necessary. Further important challenges facing the Greek economy in the long term include:  ageing populations, which in combination with low labour market participation limit potential growth, and  climate change, which will affect the country's production model and energy security. Ladies and gentlemen, Allow me at this point to refer briefly to the areas on which economic policy should focus in the future, with a view to addressing medium to long-term challenges for the Greek economy, but also short-term risks stemming from the international economic environment. These consist of:  Maintaining fiscal credibility and stability. To this end, any additional interventions to mitigate the effects of the energy crisis adopted should be temporary, targeted and tailored appropriately so as not to weaken incentives to reduce energy consumption and, at the same time, to support energy saving actions and green transition. Moreover, from 2024 onwards, Greece should aim for primary surpluses of 2% of GDP. in order to cover interest costs. Maintaining high primary rates Surpluses over a long period require a major overhaul of budget expenditure and revenue. In particular, there is a need to increase the quality and efficiency of public spending (by increasing expenditure on public investment, education, health and social protection) and to improve the structure of the tax system and strengthen tax compliance (by combating tax evasion in income taxes and VAT).  The implementation of actions to enhance the potential growth rate. In this direction, it is necessary to increase productive investment, with an emphasis on upgrading infrastructure and the green and digital transitions. At the same time, it is necessary to continue the reform effort, in particular through initiatives leading to an improvement in the business environment and the quality of governance institutions, where there are large gaps in best practices. An integral part of this effort is the timely and full implementation of the actions foreseen in the National Recovery and Resilience Plan and the full utilization of available European resources, as well as the good coordination and operational readiness of the public administration.  Addressing the twin energy and climate crises, which require accelerating and promoting investments in green technologies, improving networks and expanding infrastructure in electrical interconnections, as well as developing central energy storage systems.  Strengthening the "knowledge triangle", i.e. education, research and innovation, by adopting policies and reforms that encourage research, facilitate the diffusion of technology and enhance entrepreneurship.  Maintaining labour market flexibility and ensuring that the competitiveness gains achieved over the last decade are maintained.  Addressing labour market distortions, such as high unemployment and skills mismatch. This requires upgrading the technical education and training of workers. At the same time, immediate support is needed for the unemployed and those marginally linked to the labour market, through the implementation of effective active employment policies. In addition, it is necessary to strengthen the resilience of the Greek banking system in order to be able to provide seamless financing to Greek businesses and households. To this end, it is necessary to further reduce non-performing loans, strengthen organic profitability and qualitatively and quantitatively strengthen the capital base of Greek banks. At the same time, efforts need to be stepped up so that banks can integrate the risks of climate change, as well as achieve their digital transformation. The Bank of Greece, together with the Single Supervisory Mechanism, as competent supervisory authorities, systematically assess the resilience of the banking sector and will assist at every step of the way, safeguarding financial stability. In addition, there is a need to broaden sources of long-term financing of investments beyond bank credit and European resources, through capital markets and alternative financing. Foreign direct investment is also an important factor in meeting the economy's investment needs, which also promotes closer trade ties with countries and companies with cutting-edge technologies and facilitates participation in global value chains. This will increase extroversion and improve both the quantity and quality of Greek exports. To attract foreign direct investment, privatisation should be accelerated and emphasis should be placed on removing disincentives such as red tape, ambiguity and instability of the legislative and regulatory framework, unpredictable tax system, poor protection of property rights and delays in litigation. In closing, I would like to point out that, given that 2023 is an election year, political forces need to come together and come to an understanding in order to maintain the growth momentum by making timely and effective use of the available European funds and ensure a return to primary finances surpluses to continue the downward trend in public debt. This, undoubtedly, will lead to the recovery of investment grade in terms of the creditworthiness of Greek government bonds, which is particularly crucial given the turbulence we have recently experienced in the global financial system.

Title: Speech by Governor G. Stournaras at the 90th Annual General Meeting of the Bank's Shareholders
text: CREDIBLE ECONOMIC POLICY IS A COUNTERWEIGHT TO PERVASIVE UNCERTAINTY Speech by Bank of Greece Governor Yannis Stournaras at the General Meeting of Shareholders After two years of an unprecedented pandemic crisis, 2022 has been another year of heightened uncertainty due to Russia's invasion of Ukraine and a sharp rise in inflation. In such a volatile environment of successive crises, it is important to look for stable ones that strengthen the economy's resilience and ability to cope with challenges. In the case of Greece, the continuation of credible economic policies, particularly in the field of fiscal policy, the preservation of the significant achievements of past reform efforts and the establishment of a new reform program for the government that will emerge after the national elections, focusing on the modernization of the public sector and the upgrading of institutions and infrastructure; They must be the beacon that will guide us through the turbulent waters of the new economic reality. International environment The global economy, following the strong recovery rates recorded in 2021, slowed significantly in 2022. However, this slowdown was milder than initially estimated, despite rising inflation, mainly due to: (i) deferred demand and accumulated savings from the pandemic period, which supported consumption, (ii) a strong labour market, and (iii) temporary global policy measures to contain energy costs. Global inflation increased strongly in 2022 and proved to be higher and more protracted than initially forecast. Elevated inflationary pressures are largely driven by supply-side factors, mainly reflecting rising energy costs, while demand drivers also make a significant contribution, owing to the dynamic recovery of economies after the pandemic and extensive fiscal support measures. The dynamic intervention of monetary authorities worldwide, with the drastic increase in interest rates, was deemed necessary to signal their determination to anchor inflation expectations and to contain aggregate demand and bring second-round inflationary effects under control, preventing the emergence of a combination of continuous price-wage increases ("spirals"). Indeed, the magnitude of central bank intervention was such that last year saw the sharpest shift in monetary policy stance recorded since the war, with still uncertain implications for economic activity. Single monetary policy In the course of 2022, inflation in the euro area accelerated sharply and reached historically high levels, triggering a shift in the monetary policy stance of the European Central Bank (ECB). The upcoming normalisation of monetary policy was decided in December 2021, while the start of key interest rate hikes was announced in June 2022, when ECB forecasts suggested that inflation would be more persistent than previously estimated and would remain at undesirable high levels for a long time. Thus, since July 2022, the ECB has made successive increases in key interest rates, ending an eight-year period of negative interest rates. Cumulatively to date, key interest rates have increased by 350 basis points. The way monetary policy decisions are taken has been adapted to the current context of the uncertain economic environment. In particular, instead of prescribing the path of key interest rates by providing forward guidance from the ECB, key interest rate decisions are now taken on the basis of information and economic data gathered with a view to the next meeting of the Governing Council, when the situation of the euro area economy and in particular the inflation outlook is reassessed. as well as the intensity of monetary policy transmission. Throughout this process, the ECB maintains optionality, data-dependency gradualism and monetary policy flexibility. Alongside the interest rate hikes, the ECB adopted a number of other measures. Specifically: - Net asset purchases under the emergency PEPP programme ended in March 2022 and the flexible reinvestment programme has been in place since then, at least until the end of 2024. The possibility of using Greek government securities as collateral in Eurosystem refinancing operations was also extended, at least for as long as PEPP reinvestments continue. - In July 2022, the Transmission Protection Instrument ( TPI) was introduced to enhance the effectiveness of the transmission mechanism of the single monetary policy. - In October 2022 the terms of the targeted longer-term refinancing operations (TLTRO-III) became less favourable to align them with the normalisation of monetary policy, contributing to the shrinking of the ECB's balance sheet. - In December 2022, it was decided to start shrinking the APP portfolio from March 2023, at a predictable and steady pace. Overall, the ECB's strategy demonstrates its determination to ensure that inflation returns to its medium-term objective of 2% and that the monetary policy transmission mechanism functions smoothly by adapting all instruments at its disposal. At the same time, the ECB's policy toolbox is fully equipped to provide liquidity to the banking system; if necessary to ensure financial stability in the euro area. Greek economy Amid unprecedented exogenous shocks and pervasive uncertainty, the Greek economy has made significant progress since the debt crisis of the previous decade, showing high resilience, while strengthening the credibility of economic policy. Over the last two years, Greece has achieved strong growth in its economy, recording a real convergence of its level of prosperity towards the European average. In particular, it is estimated that in 2022 the negative output gap of the economy has been eliminated, after 11 consecutive years. In 2022, the Greek economy maintained its growth momentum, recording a GDP growth rate of 5.9% (significantly higher than the European average), despite strong inflationary pressures and the deterioration of the international environment. GDP in real terms exceeded pre-pandemic levels, driven by private consumption, exports of services (travel receipts almost reached the level of 2019) and investment. In 2021-22, foreign direct investment inflows strengthened significantly, reaching their highest levels in 20 years. Investment funds have been a key tool for financing growth, promoting productivity and jobs and introducing innovative technologies. This development is mainly due to the gradual recovery of confidence in the prospects of the Greek economy. An important role in boosting investment in recent years has been played by the acceleration of the privatization and utilization program of public property, the participation of foreign companies in the share capital of domestic companies, as well as the record number of mergers and acquisitions recorded in 2022. The strong acceleration in headline inflation (to 9.3% in 2022) due to higher international energy prices reduced households' real income and undermined the economic outlook. Gradually, over the course of the year, large and sustained increases in energy and food goods were passed on to services and non-energy industrial products, resulting in a rapid rise in core inflation (to 5.7%). The improvement in the labour market is now evident, with the unemployment rate having fallen in 2022 to 12.4%, below its 2010 level, employment growth accelerating, and labour force growth recorded for the first time since 2009. These developments are largely attributable to labour market liberalisation and reforms of the past decade; which increased flexibility and contributed to employment responding more quickly to GDP growth. The international competitiveness of the Greek economy continued to improve in 2022, despite high inflation. The improvement in competitiveness has been more spectacular in terms of unit labour costs, especially as the relevant indicator fell in 2021-22 below the levels it was before Greece joined the eurozone. This painful and far-reaching recovery of international competitiveness is largely due to the reform of the institutional framework for determining wage increases and its liberalization labour market. Progress is also being made on aspects of the structural competitiveness of the Greek economy. This progress, initiated by a series of reforms in the post-2010 period and intensified in recent years, contributes to improving the business and investment climate, offering additional benefits to outward-looking sectors of the economy. However, the current account deficit widened significantly in 2022 to 9.7% of GDP, owing to faster growth in imports of goods, especially energy, compared to exports of goods. Strengthening consumption and continued growth in industrial production and investment contributed to higher imports of goods. The current account balance was also significantly burdened by the increase in international fuel prices. Despite the widening of the current account deficit in recent years, largely due to cyclical factors linked to the evolution of the pandemic and increased international energy prices, the external sector of the Greek economy has recorded an impressive transformation. Overall, exports of goods and services as a percentage of GDP have almost doubled compared to 2010, reflecting not only the positive course of tourism and transport services, but also the significant increase in exports of goods, along with the increasing diversification of the export base of the Greek economy. Budgetary developments Despite widespread uncertainty and additional support measures, the fiscal targets of the Budget for 2022 are estimated to have been achieved with a safe margin, thanks to higher growth and inflation than initially estimated. The additional interventions did not burden the State Budget, since most of them were financed by extraordinary revenues and by the utilization of fiscal space created thanks to the better-than-expected course of economic activity and the overperformance of tax revenues. According to the Bank of Greece, the primary deficit as a percentage of GDP for 2022 is estimated to be close to zero. Therefore, it will be significantly better than expected despite adverse conditions, enhancing the country's fiscal credibility. This would make it safer to achieve the primary surplus target in 2023, at a time of heightened uncertainty and a significant slowdown in growth. Greece managed in 2021-22 to achieve one of the largest fiscal adjustments in Europe and to record cumulatively the largest decline in public debt, which returned to levels below pre-pandemic levels. Compared to 2020, it is estimated that debt decreased by about 35 percentage points of GDP to 171.4% in 2022, with 2/3 of the decline occurring in 2022. The sustainability of public finances is an important factor in the ratings of international agencies, two of which in 2022 and another in 2023 upgraded the country's credit rating one notch below investment grade, while another has upgraded the economy's outlook to positive. Banking sector Bank credit to the private sector recorded a notable acceleration in 2022, remaining at a higher level than in previous years. In fact, the average monthly net flow of credit almost tripled year-on-year. The rise in economic activity and the increase in inflation, which has inflated the financing needs of businesses due to the increased cost of raw materials and energy, fuelled demand for bank loans. On the supply side, the Eurosystem's provision of liquidity, the ongoing increase in bank deposits and the significant decline in the ratio of non-performing loans (NPLs) had a positive effect. Deposits continued to strengthen in 2022, although their annual growth rate slowed. Private bank deposits recorded a cumulative increase of 8.6 billion. euro in 2022, which corresponds to about 1/2 of the flow of 2021. The increase in household deposits is mainly linked to higher disposable income (in nominal terms), supported by employment growth and fiscal support measures. The increase in business deposits is due to the marked recovery in turnover and tourism receipts. The increase in the key ECB interest rates gradually affected domestic bank interest rates. Bank borrowing costs increased in 2022 for all types of credit, both to non-financial corporations (NFCs) (50 bps) and to households (consumer loans: 50 bps, housing loans: 36 bps). On the other hand, deposit rates remained at very low levels in 2022, due to the smaller and lagged integration of market rate increases into deposit products. Extensive restructuring of the banking sector in Greece has taken place in recent years, making banks less vulnerable to financial market turbulence than in the past: - Banks have largely cleaned up their balance sheets, addressing the NPL problem mainly through the Hercules programme and the corresponding government guarantees. However, the NPL ratio continues to be among the highest in Europe, while the bulk of NPLs moved from banks' balance sheets mainly through the loan securitisation process; remains a problem for debtor businesses and households. - The improvement in balance sheet quality and the significant reduction in provisions, as well as the increase in interest rates, favoured the profitability of Greek banks. The return of banks to profitability in 2022 is a remarkable development, because, among other things, it creates the conditions for (a) further strengthening their capital base, (ii) increasing their ability to finance sound business plans and (iii) improving their quality of their capital by reducing the deferred tax asset on their own funds. - Capital ratios are maintained at a satisfactory level, above the supervisory minimum. High capital adequacy reflects a bank's resilience against a shock that would damage its balance sheet, so that it can absorb any losses. At the same time, liquidity conditions have improved with increased deposits and stable access to capital markets. The Greek banking system has particularly high liquidity ratios not only compared to the past, but also compared to banks in other euro area countries. High liquidity shows how quickly the banking system can respond to shocks. - The exposure of Greek banks' balance sheets to interest rate risk is limited, given that the largest proportion of the Greek government bond portfolio concerns maturing securities that are therefore not affected by price changes, and that banks apply interest rate hedging practices. Overall, the figures show that the Greek banking sector is now in a better position than in the past to absorb the shocks from international markets observed recently, coupled with the continued support it receives from the ECB. This is also a consequence of the adoption of a much stricter regulatory framework for banks' regulatory capital and liquidity. A noticeable difference in Linked to the global financial crisis of 2008 is the fact that since 2014 there has been a harmonised supervisory approach at euro area level by the Single Supervisory Mechanism (SSM) that enhances overall systemic stability in the euro area. It should be noted that supervised institutions undergo stress tests on a regular basis and continuous and thorough audits. Predictions According to the latest estimates by the Bank of Greece, the Greek economy is forecast to grow at a rate of 2.2% in 2023, well above the eurozone average, but clearly lower than in 2022. Consumption and especially investment will continue to contribute positively to growth, while the tourism sector is showing positive prospects again this year. despite continued uncertainty. The upward revision of the growth forecast for 2023 against previous estimates is due to the carryover effect for this year based on the better performance of the economy in 2022. Headline inflation, while remaining at relatively high levels, is expected to decline significantly in 2023 to 4.4%, reflecting the expected decline in energy prices as well as a negative base effect. The current account deficit is projected to decline both in absolute terms and as a percentage of GDP, although it will remain high. The expected de-escalation of energy prices combined with The slowdown in domestic consumption spending will have a dampening effect on imports of goods. At the same time, the recovery of the global economy  albeit at a decelerating pace  will have a positive effect on Greek exports of goods. On the fiscal front, with the lifting of exceptional support measures, fiscal balance is expected to be restored. Based on the available data and the interventions that have been announced, the Bank of Greece estimates that in 2023 the general government budget will return to a primary surplus of 0.7% of GDP, after three consecutive years of deficits. It is also noted that there will be a primary surplus even in structural terms, i.e. excluding the effects of the economic cycle and one-off measures. This means that the The budget structure is such as to generate primary surpluses without the need for additional measures, which is a consequence of the structural fiscal adjustment and reforms of previous years. The country's ability to generate permanent structural primary surpluses is an important element of fiscal policy credibility and, in combination with the favourable characteristics of the public sector This makes the dynamics of the debt-to-GDP ratio particularly resilient to negative shocks over the medium term, boosting international investors' confidence in the prospects of the Greek economy. Sources of risk and uncertainty The adverse international macroeconomic environment is weighing on the prospects of the Greek economy in 2023, which is why credible policies are required. Mitigating the impact of the energy crisis and maintaining growth momentum in the period ahead are the main challenges facing economic policy. More specifically, risks to the prospects of the Greek economy are: (1) the deterioration of the external environment due to adverse geopolitical developments, (2) higher and more persistent inflation; (3) a possible prolonged electoral period; which would increase political uncertainty, (4) a slower-than-expected absorption rate of NGEU funds, (5) the halt in reform implementation or the reversal of past reform changes, with negative effects on economic productivity enhancement and business competitiveness, and (6) the emergence of a new generation of NPLs, due to rising interest rates and the impact of the energy crisis; after the phasing out of state support measures. On public finances, increased fiscal challenges require fiscal prudence and responsibility. In an international environment of rising interest rates, commitment to restoring fiscal balance remains crucial. This is because rising borrowing costs and slowing growth rates limit the positive contribution of the implicit-nominal growth differential, gradually weakening the initially beneficial effect of inflation on reducing the debt-to-GDP ratio. Consequently, Fiscal prudence is needed so as not to undermine the continued downward trend in public debt. Turning to the banking sector, monetary policy tightening and the slowdown in economic activity are expected to weigh on credit growth to the private sector in 2023. The increase in credit costs will limit the ability of private sector borrowers to repay with floating rate loans, especially households, whose real income has already been squeezed by inflation. At the same time, the imminent slowdown in economic growth in 2023 will increase the credit risk of non-financial corporations and households; due to the deterioration of their financial situation. In a globalised world, risks lurk and regional disruptions can quickly take on international dimensions. This underlines both the importance of the resilience of domestic banking systems and the need for supervisors to ensure financial stability conditions. At euro area level, the ECB's strong supervisory framework and toolbox provide safeguards to safeguard financial stability in the event of negative effects on portfolios due to monetary policy tightening bonds and the quality of the loan portfolio. Policy recommendations A tightening of the monetary policy stance is necessary to achieve the objective of reducing inflation to 2% over the medium term. Raising key interest rates and keeping them above their neutral levels would avoid the risk of destabilising inflation expectations and second-round effects from a possible price-wage combination. However, the comparatively larger contribution of aggregate supply factors to the recent rise in inflation, particularly in the euro area, calls for measures other than monetary policy; such as those related to energy policy, minimizing labour market constraints and the production of raw materials. The current economic context calls for complementarity between monetary and fiscal policies. Ensuring the tightening of the fiscal stance during monetary policy tightening requires fiscal prudence and discipline. Under the current circumstances, any support measures should be financed by making use of available fiscal space and should be: (1) temporary, (2) targeted and (3) adapted to the need to address the energy crisis and provide incentives to reduce energy consumption. Moreover, the design of a coherent and credible medium-term fiscal framework is essential at a time of heightened uncertainties. Therefore, the revision of the Stability and Growth Pact and the formulation of new, credible fiscal rules are key preconditions to strengthen the resilience of the euro area as a whole to future shocks. The upgrade of the Greek State's credit rating to investment grade is a very important objective for economic policy in the coming period. In this direction, the key factor is the preservation of fiscal credibility, by achieving sustainable primary surpluses in the medium term of 2% of GDP. The acquisition of investment grade would lead to a very large expansion of the investment base for Greek government bonds, attracting new high-quality investment funds, thus containing the upward effects on their yields of the tightening of international monetary and financial conditions. It would also have a positive impact on Greek businesses and banks by reducing their borrowing costs and attracting new capital. Productive investment and reform implementation will strengthen the economy's resilience, overall productivity and potential output. Therefore, emphasis should be placed on the dynamic implementation of the actions foreseen in the "Greece 2.0" plan, which put the economy on a solid path of strong growth. Increasing public and private investment and accelerating structural changes for the digital transformation, green transition and employment growth will shield the economy against future crises and consolidate sustainable and inclusive economic growth. The improvement in the competitiveness of the Greek economy should continue, keeping wage increases moderate. At the same time, addressing the current account deficit is also a major challenge. The relatively high deficit, even after the correction for high energy prices, suggests the need for (i) further improvement of structural, wage and price competitiveness, and (ii) an even greater inflow of investment capital from abroad to cover its remaining deficit current account. In the labour market, upgrading technical education and training and retraining of vulnerable social groups will help address the problem of mismatch between jobs sought and offered. Interventions to increase the participation of women and young people in particular in the labour force are also needed. For the banking sector, achieving sustainable profitability is important both to preserve its soundness and financial stability and for banks to provide the necessary credit to the real economy. At the same time, a stronger effort is needed to further reduce NPLs, especially when the full impact of the energy crisis has not yet been recorded; inflation and rising interest rates on the quality of banks' loan portfolios. Finally, the prospects of the Greek economy also depend on developments in European integration. The completion of the Banking Union, with the establishment of a European deposit insurance scheme and the establishment of a common, uniform framework for financial crisis management in the European Union, is key to ensuring financial stability and the smooth transmission of monetary policy to member states, making the euro a strong international reserve currency. *** Despite the successive and multi-layered crises of recent years, the Greek economy has shown remarkable resilience. This is due both to the continued implementation of reforms and to the implementation of credible policies. A decisive contribution to the recovery of the Greek economy and the consolidation of a climate of confidence was the support of European institutions in the economic policy followed. For example, the possibility to purchase Greek government securities in the ECB's PEPP programme and the extension of their waiver from collateral eligibility rules for as long as programme reinvestments continue have contributed significantly to the smooth transmission of monetary policy. At the same time, Greece is one of the countries with the greatest expected benefits from the utilization of NGEU resources. The country's performance in absorbing the resources of the European Structural and Investment Funds is also remarkable. Overall, this European institutional support was a consequence of the preparation and implementation of credible medium-term fiscal and reform plans, which was acknowledged by international agencies and investors. This practical support has improved the medium-term growth prospects of the economy and strengthened the sustainability of public finances. The benefits of reforms are now evident in the economy, with measurable and indisputable results. The continued implementation of credible economic policies is a prerequisite for further support from the European institutions and the strengthening of investor confidence, with the ultimate goal of regaining and maintaining investment grade. Moreover, the disbursement of NGEU-critical development funds depends on the implementation of further structural changes and the promotion of credible investment projects. At the same time, countries' participation in the ECB's new Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI) is conditional on adherence to fiscal rules and the adoption of prudent and sustainable macroeconomic policies. The greatest risk to the prospects of the Greek economy, in a period of successive crises and increased uncertainty, would be the loss of credibility of the economic policy pursued, which has been so difficult to recover, and a return to bad practices of the past. It is true that prolonged political uncertainty may undermine the climate of trust that has been built up in recent years. However, the most significant risk to the economy is a return to ineffective policies of the past and the halting and/or reversal of reform efforts. Memories of the painful adjustment achieved in previous years are still fresh enough to remind us of the high economic and social costs involved in correcting chronic imbalances in the economy. Therefore, given that 2023 is a year of national elections, prudence and responsibility of political forces are required, as well as support for national economic targets, in order to maintain confidence in the prospects of the Greek economy. Policymakers should agree to implement key economic policy commitments to preserve what the Greek economy has achieved over the past decade and the sacrifices of the previous period, for the benefit of generations to come. Greece has a historic opportunity to complete the transformation of its economy, making it more resilient against future crises and converging towards the European average. The experience of the decade-long debt crisis, the consolidation of the value of fiscal responsibility and the recognition of the benefits of implementing reforms have contributed to the maturation of Greek society, helping it understand the new international economic environment. The political will for fiscal responsibility and the implementation of credible reform policies is a factor that helps transform crises into opportunities for the country to definitively overcome its long-standing weaknesses, transform itself into a modern, sustainable, extrovert and competitive economy and demonstrate adaptability and resilience in a highly uncertain international environment. Watch here the speech of Bank of Greece Governor Yannis Stournaras at the 90th Annual General Meeting of the Bank's Shareholders.

Title: Speech by Bank of Greece Governor Yannis Stournaras at the Hellenic Institute of Internal Auditors on "The credibility of economic policy and the challenges of the banking sector and its supervision"
text: Address by the Governor of the Bank of Greece's Yiannis Stournaras at Elliniko Institute of Internal Auditors on "The credibility of economic policy and the challenges of the banking sector and the supervising it' 16/05/2023 - Speeches 2nd B3rd And 9 Type: Horse Tree, KibK M3P39IPith & Public: ibth  -   -  Ladies and gentlemen, I am pleased to have the opportunity to participate in today's event of the Institute of Internal Auditors of Greece and share with you my thoughts on the challenges and prospects of the Greek economy, but mainly on the challenges faced by the Greek banking system and its supervision, as well as on the importance of internal audit. risk management and compliance. The Greek economy, amid unprecedented exogenous shocks and pervasive uncertainty, has managed to make significant progress since the great debt crisis of the previous decade, showing high resilience, while at the same time the credibility of economic policy has been strengthened. This is the result of major fiscal adjustment, deep public debt restructuring, far-reaching reforms and restructuring of the banking sector. These significant changes have largely corrected key macroeconomic imbalances. The country's ability to generate structural primary surpluses of around 2% of GDP is a very important element of economic policy credibility. This, together with the favourable characteristics of the public debt structure as a result of its radical restructuring, makes the dynamics of the debt-to-GDP ratio highly resilient to negative shocks in the medium term, and debt sustainable in the long term, thereby enhancing confidence in the prospects of the Greek economy. Competitiveness in terms of relative prices and labour costs has improved significantly since 2010. This painful and far-reaching recovery of international competitiveness is largely due to the reform of the broader institutional framework for determining wage increases and the liberalisation of the labour market. In 2021-22, foreign direct investment inflows strengthened significantly (amounting to 2.8% and 3.1% of GDP respectively, compared to an average of 0.9% for 2002-18) and were a key tool for financing growth, promoting productivity and employment and introducing innovative technologies. Combined with the increased flow of resources from the European Structural Funds and the Recovery and Resilience Fund, which is estimated to be at least 3% of GDP per year over the next five years, they ensure significant resources for the country's development, energy transition and digital transformation. The banking sector has also undergone extensive restructuring in recent years. Banks have largely cleaned up their balance sheets, addressing the problem of non-performing loans. Liquidity conditions have improved with an increase in the stock of deposits and stable access to capital markets. Capital ratios remain at satisfactory levels, above the supervisory minimum, while profitability improved significantly in 2022. A decisive contribution to the recovery of the Greek economy in recent years and to the consolidation of a climate of confidence has been the support of the European institutions in the economic policy pursued. The possibility of purchasing Greek government securities in the emergency purchase programme due to the pandemic (Rapathipio Epithgothpou Despite the lack of investment grade of these securities, and, as already mentioned, Greece's participation in the European Recovery Instrument (NTHI), are two important examples of this contribution. Despite progress in many areas and the rise in the ranking scale in recent years, the Greek economy still has persistent structural problems, leaving it still relatively low in structural competitiveness indicators. Examples of such inherent weaknesses are delays in the administration of justice, bureaucracy and inefficiency that persists in some areas of public administration, lack of basic infrastructure, low participation of women and young people in the labour market combined with unfavourable demographic developments, delays in completing the national land register, insufficient fight against tax evasion, deficiencies in the so-called "knowledge triangle" (education - research - innovation), quasi-oligopolistic conditions in specific markets for goods and services, and distortions in the energy market. The country's GDP is still significantly below 2008 levels, public debt remains the highest in the eurozone, and the current account deficit stands above 6% of GDP. As challenges to global financial stability remain high with successive crises and pervasive, heightened uncertainty, the biggest risk to the prospects of the Greek economy would be a loss of credibility, which has been so difficult to recover, and a return to past practices. Prudence, responsibility and commitment on the part of economic policymakers are needed to preserve the sacrifices of the previous period and to continue the progress made. The primary task of the next government should be (a) the reform programme that will improve structural competitiveness and increase the total productivity of the economy and (b) the return to primary, structural fiscal surpluses of 2% of GDP, so that this year the investment grade can be recovered, maintained, and exceeded in the medium term. which will have favourable multiplier effects on all sectors of the economy. But allow me to focus the main part of my speech on the financial sector. 2022 was a landmark year for the Greek banking system as, after several years, there was a spectacular improvement in all areas, so that we can now talk about a gradual return to normality. More specifically: The quality of credit institutions' loan portfolios improved significantly. The ratio of non-performing loans (NPLs) to total loans stood at 8.7% in December 2022, compared with 12.7% in December 2021, with a total stock of NPLs of 13.2 billion. euro, down 28.2% year-on-year. For the first time since 2009, the system is again with a single-digit NPL ratio. It should be noted that the overall reduction in NPLs from their highest level recorded in March 2016 now stands at 88% or 94 billion. euro. This decrease reflects progress in loan consolidation efforts portfolio of banks, mainly through securitisation of loans using the state guarantees of the Hercules programme'. Banks have resumed funding to the real economy. According to Bank of Greece data[1], in December 2022, the annual growth rate of total private sector financing stood at 6.3%, while the annual rate of change in the financing of non-financial corporations (NFCs) stood at 6.3% stood at 11.8%. In 2022, Greek banks recorded profit after tax and discontinued operations of 3.6 billion. euro, returning to profitability after several loss-making years. This development was decisively contributed by the increase in non- recurring income as well as the formation of reduced provisions for credit risk due to improved asset quality. At the same time, principal banking revenues, in particular net interest income, increased during the 2nd half of the year, as banks benefited from an increase in key interest rates and the normalization of monetary policy. It is also worth report progress in reducing operating costs. The capital adequacy of banking groups strengthened significantly in 2022, mainly due to the increase in banks' regulatory own funds through profitability and, secondarily, due to the issuance of additional capital instruments. Specifically, the Total Capital Adequacy Ratio increased to 17,5% in December 2022, from 16,2% in 2021. Incorporating the full impact of IEK8 9 (IFRS9), the Index stood at 16.4%. Finally, liquidity conditions remain satisfactory. In the course of 2022, deposits continued their upward trend, although their annual growth rate decelerated, reflecting strong economic growth, despite the negative impact of high inflation. The upward trend in deposits contributed to a significant extent to the fact that the liquid assets of Greek credit institutions remained at a high level despite the early and partial repayment of loans in the framework for the ECB's longer-term refinancing operations ( TITKO-III). In recent times, risks to global financial stability have increased. The persistence of inflationary pressures, despite the normalisation of monetary policy, combined with increased geopolitical risks (such as The Russian invasion of Ukraine and the tension in relations between the US and China), create high uncertainty and risks surrounding the international financial environment. The recent banking turmoil in the US and Switzerland has demonstrated the speed of risk contagion and diffusion in the modern financial environment. The weaknesses of individual banks, under conditions of impaired investor and depositor confidence, are growing and spreading rapidly both to other credit institutions within the country where these banks are located and internationally, due to the interconnectedness of financial markets worldwide. Therefore, safeguarding financial stability requires further strengthening of the financial system. As mentioned above, the banking sector in Greece has made significant progress in recent years and has strengthened in order to be better able to cope with potential turbulence and shocks, such as those we have experienced recently. However, while the outlook for the near future looks positive, challenges remain, such as further improving asset quality to the European average, amid pressures on the financial situation of households and businesses due to inflation, rising interest rates and slowing economic activity. At the same time, the challenges are to achieve sustainable profitability and to further quantitatively and qualitatively strengthen banks' capital adequacy, which is below the average for credit institutions directly supervised by the ECB (LCI of 19.4% in December 2022). The turmoil in the US banking system shows the importance of prudent and adequate risk management and internal control practices in a credit institution, together of course with an effective supervisory and crisis management system. Although it is still too early to draw conclusions from the recent crisis, it is evident that in most cases of failing banks, basic risk management and internal control practices were not followed, as a result, inter alia, of the "relaxing" supervision of small and medium-sized credit institutions by competent authorities in the US since mid-2019. It is also a fact that this risk, which often manifests itself through the massive withdrawal of deposits and the draining of banks' liquidity, in today's era of digital, in-person banking (a9/1) and instant payments, can now be realised with impressive speed, compared to the past and our recent experience. The successful implementation of risk management practices by financial institutions in today's era is a significant challenge due to the increased digital transformation of the financial system, the adoption of technological innovation and the ever-expanding interconnectedness of financial institutions with each other and with third-party technology providers or companies. It is a fact that the extensive use of technology, information technology and telecommunications by companies in the financial sector has contributed, among other things, to a more efficient management of business resources, to better supervision and more effective control of all their activities, but also to their geographical expansion at low cost. Moving to a more technology-driven financial services market presents many benefits for financial institutions, which include reduced costs, improved customer experience and increased transaction speed, reduced account opening time, and instant access to online services. But it also creates new risk areas for which it is important to follow best risk management practices as well as to closely monitor and comply with the correspondingly evolving regulatory framework as soon as possible. I would like very briefly to focus on some of those areas that concern us as supervisors and where we already have to develop knowledge and tools in order to ensure financial stability and confidence in the financial system: High dependence on technological infrastructure exacerbates risks to cybersecurity and data protection. Last year's European Parliament report Systemic Risk Board on "Systemic risk mitigation in cyber risks", he stressed with particular emphasis that cyber risks are constantly evolving, attacks are becoming more complex and potential targets can easily be located in different sectors or countries. Financial institutions need to upgrade their digital operational resilience to be able to deal with a wide range of complex threats, as they are already doing for more traditional financial risks. In the context of open banking, we consider it extremely important that communication between financial institutions takes place in a secure and structured way, through Application Programming Interfaces - APIs, such as those implemented by account servicing providers under the revised Payments Directive - P8D2, leaving behind less secure practices of extracting data from providers' websites. Also, new types of risks or different aspects of existing risks may arise in the near future from the widespread use of innovative forms of financial instruments or services such as crypto-assets and decentralised finance. The transition from traditional face-to-face (I3i-Io-I3i) interaction with the customer to non-face-to-face (PDO 3-3) online interaction channels on a remote basis, creates a number of challenges in terms of their compliance with the institutional framework for the prevention of Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing (AML/CFT). These challenges are addressed both to the supervisory authority which has to shield the system through its regulatory role, and companies in the financial sector that will need to adapt their business practices in order to remain competitive, while assessing and effectively addressing new and emerging risks associated with AML/CFT. Another concern from the point of view of cross-border financial stability is the over-reliance of financial sector entities on a limited number of third-party providers, such as technology giants - Bi9T, for outsourcing operations or providing technological infrastructure and services. This is particularly important in the context of the migration of critical infrastructures and services to cloud computing, which can lead to risks data aggregation, business continuity and governance. Artificial intelligence, including machine learning, equips Financial institutions with tools that can enhance their capabilities in a variety of business areas. Indicatively, I mention downloading and automation decisions and estimates of development figures, detection of fraud, threats to the cyber and money laundering and terrorist financing, operational risk management, market monitoring, improved customer experience in remote contact with the organization and regulatory compliance. However, it may entail risks in terms of the ability to explain the results of AI models, as well as bias or inaccuracies due to the data fed into the models. In any case, institutions should be able to justify decisions taken with the help of an artificial intelligence tool. It is important to mention that, at the level of corporate governance, the digital transformation strategy of an institution should have the approval and full support of its board of directors and there should be harmonisation between it business strategy and IT strategy. Digital transformation is a continuous and complex process and institutions must implement it in a holistic, complete and centralized way, with a clear delimitation of responsibilities and responsibilities and adequate support and involvement of the services that constitute the second and third line of defense. For some of the areas I mentioned above, significant initiatives have already been taken at national level by government and supervisory bodies in order to mitigate risks within an optimal regulatory framework or practices. In this context and responding directly to market needs, the Bank of Greece in May 2020 issued Executive Committee 172 specifying the terms and conditions for remote electronic identification of natural persons. In the same direction, on the initiative of the Minister of Foreign Affairs. Digital Governance, in 2021 the electronic service THYON-KYO was launched, through which credit institutions (PD) and financial institutions (XO) can obtain in digital form the identity data of their customers of natural persons from the primary registers and information systems of the State, as an alternative to the presentation of the original documents in physical form. These steps have significantly contributed to enhancing the security and reliability of the implemented remote authentication process of customers and to improving the level of compliance of credit institutions with their obligations under the AML/CFT prevention framework. Important developments were also the adoption of a harmonised outsourcing framework (Executive Committee 178/5/2020), which specified the obligations of institutions when outsourcing activities to cloud service providers, as well as the adoption of individual acts implementing secondary legislation relating to payment services under P8Z2. Also, in order to enhance its ability to understand in a timely manner the developments taking place in the context of the digital transformation of the financial system, the Bank of Greece has created the Innovation Hub and the Protected Regulatory Environment as mechanisms to facilitate innovation in recent years. However, we expect many relevant important actions to be taken in the medium term, both by the market and by competent supervisory and regulatory authorities at European and national level. The European Commission's initiatives on the Regulation on Digital Operational Resilience of the Financial Sector, known as OOPs, and the Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation, known as MIOPA, are key examples of reform aimed at closing regulatory gaps in the area of supervision of digital financial services and products.
