Similarly, the long-awaited EU anti-money laundering and countering the financing of terrorism package, known as AMI_ Rao, aims at a fundamental overhaul of the European regulatory and supervisory framework in this area. The primary focus is on establishing a new Regulation with common, uniform rules and obligations for all institutions and the creation of a new European supervisory authority, known as AMI_A (AMI_APIping), with strong powers and responsibilities, including the exercise of direct supervision over selected high-risk obliged entities. On the supervisory side, we will have to familiarise ourselves with and implement the new framework, while on the supervisory side, credit institutions will have to comply by developing appropriate mechanisms. The digital transition of financial services is a dynamic, constantly evolving process that has an impact not only on the business model but also on the entire risk profile of institutions, operations (CBC3iiop8) and corporate governance. In order for an institution to effectively manage new and emerging risks, training, up-to-date and specialized knowledge is required at all levels of organization, from the operational officer to the members of the Board of Directors of the institution. Equally important is the demonstration of readiness and alertness in the control mechanisms from the 2nd and 3rd lines of defense (IOd) to identify, assess and address risks (IT, eighthG, IAWA, MI/TE, BUSINESS CONTINUITY, ETC.) and to develop prevention and control mechanisms in compliance with regulatory requirements. In any case, addressing the challenges and new risk areas associated with new technologies requires close cooperation both between executives of different specialties in different business units within the institution itself, as well as with the supervisory authorities, aiming at the common goal of remaining competitive, responding to consumer needs and following technological developments, while shielding the security and stability of the system. In closing, I would like to make a reference to the European Commission's recent proposals on the crisis management framework, which are moving in the right direction, filling existing gaps and significantly strengthening the resolution framework. At the same time, however, initiatives to complete the Banking Union with the creation of the third pillar, a pan-European bank deposit insurance scheme, should be stepped up (Euratom Oooodi Iordib 8th Ioth - EDI8). Taking into account that the digital transformation of financial institutions can accelerate the transmission of crises, as I mentioned above, the adoption of this framework should proceed at a fast pace in order to be able to prevent and effectively address the challenges created by the modern functioning of the market. Title: Speech by Bank of Greece Governor Yannis Stournaras at a TMEDE event entitled: "The institution of microfinance and prospects for the Greek market"
text: Speech by Bank of Greece Governor Yannis Stournaras at a TMEDE event entitled: "The institution of Microfinance and the prospects for the Greek market" 20/06/2023 - Speeches Ladies and gentlemen, I am glad to have the opportunity to participate in today's TMEDE event and share with you my thoughts on its challenges and prospects microfinance in Greece. Starting with basic concepts, microfinance today includes a set of financial products aimed at low-income individuals and micro-legal entities, usually excluded from the banking sector, mainly because of their inability to provide collateral to guarantee the loans they receive. Among the various financial products included in microfinance (microinsurance, savings, money transfers, etc.), the best known is microcredit, which I will call microfinance here in the broad sense, as it is widely used. Looking back, microfinance was first implemented in the 1970s, under the guidance of Myiapithp Yypye, a Bangladeshi economist who was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2006 for creating the Obpithp BbpK, the "bank of the poor". Shocked by a terrible famine that caused 1.5 million people to live in his country. victims, He thought that if people had access to credit, they could increase their income or diversify their economic activities more profitably. By lending small sums of money to the financially weak, he believed that they would improve their lives enough to be able to return them to him. So he could lend further without having to donate them, and in this way he could help many more people. Interesting theory but ineffective, because initially many of the borrowers did not repay these small loans. Hyhyye assumed that this was either because they had used the money with wrong way (for consumption or for ill-conceived micro-enterprises) or in that they were not trustworthy. Improving on his original theory, he brought to the system certain Amendments: Lending to poor rural women was preferred (because they were less likely than men to abuse the loans and were more reliable to repay them). She organized women into groups of five, who collectively took responsibility for repaying their loans, thus creating a "social" (e.g. the elected president of the group is entitled to a loan only when all members of the group have fulfilled the terms of their loans). It developed simple, standardized financial products that required regular, small payments to be repaid. It recruited and trained young school graduates to provide the relevant services in order to minimize corruption. As a result, 0c3pith Bahk of Bangladesh was founded, which was established as a parastatal organization ("p3C38I3333beg") and today has an emblematic role in the world of microfinance. It is tangible proof that the poor can be "financeable" ("03c3i3i)"). In the same line was Miiop Epthaip3p[1] who advocated that: "The poor remain poor not because they are lazy, but because they don't have access to capital." From the above it is evident that microfinance can be a valuable tool when properly used for the creation or development of businesses and the improvement of household living conditions. Microfinance has proven to be a powerful weapon in the fight against poverty, having a positive impact on borrowers as their income level increases after receiving the loan. Through the increased Individuals can lift themselves out of poverty, ensure better nutrition and education for themselves and their families, and break the cycle of intergenerational poverty. Microfinance also plays a central role in empowering women, who often face barriers to accessing financial services. By granting microloans to women, they are given the opportunity to do business, but also to become decision-makers both for themselves and for the communities in which they operate. The consequence of women's economic empowerment is the improvement of their economic and social status, access to better health care, but also increased educational opportunities for future generations. We see, therefore, that the inclusion of the economically weak and women in economic activity promotes the creation of a fairer and more inclusive society. Through innovative delivery channels and digital applications, microfinance bridges the gap, ensuring that financial services are accessible to all. At the same time, a significant positive impact is also observed on the sustainable development of an economy, as aspiring entrepreneurs are given the opportunity to start or expand their small businesses, creating employment opportunities and enhancing income generation. By promoting entrepreneurship, microfinance promotes local economic development, fosters innovation and builds resilient communities. This is why I believe that households should be encouraged to seek investment opportunities that will increase their demand for financing. But there are some who question the positive effects of microfinance, considering that it is possible that borrowers use the money they receive to meet their basic needs, rather than invest it in business activities, thus not generating new income. Although this risk exists, I believe that the benefits of microfinance outweigh the risks. For this reason, the strengthening of the institution is imperative. As we have seen, in the developing countries where it is structured, the alternative financial model of microfinance is a driving force for development and, above all, a tool for combating poverty. In Europe, on the other hand, the promotion of microfinance is more part of political initiatives to combat social exclusion and create opportunities to return to employment. Indirectly, Microfinance is presented as a lever to combat poverty, offering those who benefit from it the opportunity to escape social exclusion by setting up or taking over a business. Microfinance has been a growing area of activity in recent years, especially in Eastern Europe. Its penetration potential remains high, taking into account the impact of the current low economic growth on disadvantaged populations and the need to ensure their social and financial inclusion. In Europe, the sector is heterogeneous, due to the diversity of actors and business models, and the different legal and institutional frameworks applied in each country. Therefore, lending practices in the sector vary considerably depending on the type of institution providing the microcredit, its legal status, the institutional environment in which it operates and its ability to apply sound and efficient management procedures. The majority of microfinance providers are non-banks microfinance (94%), which operate as NGOs, non-bank financial institutions (NPIs), government bodies and cooperatives. In Eastern Europe, microfinance is mainly provided by cooperatives and non-bank financial institutions, while the microfinance sector in Western Europe is dominated by banks and NGOs. According to a study by the European Microfinance Network (European Microfinance Network ) in 2022, 80% of microfinance institutions rate their situation as good or very good and 71% of microfinance institutions believe that their business situation will improve in the next 12 months. According to 2021 data, the value of the total microfinance portfolio in Europe is estimated at 4.3bn. from 3.9bn. euro in 2020 (9%) and the number of active borrowers was 1.4 million. from 1.2m. in 2020 (20%). 84% of microfinance institutions have digital solutions that support clients in applying for and managing or repaying a loan. Finally, according to the same study by the European Microfinance Network, access to finance is seen by NGOs as a major challenge. For banks too, the adoption of relevant regulatory rules raises a variety of concerns. Having a strong propensity for growth, microfinance institutions see low customer potential as the main obstacle to the development of their sector. Low and volatile incomes, limited financial capabilities and low digital competence of customers are perceived by many microfinance institutions as the main challenges to be addressed. However, it should be noted that the trend of digitalisation, accelerated by IoKaonni and the need for remote work and communication with customers, has led to the introduction of new digital solutions. The growing demand for new alternative forms of financing, as reflected at European level, has created the need for an institutional framework in Greece for two reasons: making it easier for micro-enterprises to access finance and the strengthening of social groups to tackle unemployment and social exclusion. Law 4701 of 2020, in the spirit of the European Code of Good Practice for the granting of Microcredit, laid the foundations for the development of the sector. It was established primarily to fill the funding gap that exists in business activity and mainly affects those who are starting out in business, because one of the main problems faced by micro-enterprises is their access to bank lending, in particular due to the inability to provide the collateral required by EU banking legislation. The law also recognised the importance of microfinance institutions providing business education advisory services to beneficiaries of microfinance. Thus, and in this spirit, the law made this possibility compulsory. In this way, the law on microfinance institutions aims to form a new pillar, parallel to the banking system, for raising capital from natural and legal persons who develop or have the potential to develop a business/professional activity. This new pillar complements and does not compete with banks and comes to meet needs that banks did not cover until now. In addition, this law provides for the possibility of granting appropriations aimed at strengthening public policies or the social and economic integration of vulnerable social groups, in particular by covering expenses directly or indirectly related to their education or further education. The aim is to create new jobs, boost entrepreneurship, reduce the shadow economy, promote a healthy business culture and support growth. Let us now see what the provisions of the law provide, starting with the concept and legislative status of microfinance institutions. As a foundation Microfinance means the legal entity based in Greece that provides microfinance, i.e. loans up to 25k. Regarding the activities of microfinance institutions, they may indicatively provide microfinance up to 25th, as follows: (a) all forms of credit, either to cover investment needs or as working capital, (b) leasing products for the acquisition of equipment; (c) stand-alone guarantees, which may not be used to obtain loans from other financial institutions; Beneficiaries of these forms of credit are micro-entities, natural persons for the purpose of setting up micro-entities, natural persons exercising individual business activity and Social and Solidarity Economy Bodies. In addition to the above-mentioned credits, microfinance institutions may grant forms of credit aimed at strengthening public policies or the social and economic integration of vulnerable social groups, up to 25th. These appropriations relate in particular to the fight against unemployment. The beneficiaries of this fourth form of credit are natural persons belonging to vulnerable social groups and natural persons seeking to cover expenses related to their education. Microfinance institutions are also required to provide business education and mentoring advisory services to beneficiaries. As regards the conditions for granting microfinance, microfinance does not require the beneficiary to provide security in rem, but may be required to provide some guarantees. The repayment period of loans may not be less than twelve months nor exceed ten years, and the beneficiary shall be entitled to early repayment. To protect the beneficiary, the law requires transparency in loan termsby their mandatory inclusion in the contract between the beneficiary and institution and also requires the precise specification of standard information for advertising and marketing the products of those institutions. Finally, the law provides for the participation of these institutions in programs funded by the Public Investment Program, provided that they have previously received certification of compliance with the European Code of Good Practice for Microcredit Granting. The Bank of Greece has been designated as the competent authority responsible for the authorisation and supervision of microfinance institutions. A legal person wishing to obtain authorisation shall submit an application to the Bank of Greece, accompanied by the required data and supporting documents. This ensures that the suitability of its shareholders, its management and the relevant director to comply with the provisions of the legislation on the prevention and suppression of money laundering and terrorist financing is ensured. Abreast evaluate the organizational governance framework, the policies followed and procedures, as well as internal control mechanisms. In order to monitor institutions' compliance with the provisions of the institutional and regulatory framework, the Bank of Greece supervises and controls microfinance institutions, receiving, inter alia, supervisory reports also submitted by licensed microfinance institutions. Since the entry into force of the law, three microfinance institutions have been licensed by the Bank of Greece. These are the institutions "T.M.E.D.E. MioGoithithoth doiiopd", "MioiodPITHi" and "AFI MioGoithioth S.A." which received a license in January 2022, March and May 2023 respectively and are expected to start their activity in the next one interval. It is worth noting here that since 2014 AFI and since 2018 Mio8iti3C (as MioGOviaG) have been active as civil non-profit companies in the field of microfinance, mediating specific banks for the disbursement by them of microloans to customers, which the companies themselves had approached and initially evaluated. Regarding the obstacles and prospects for microfinance institutions to operate in Greece, we understand that the Greek regulatory framework is demanding in terms of the licensing and prudential regime imposed on microfinance institutions. It should be noted, however, that it is based on the provisions of the landmark European Code of Good Practice for microcredit (" 0thpi8cI") for the sector in Europe, while protecting the beneficiaries of microcredit. At the same time, the rules set out aim to ensure the viability of microfinance institutions. To enhance the sustainability of institutions, effective policies and improved regulatory frameworks need to be ensured, allowing institutions to play a key role in reducing inequalities and fighting poverty. Applying the national institutional and regulatory framework, microfinance institutions in Greece should build on decades of international experience in the microfinance sector so as not to repeat past mistakes. They should assess prospective borrowers, their risk profile and business idea, providing the right products for their lending, adopt the necessary microfinance monitoring mechanisms, recruit competent staff and provide appropriate advisory services. At the same time, access to financing and guarantee mechanisms is necessary for the development of the institution of microfinance in Greece. Such mechanisms are provided, among others, by European bodies, such as the European Guarantee Fund, the Hellenic Development Bank, and the Ministry of Development. In conclusion, the European and global experience gives encouraging signals for the prospects of the economic model of microfinance in Greece, taking into account that microfinance is one of the few tools available for those usually excluded from the banking system, including micro-enterprises. Despite any problems and failures, this institution can support national, European and global efforts to finance financially weak individuals and micro-enterprises, alleviate poverty, increase incomes and living standards, reduce unemployment and ultimately growth. I also believe that the existence of a strong institutional regulatory framework for the granting of microfinance in Greece lays solid foundations for the smooth and successful development of the institution in our country, addressing in a timely manner one of the challenges currently encountered at global level, which is, as I mentioned at the beginning, an appropriate regulatory framework for these institutions. Finally, the development of the institution may help, to some extent, to mitigate the current climate of economic uncertainty at global level, from high inflation and existing geopolitical risks. Title: Speech by Bank of Greece Governor Yannis Stournaras at "FinForum 2023: The Day After" entitled "Challenges and opportunities for the Greek financial system"
text: Speech by Bank of Greece Governor Yannis Stournaras at the "EUPOGYITI 2023: Teth Thg AUTHG" entitled "Challenges and opportunities for the Greek financial system" 11/07/2023-Speeches Ladies and gentlemen, It is a great pleasure and honor for me to address the opening speech at today's workshop, which has a very rich and interesting program. I will refer to Greek banks and private insurance companies, which make up the Greek financial system. I will start with the banks, but before I talk about the challenges and opportunities they face today, I would like to make a brief reference to the very long way they have travelled in recent years in terms of cleaning up their balance sheets and improving their financial figures: Over the past decade, Greece has experienced one of the most severe financial crises in postwar world economic history, with heavy consequences for the domestic banking system. At the beginning of 2016, almost half of Greek banks' loan portfolios were non-performing. In some sub-sectors of the loan portfolio, such as SMEs and micro-enterprises, the share of non-performing loans amounted to around 2/3 of the total. It is understandable that in these circumstances, banks were unable to perform their important intermediary role in the economy. Since then, Greek banks have seen a very large reduction in non-Greek banks. of performing loans, especially after the option of asset protection through the granting of a state guarantee, known as Hercules, and currently have a single-digit ratio, which stands at 8.8%, according to data for the first quarter of 2023, compared to 45% in March 2016. At the height of the crisis, banks were highly dependent on the Central Bank's emergency liquidity assistance (EIA) mechanism for their funding, amid continued deposit outflows and market inaccessibility. Today, banks fully respect supervisory liquidity ratios and have a stable and growing deposit base, with full market access, despite the fact that they do not have investment grade. Finally, during the crisis years, Greek banks recorded cumulative significant losses, stemming mainly from credit risk, P8I and the inability to substantially expand their activities. As a result, it took several rounds recapitalisations of significant (but also some less significant banks) in order to avoid the possibility of their collapse, while several credit institutions were placed in resolution. Today, Greek banks are showing significant profitability, both due to improved asset quality and high interest margins, as well as due to credit growth and high Greek banks have one of the lowest cost-to-income ratios in the eurozone. The high profitability, combined with other capital enhancement actions, led Greek banks to have an average Capital Adequacy Ratio above the minimum thresholds. It is evident from the above that Greek banks today have much improved figures compared to the past and have returned to normality. And this is something that crystallizes in both the market assessment and the supervisory assessment. But risks to global financial stability have increased over the past year and European banks face significant challenges. Specifically: The outlook for economic growth in the global and especially in the European economy remains uncertain, amid high geopolitical risks and increase in interest rates which has become necessary to tackle high inflation. Some analysts even speak of a new trilemma facing the authorities as they will have to deal with high inflation through monetary policy, while ensuring financial stability and positive growth rates. This combination (i.e. high inflation and elevated interest rates) is putting pressure on households and some businesses, in particular variable rate borrowers and "vulnerable" borrowers, such as those on the path to recovery from the pandemic. Therefore, the possibility should not be excluded deterioration of their asset quality in the period ahead. This challenge is even more important for Greek banks, which  despite significant improvement  are still far from the eurozone average in terms of NPL ratio. The increase in interest rates has provided a strong boost to banks' net interest income in the short term, but in the medium term it may increase their credit risk, operating and liquidity costs, especially for banks that need to meet the targets for minimum EI levels, i.e. the minimum liabilities indicator required by the European Resolution Authority. Moreover, in an environment of high interest rates, demand for new loans and/or repayment of existing loans is expected to decrease, especially from companies with excess liquidity. For Greek banks, sound credit growth is a necessary ingredient for achieving sustainable profitability in order to strengthen their but also to gradually reduce the percentage of the deferred tax asset on their own funds. Rising interest rates and market volatility also pose risks in the financial sector outside the banking system (HOH-03 BCL Toxicid) that may affect banks secondarily. The real estate market (particularly commercial real estate, or commercial real estate ) is on course to correct and may expose some banks to losses. New risks are also emerging, such as those related to climate change or cyber-attacks (octocth 3/3i). Finally, markets remain vulnerable to negative news. A typical example was the recent turmoil in the banking system in the US and Switzerland that had a serious negative impact on markets. Particularly in the case of the collapsed American banks and the rescue of Otvaii Diadif (08) by IIB8, I would like to point out that these are events that have seriously troubled the competent authorities, but they appear to be isolated cases where the increase in interest rates has revealed serious weaknesses in the their business model and risk management, along with significant gaps in the implementation of the supervisory framework. This turmoil has also shown how important it is to maintain confidence in the banking system, especially in today's digital age, considering the possibilities offered by digital banking. It also highlighted the importance of prudent risk management and internal control practices within credit institutions and robust supervision by competent authorities. It is important at this point to stress that European and Greek banks do not have the weaknesses identified in the US, as most of their deposits are insured, have a different asset structure with more loans on their balance sheet, have ample high-quality liquid assets, have strong internal control and risk management systems, and, as regards Greek banks, they are supervised by the ECB and the Bank of Greece. The creation of 88M, the single European supervisory mechanism, proved to be a very good choice, since, among other things, it eliminated national biases in the supervisory process. Despite these serious challenges (which, as I mentioned above, concern all banks in the euro area) and the uncertain economic environment, Greek banks have significant opportunities to expand their activities and further strengthen their activities. their fundamentals. Specifically: In the near future, Greece is expected to regain investment grade. This will have beneficial effects for the economy as a whole, as it will boost, through investment, economic growth and facilitate access to markets at lower (current) costs of raising capital. Given that banks have plans for significant bond issuances and capital instruments, it is understandable that regaining investment grade status will have significant positive effects. The economy will benefit in the coming years from the implementation of the important reforms already announced by the government as well as from the utilization of resources from the European Union Structural Funds and the Recovery Facility and Resistance. It is understood that the opportunities created for the Greek Banks to expand their loan portfolio are important, with all that this entails to enhance their profitability and capital adequacy. In light of the positive prospects for the Greek economy and the significant We can now say with certainty that the Greek banking system, like the Greek economy, has ceased to be the "black sheep" of the Eurozone and can now look to the future with optimism. The results of the EU-wide stress test (Itsdi), which will assess the resilience of Greek and European banks to an adverse scenario, are expected at the end of the month. Finally, I believe that the European banking system (including Greek banks) will benefit significantly from possible progress in the discussions currently taking place in the European Union on the introduction of an effective Crisis Management Framework. In this regard, I should mention that in April 2023, the European Commission published its proposals for the revision of the framework for crisis management and deposit insurance. The main points of the revision include: a) the possibility of extending the application of resolution measures to small and medium-sized credit institutions, b) strengthening the role of national Deposit Guarantee Funds with the possibility of their participation in the financing of crisis prevention, consolidation measures, or (c) other amendments, such as improvements to early intervention measures and the framework for cooperation between supervisory and resolution authorities. The proposals on the table are a step in the right direction to ensure smooth crisis management in the banking sector and to protect depositors. However, it highlights the need for additional changes concerning, inter alia, ensuring the effectiveness of the framework in the event of a systemic crisis, as the existing framework is designed to address limited crises. To this end, it is primarily necessary to adopt a common European deposit insurance fund at banking union level to consolidate depositor confidence, especially in the event of cross-border shocks and systemic crisis. The other important sector under the supervisory responsibility of the Bank of Greece is that of private insurance companies. It is more than seven years since the European supervisory framework "Solvency II" entered into force in 2016. Greek insurance companies, which operate under this framework, have effectively addressed all the challenges of previous years, while maintaining their capital adequacy at high levels. The effects of the recent pandemic, the energy crisis exacerbated by the war in Ukraine and the generalised surge in inflation are some examples of these challenges. The Greek insurance market has undergone extensive transformation in recent years, due to mergers and acquisitions. Today the sector faces a number of additional challenges. Especially: Greece is a country exposed to natural disaster risks (mainly earthquake risk), for which insurance penetration is disproportionately low, which implies a gap in insurance protection for Greek citizens. Gaps in protection from private insurance also exist in relation to other risks, such as pensions, health insurance, general liability, etc. But on the specific issue of natural disaster risks, the Greek insurance sector has the skills, knowledge and ability to play an important role in filling the gap. As insurance undertakings need to reduce their exposure to insurance products with long-term guarantees, low or even negative interest rates prevailing over the last decade have increased the number of investment-related insurance products (products). One of the priorities of the Bank of Greece is to ensure the best possible treatment of policyholders and the availability to them of products offering satisfactory value for money. In this context, insurance undertakings should continuously evaluate their business practices relating to the insurance product design and development process, their pricing, advertising and distribution, and finally the management of potential insurance claims. Climate change is a serious challenge. The Bank of Greece has repeatedly stressed the importance of the contribution of private insurance to tackling the effects of climate change, since its role is twofold. On the one hand, insurance undertakings absorb losses that would otherwise be borne by individuals, undertakings or the State. On the other hand, insurance undertakings, as institutional investors, may select investments that protect the environment and promote a green and sustainable economy (principles E83). Insurance companies will also have to respond to the challenges of the new digital age. First, by leveraging technological innovations to improve their operations, as well as the services they provide to policyholders. And second, by providing insurance against cyber-attacks to individuals, but mainly to Greek businesses. In closing my position today, I would like to conclude that the Greek financial system is clearly healthier and more solvent than in the past and is able to absorb shocks from the possible implementation of an adverse scenario for the Greek economy, e.g. a severe shock from abroad. However, this does not mean complacency, as the challenges to financial stability remain high and vigilance is needed both on the part of management, mainly banks but also private insurance companies, and on the part of supervisors. In any case, I think that after a difficult period, it is now justified for the Greek financial system to look to the future with optimism. Thank you and I wish you every success in today's workshop.

Title: Speech by Bank of Greece Deputy Governor Christina Papaconstantinou to the staff of the Central Bank of Cyprus entitled: "Modern challenges: building on experience"
text: Speech by Bank of Greece Governor Christina Papaconstantinou to the staff of the Central Bank of Cyprus entitled: "Modern challenges: building on experience" 05/09/2023 - Speeches It is a great pleasure for me to be at the Central Bank of Cyprus today. I would first of all like to thank Governor Herodotou for his invitation and warm hospitality, as well as all of you for your presence. In my speech, I will refer to the developments and prospects of the Greek economy at the current juncture and the experience we have accumulated during the past years of crises and reforms. The Greek economy has shown considerable resilience, despite successive exogenous shocks in recent years  the pandemic (Othney-19), the war in Ukraine and the energy crisis, as well as the recent turbulence in capital markets centred on the banking system, which created an adverse economic environment and led to increased uncertainty. Greece has returned to a strong growth trajectory, recording GDP growth rates of 8.3% in 2021 and 5.9% in 2022, higher than the eurozone average, as has Cyprus. As a result, the losses in GDP due to the pandemic crisis have been recovered and a real convergence of the country's level of prosperity towards the European average is taking place. In particular, growth in 2022 was mainly supported by higher private consumption, despite a deterioration in households' real disposable income due to strong inflationary pressures. Both exports of services, mainly due to the good performance of tourism receipts, and investment, supported inter alia by the utilisation of LMVI resources, made a positive contribution to growth. Growth in Greece is expected to slow this year, as a result of the downturn in economic activity in the euro area and milder growth in domestic private consumption. The decline in the pace of recovery in private consumption is due to the impact of inflation and the withdrawal of financial support measures on households' disposable income, as well as to the weakening impact of deferred demand. Despite the challenges, the Greek economy maintains a significant part of last year's growth momentum, as confirmed by available data, and continues to perform better than the euro area average. Greece's medium-term growth prospects are positive, supported by available European funds and the implementation of the National Recovery and Resilience Plan, as well as, of course, by the favourable characteristics of public debt. At the same time, the expected recovery of investment grade status in 2023 will provide a significant boost to the financing of the Greek economy, including the Greek banking system, and strengthen its capacity to withstand external shocks. Progress made since the euro area debt crisis has contributed to the resilience of the Greek economy. During the three economic adjustment programmes, the "twin" general government and current account deficits were tackled through hard work, cost competitiveness was restored and reforms were implemented, such as in the social security system, the labour market, goods and services markets, the business environment and public administration. The reform effort continued after the completion of the adjustment programmes. At the same time, the capital adequacy and liquidity of the Greek banking system improved and the stock of non-performing loans (NPLs) was significantly reduced, allowing the banking system to perform its intermediary role. In my view, there are many important lessons, at national and European level, from previous crises and economic adjustment programmes in terms of designing and, in particular, implementing economic measures and structural reforms. This experience has highlighted the importance of credibility, continuity and consistency in the conduct of economic policy, ownership of economic adjustment programmes, trust in institutions, but also trust between social partners, as well as understanding and consensus between different political forces. To this I will add the importance of effective public administration for the implementation of policy measures. When these conditions coexist, the costs and duration of economic adjustment can be mitigated and structural breakthroughs can be successfully completed, bringing long-term benefits to the economy. The economic adjustment programmes in Europe were the product of ongoing negotiations at both technocratic and political levels. For this reason, it was necessary to establish and maintain the credibility of national actors in a timely manner with practical evidence of their ability to implement demanding policies, in order to ensure the trust of European partners and thus maintain at national level certain degrees of freedom in the final formulation of adjustment programmes. Greece and Cyprus faced different challenges during the eurozone debt crisis and entered an economic adjustment programme at different junctures. Cyprus eventually met a broad internal consensus on the programme and this made it easier for it to honour its commitments. In Greece, the lack of consensus and the breakdown of trust of our European partners have prolonged the economic and social shocks. At this point I will address the issue of political willingness and commitment to implement necessary structural reforms. We know from international experience that the implementation of reforms is subject to significant challenges, particularly because the benefits of reforms are spread while the costs are concentrated. That is why we find that reforms, whether at national or European level, They take place mainly in the aftermath of crises, as in the case of the eurozone debt crisis. However, as a result of this practice, the cost of reforms increases, especially when the mix of structural and other policies is inappropriate, while the emergence of reform fatigue is favoured.In fact, in the context of economic adjustment programmes in Europe, it was found that, in the absence of national ownership of reforms, support for their completion at institutional and administrative level was affected. Similarly, necessary revisions of the common European framework are often carried out late, which both incites anti-European sentiment and reduces Europe's ability to deal with new disruptions in a timely manner. It is therefore legitimate and necessary for structural reforms to be implemented preventively in times of economic recovery and not only after crisis episodes in times of recession. I believe that this change of direction is now being helped by European initiatives that create the right incentives for the implementation of structural policies. A prominent example is the recovery instrument (NEy), at the core of which is the Recovery and Resilience Facility. Member States have drawn up "Recovery and Resilience Plans", setting out reform and investment programmes themselves, as well as targets, milestones and estimated costs. In this way, national governments themselves have ownership, commitment and responsibility for national plans. At the same time, the progress of their implementation is subject to systematic control and disbursements from the NHS are linked to the fulfillment of targets and milestones. This creates the conditions for the success of the European project, through a process that links the inflow of capital with the implementation of measures that will magnify the final footprint of these funds on the economy. The proposed new economic governance framework of the European Union, currently under negotiation, is a European initiative that encourages the reform effort. Under the new framework, member states will formulate medium-term fiscal-structural plans, setting their fiscal targets, as well as structural measures and investments for sustainable and inclusive growth. Here, too, emphasis is therefore placed on strengthening national ownership and project ownership. At the same time, the new framework gives governments more flexibility and incentives to make necessary structural interventions. If there is one lesson we can learn from past experience, both in the case of the debt crisis and in the crisis brought about by the EU-19 pandemic, it is that coordinated and harmonised action at European Union level can bring significant benefits for all Member States and favours an effective and rapid response to shocks. Ladies and gentlemen, It is a given that we cannot rest on what we have already conquered. Today's challenges are many and complex, and economic policymakers need to be prepared and far-sighted to identify new sources of risk. Among the common long-term challenges I could not omit those linked to climate change, technological progress and an ageing population. More directly, the challenges facing EU member states are mainly linked to the effects of the energy crisis and high inflation, which worsen the financial situation of households and businesses, thus undermining growth dynamics. To avoid fuelling inflationary pressures, budget support needs to be based on measures targeted at the most vulnerable, temporary in nature and tailored to incentivise a reduction in energy consumption and the transition to a greener economy. At the same time, prudence and responsibility in the conduct of fiscal policy are essential. Moreover, maintaining the restrictive fiscal stance in the euro area supports monetary policy in alleviating inflationary pressures. In the case of Greece, the high debt leaves no room for fiscal easing and makes it imperative to achieve short-term targets. The Greek economy is also facing challenges that are exacerbated by the current conjuncture (adverse macroeconomic environment, high inflation and increased interest rates), but are also related to chronic weaknesses. Some of these challenges I believe that the Cypriot economy is also facing: High public debt as a percentage of GDP. In the medium term, its favourable Characteristically, in terms of its structure, as it is primarily a debt to the official sector, and its low service rate, ensure its sustainability. However, these features are not permanent, as favourable loans are gradually coming to an end. were granted under the MoUs and are replaced by new borrowing on market terms. Therefore, we have an important window of opportunity that must be seized by maintaining prudent fiscal policy to ensure the achievement of primary, cyclically corrected, surpluses of 2% of GDP. The high current account deficit. A small open economy that is in the process of recovery and convergence towards the European average is bound to have a negative balance, due to the increased needs for imports of productive inputs. Despite the significant increase in Greek exports compared to the period before the debt crisis (at a rate exceeding the corresponding average of Eurozone) and the increase in their share of world exports, the persistent current account deficit reflects the low structural competitiveness of the Greek economy and the inability to attract foreign capital, as well as the economy's dependence on imports of goods. Non-performing loans and high private debt. Although a significant consolidation of Greek banks' loan portfolios has been achieved, the NPL ratio remains significantly higher than the European average, negatively affecting the quality of their capital. After all, regardless of who manages it, the Private debt remains high, limiting the potential for new borrowing and investment. Additional risks to banks' asset quality over the medium term are posed by pressure on household and corporate income from high inflation and rising interest rates. Rising interest rates boost Over the medium term, however, banks' profitability may affect credit risk costs, operating costs and liquidity raising costs. Sustainable profitability growth requires an increase in credit growth, which is associated with an increase in demand for loans, which is discouraged by rising interest rates. High unemployment. Unemployment in Greece remains very high compared to the European average, especially among young people, women and the long-term unemployed. At the same time, labour market participation remains relatively low and skills are mismatched. To some extent, the above challenges are the result of structural weaknesses of the Greek economy that have not yet been effectively addressed, thus acting as a brake on growth, reducing the investment gap, further increasing exports and attracting foreign direct investment, consolidating private debt and reducing structural unemployment. In the case of Greece, despite the progress made, we recognise remaining distortions of competition in goods and services markets, the lack of an integrated land registry, the low quality of governance institutions and the low effectiveness and efficiency of public administration, obstacles to doing business, delays in the administration of justice, weaknesses in the education system and deficiencies in the "knowledge triangle". In order to address the structural weaknesses of the Greek economy and thus lay the foundations for correcting macroeconomic imbalances, targeted interventions are needed as part of a long-term and ambitious reform programme. The reform and investment programme outlined in the national Recovery and Resilience Plan is in this direction, as it includes, inter alia, structural actions to improve the efficiency of the judicial system and modernisation of public administration. At the same time, it provides for actions that facilitate the green and digital transitions, such as energy upgrading of buildings, investments in 50 networks, digital transformation of the state, etc. Therefore, the timely and full implementation of the plan, making the best use of available European funds, emerges as a key policy priority. As regards NPLs in particular, steps towards a full consolidation of the loan portfolio of Greek banks and the effective management of private debt by loan and credit servicing companies should continue. I note that a smooth resolution of the private debt problem requires well-functioning institutions such as the judicial system. This underlines the interaction of different policy areas and the importance of targeted structural measures. At the same time, all stakeholders should be vigilant in order to prevent a new generation of NPLs from emerging as a result of households and businesses making it difficult to meet their debt obligations. The special arrangements put in place by the Greek systemic banks to facilitate vulnerable and consistent borrowers are in the right direction. Adherence to fiscal, investment and structural targets and the successful handling of structural challenges will consolidate the credibility of Greece's economic policy, safeguarding the hard-won trust of our European partners and markets, as well as of citizens. Ladies and gentlemen, Greece and Cyprus have been inextricably linked over the centuries through their common history and language. They are also linked by a common European identity and membership of the euro area. I am convinced that this allows us to face the serious challenges of the present and the future, just as we faced the crises of the recent past. The common goal and priority of the two countries is the active participation in the European dialogue for the formulation of new policies and actions in Europe. We must and can contribute to institutional developments in the EU in a way that focuses primarily on what we identify as common goals, and not by highlighting what differentiates us, in a spirit of consensus and cooperation. Thank you.

Title: Keynote speech by Dimitris Malliaropulos, Chief Economist and Director of Economic Analysis and Research of the Bank of Greece, at the World Banking Forum, titled: Banking Around the World Today
text: Keynote speech by Dimitris Malliaropulos, Chief Economist and Director of Economic Analysis and Research of the Bank of Greece, at the World Banking Forum, titled: Banking Around the World Today 21/09/2023 - Speeches It is a great pleasure to participate in this years summer event by the World Banking Forum, hosted in a city with a long history in trade and financial activities. Throughout the decades, banks around the world have experienced major transformations to keep pace with changing economic needs, often the result of various crises. Today is no different, although several forces including globalisation and digitalisation, have increased the complexity of the challenges, as well as the uncertainty about the outcomes. Today the banking industry is facing challenging macroeconomic conditions, following multiple supply (and demand) shocks that hit the global economy, combined with profound structural shifts relating to the green and digital transitions. In what follows, I will discuss in more detail the implications of the global macro-financial environment for banks, touching upon the lessons learnt from the recent bank episode in the US, before I move to the state and prospects of European banking amid the new geo-political realities. Finally, I will share with you my take on the most pertinent structural issues banks are likely to confront in the next five years. The current macro-financial environment faced by banks can be summarised in three elements: economic slowdown, persistent inflation and, probably, high interest rates for longer. Over the past three years, our economies have been hit by a back-to-back triple shock: the pandemic, the war in Ukraine and an energy/cost-of-living crisis. The compounded effect of these shocks has been significant, pushing economic activity down and prices up. To support incomes, governments increased spending, which together with excess post- pandemic private savings and a resilient labour market, have sustained aggregate demand. To tame very high inflation, central banks globally embarked on an unprecedented, synchronised and aggressive tightening of monetary policy. Since the start of the recent tightening cycle and in about one and a half years, the fed funds rate has increased by 525 basis points, the Bank of Englands official rate by 515 and the ECBs deposit facility rate by 450 basis points. As a result of monetary policy tightening, lower energy prices and a normalisation of supply chains, headline inflation has abated, but underlying inflationary pressures remain elevated and persistent. Meanwhile, activity has softened, but a hard landing has been avoided, at least for now. Looking ahead, global GDP growth is forecast by the IMF[1 ] to weaken to 3% in 2023 and 2024, under the weight of still high inflation and tighter monetary and financial conditions. This growth is well below the historical average of 3.8% in 2000-2019. It also masks significant regional divergences, with a pronounced deceleration in advanced economies, but brighter spots in emerging markets. Chinas more-subdued-than-expected recovery poses a downside risk to global growth. Global headline inflation is set to fall to 6.8% in 2023 and 5.2% in 2024, while core inflation is expected to decline more gradually. Its persistence reflects the lagged pass-through of past shocks, high corporate profit margins, and strong nominal wage increases, which combined with weak productivity growth lifts unit labour costs. Services are labour-intensive but also less sensitive to interest rates, increasing the lag and decreasing the efficiency of monetary policy transmission. However, to date, wage-price spirals do not appear to have materialised in the average advanced economy, while longer- term inflation expectations remain anchored. If there is one thing characterising the current macroeconomic environment, that is uncertainty around the global growth prospects and the disinflation process, even in the absence of additional shocks. Elevated and multi-layered uncertainty complicates the task of central banks. For example, there is still debate on the drivers of inflation, whether these are dominated by supply or demand factors, their dynamics and cross-sectional price spillovers. Another area of uncertainty relates to wage developments and second-round effects on inflation. Is the tightness in the labour market cyclical, due to supply and demand dislocations caused by the pandemic, or more structural due to demographics and skill mismatches? How strong will nominal wage demands be to compensate for real wage losses and to what extent will high profit margins absorb wage increases? Can we engineer a soft landing, where labour market rebalances through a decline in excess labour demand rather than a large increase in unemployment? Do we account for non-linearities in the relationship between inflation and labour market slack and how important are they in explaining the recent surge in inflation?[2] And to complicate policy further, let us not forget that the levels of neutral interest rates and the lags of monetary policy transmission to the real economy are difficult to estimate with confidence. Thus, there is always uncertainty about the precise level of the required monetary policy tightening, in real time, and how it affects economic activity and inflation. To mitigate the uncertainty surrounding the medium-term outlook, the ECB has made future decisions contingent on three criteria: the inflation outlook, the dynamics of underlying inflation and the strength of monetary policy transmission. In the current environment, this means, quoting ECB President Christine Lagarde at the 2023 Jackson Hole meeting setting interest rates at sufficiently restrictive levels for as long as necessary to achieve a timely return of inflation to our 2% medium-term target.[3] In the same vein, Fed Chair Jay Powell noted that we are prepared to raise rates further if appropriate, and intend to hold policy at a restrictive level until we are confident that inflation is moving sustainably down toward our objective. In other words, interest rates are likely to be higher on average through the course of the cycle. Higher interest rates are affecting banks balance sheets. On the asset side, credit expansion to households and corporates has slowed sharply amid tighter lending standards and reduced loan demand. Bank lending surveys in the US and Europe suggest that credit growth will remain sluggish in coming months. Banks higher risk perceptions and lower risk tolerance continued to be the most significant factors contributing to the tightening. Asset quality has also deteriorated amid higher debt servicing burdens and rising debt distress and defaults among borrowers, adding pressure on banks earnings and impairment costs. The fact that the bulk of new term loans to non-financial corporations are at a variable rate in many advanced economies, including the euro area, increases credit risk at this juncture. In the EU, as loans under the various national COVID-19 guarantee schemes mature over the coming months/years, bankruptcy declarations may increase further.[4] On the liability side, banks cost of financing, including through bond issuance, has gone up and we might not get back to the low levels of yields that preceded the pandemic for some time to come. Deposits have also shifted from current accounts into higher-yielding time deposits, at a record rate in the euro area.[5] Yet, as the interest rate pass-through on loans still significantly exceeds the pass-through on deposits in the EU and the US, net interest income continues to support bank profitability.[6] This trend could reverse as excess liquidity, relating to past QE and low- cost re-financing operations, dries up and bank competition for deposits increases. The bank failures in the US and Switzerland in the first half of the year reminded us that shocks in the banking system can emerge at any time, the root cause being poorly managed leverage. They also highlighted the role of interest rate risk in the financial system. Banks hold large quantities of sovereign debt, with exposures increasing after the pandemic along with the risk of bank-sovereign doom loops. Losses on government bond holdings and other interest rate sensitive exposures could sap banks capital and trigger bank runs, as the SVB failure illustrated. Problems could be compounded if sovereigns creditworthiness was downgraded. From a policy perspective, the banking turmoil highlighted the importance of post-GFC financial sector reforms for the resilience of EU banks to shocks and contagion. The US regional banking distress has not materially spilt over to euro area banks despite an incomplete banking union and lower deposit insurance levels. This reflects stickier deposits, more limited scope for unrecognised mark-to-market losses, less acute commercial real estate concerns, and less significant banks being a smaller universe. More generally, euro area banks score better on several measures of solvency, liquidity and funding stability compared to the US ones.[7] Yet, there remains room for improvement and harmonisation to build a crisis management framework suited for all types of banks operating in the EU, including for small and medium- sized banks. The latest proposals by the European Commission for a consistent and effective framework for managing banks in distress is a critical part of the Banking Union. However, the onus for building resilience and liquidity preparedness sits first and foremost with the financial institutions; for example, improve stress testing and risk management practices to include correlated risk, and increase transparency and information-sharing on exposures. The event has also illustrated that banks need to be mindful of the role of technology and social media in deposit runs and the dangers from exposure to crypto-assets, and protect themselves accordingly. Overall, the EU banking sector remains robust, based on the results of the 2023 stress tests published by the European Banking Authority (EBA) and the ECB in July.[8] Resilience reflects banks robust capital position, and the positive impact of significantly higher net interest margins on bank profits so far. However, the EBA stressed the importance of remaining vigilant and called for both supervisors and banks to be prepared for a possible worsening of economic conditions. It is clear that financial stability risks from asset repricing are growing. In this context, I would like to highlight the importance of geopolitical tensions. The unprecedented shocks that hit recently the global economy following Russias war in Ukraine have exacerbated geoeconomic rivalries and prompted governments to impose trade restrictions and adopt policies that reduce their countries external trade dependence, especially in sectors of strategic importance. In addition, multinational firms are increasingly adopting risk diversification policies, such as near/ friend/re-shoring, to increase their resilience of their global supply chains to shocks. In this new global map, the future of global trade integration looks increasingly uncertain. Trade fragmentation may have (potentially important) implications for the global economy in terms of volatility, economic growth and inflation, but it will also affect financial markets and cross-border banking. As the ECB recently noted, a potential intensification of geopolitical tensions may further increase repricing risks in financial markets.[9] As the world becomes more geo-economically fragmented, cross-border banking would become more difficult, more local and more costly. For example, the war in Ukraine or the US-China conflict (although they have a limited direct impact on European banks) are adding pressures that are speeding up financial fragmentation regionally and globally. The implications for financial stability could be significant. These include potential capital flow reversals, disruptions of cross-border payments, impact on banks funding costs, profitability, and credit provision, and more limited opportunities for global risk diversification. [10] In the EU the answer is to complete the Banking Union. Without this, times of stress will always raise fragmentation risks. In the next five years, what are the challenges that banks in the world will be facing? I would like to focus on three challenges: the increasing role of non-bank financial intermediaries, climate-related financial issues and digital transformation. The structure of the global financial system has changed in the last decade. Low interest rates, easy liquidity and lighter regulation compared to banks, have supported a rapid expansion of non-bank financial intermediaries (NBFIs), which now hold almost 50% of global financial assets, a larger share compared to that of banks.[11] It is unclear how higher policy rates will be transmitted through the NBFIs, since many have not been stress-tested for an interest-rate or a cash-flow (recession) shock. There is also lack of granular and reliable data to monitor the sector as a whole. A major concern of policymakers and investors is the rising interconnectedness of NBFIs with banks, both as lenders and borrowers. The Fed in its latest Financial Stability Report shows that US banks have 2 trillion of credit commitments outstanding to global NBFIs, while the ECB and the Bank of England highlight the systemic risks from NFBIs providing funding to the banks.[12] The ECB also highlights in its Financial Stability Report, May 2023, that any turmoil in the NBFI sector is likely to disproportionately affect large, complex, systemically important banks. For example, bond market turbulence could trigger liquidity stress in some NBFIs like hedge funds and then spill over to the whole ecosystem as they sell off their assets, reducing their prices, and withdraw funding from one another. Aside financial stability risks, banks could also face more competition from non- banks in attracting savings and providing credit, necessitating tighter regulation of non-banks to ensure a level-playing field. That said, the collaboration with FinTech startups and other technology providers poses an opportunity for banks to tap specialised expertise, access innovative products and realise efficiency gains. The second set of challenges banks will face relates to climate change. This expands from proper measurement and hedging against climate-related financial risks on banks balance sheets to financing the vast investments required for climate mitigation and adaptation. There is a need for sustainable finance products, such as green loans and bonds, and funds with environmental, social and governance standards. The latest ECBs climate stress tests show that an accelerated green transition significantly reduces credit risk for banks. Finally, let me touch upon the multi-dimensional challenge of digital transformation. Banks are called to adjust their business models, operations, products and services to the new digital realities. Physical networks are scaled back in favour of e-banking and e-branches, which in turn increases cyber-threats. Large parts of the front-end of banking are now self-driven via apps, while large parts of the back-end are now composed of third-party providers of cloud computing.[13] Digital neo-banks, such as N26 and Revolut, and big tech companies challenge incumbents. Blockchain technologies enable the introduction of digital currencies, including those by central banks, making payments faster and cheaper. Also, data is turning into a product that has the potential to transform the foundations of banking. The world is changing and along with it banking. The challenges and risks faced by banks today are multiple and complex, stemming from a geo-economic environment in transition, technological disruptions and regulatory reform. The banking sector must cope with lower growth, persistent inflation, higher interest rates and growing fragmentation. These are great challenges. Banks would need to adapt strategically by enhancing their financial, technical and business capabilities to navigate through heightened uncertainty, compete, grow and remain profitable and relevant in the new global landscape. Thank you! [1] IMF, World Economic Outlook Update July 2023. [2] The relationship between labour market slack and inflation is likely nonlinear, steepening in a tight labour market. This means that a small change in labour market tightness could result in a more substantial change in inflation. It is difficult to know with precision how steep that relationship is in real time or how it might evolve as labour market tightness changes.
