Title: Speech by Governor Yannis Stournaras: "The role of small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in the Greek Economy" at the conference organized by GSEVEE and EEA: "The challenges of small businesses in a changing economic environment"
text: Giannis_Stournaras_45191_Greek Speech by Governor Yannis Stournaras: role of small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in the Greek Economy" at the conference organized by GSEVEE and the EEA: "The challenges of small businesses in a changing economic environment' 22/09/2023 - Speeches  The participation of SMEs in the Greek economy SMEs are the main basis of the economy, both at national and European level. In Greece in 2022, SMEs were 731,829 and constituted 99.9% of enterprises in the non-financial sector, employed 83.5% of employees or 2.2 million people and generated 57% of value added or 34.8 billion. euro[1]. Due to their increased weight in the economic and social fabric, they are of key importance for Greece's twin transition to a green and digital economy. However, SMEs differ significantly from each other. They range from liberal professions and micro-enterprises in the service sector to medium-sized industrial enterprises, and from traditional crafts to high-tech start-ups. The dominant sector of activity of SMEs in Greece, including sole proprietorships, is wholesale and retail trade, followed by professional and technical services, accommodation, construction and transportation and storage. The share of micro-enterprises (with less than 10 people) in employment is higher in Greece than in the EU. Specifically, in Greece 94.5% of enterprises are micro and employ 55.8% of employees and generate 30.6% of value added[2], The greater presence of micro-enterprises in Greece is also linked to the large number of self-employed who constitute about 30% of the employed. The extensive presence of one-person and micro-enterprises is a dominant and problematic feature, as productivity in these enterprises is generally low and below the European average. However, although the small size of SMEs is generally considered problematic, in some cases it can be an advantage. For example, in high-tech activities, the presence of many small enterprises is expected and useful when they are at an early stage of the scientific and business cycle that allows flexibility, with a view to growth thereafter, or interconnection with other enterprises (see Pissarides Report, 2020)[3], At the same time, in more traditional sectors such as retail, tourism, Catering, culture and entertainment, the presence of small businesses with special characteristics can help in quality specialization and provide significant value. According to a recent study by the European Commission (2023), 69.1% of SMEs[4] in Greece are active in low-knowledge-intensive service sectors and low-tech manufacturing, employ 76.6% of employees and generate 66.3% of the added value of SMEs[5], Therefore, in contrast to the European average[6], Greek SMEs are more active in service and manufacturing sectors with low technological and cognitive content, This negatively affects the productivity of the Greek economy and limits the production and export capabilities of technology and knowledge-intensive products and services. Nevertheless, as the European Commission (2023) points out, Greece has made significant steps forward in terms of innovation, encouraging the circular economy, costs of starting a business and costs of resolving insolvency[G].  The main challenges faced by SMEs Since the beginning of 2020, due to the Oonia-19 pandemic, but also due to the Russian invasion of Ukraine, SMEs have faced unprecedented economic uncertainty. Moreover, in 2021-2022, SMEs faced difficulties in recruiting new staff to respond to an unexpectedly strong recovery in demand, while inflation rates increased drastically, particularly in 2022, also causing increases in interest rates, which in turn reduces access to finance. Increased energy costs and increased raw material prices are putting additional pressure on businesses. Rising costs for SMEs increase the likelihood that they will face larger delays in paying their invoices, which, combined with difficulties in accessing finance and increased interest rates, can lead to more bankruptcies. At the same time, the increase in interest rates to counter rising inflation reduces expectations of new investment, especially by SMEs. According to a study by the European Commission[8] , an increase of one percentage point in interest rates was found to reduce the likelihood of SMEs reporting positive investment expectations by 0.83 percentage points compared to 0.65 for large companies. The impact on business profitability of rising inflation is divided into short- and medium-term: inflation first reduces profitability as production costs rise, but then increases it when firms pass costs on to consumers. The ability of businesses to pass on costs varies greatly and depends on their position in the value chain, how flexible demand for specific products is to price changes, types of customers, size and ecosystem to which the business belongs. Key indications suggest that SMEs are less likely to pass on costs to the final consumer than large companies, thereby eroding their profit margins. In addition to dealing with extremely extreme economic conditions over the past two years, Greek SMEs are facing additional significant challenges, which are also related to the structural characteristics of the Greek economy and the necessity of the green and digital transition.  Increased energy costs and shortages in know-how, expertise and staff training are much more visible in Greek SMEs, due to their very small size. Due to their small size, Greek SMEs are less likely to engage in international trade as exporters. According to a survey by the European Investment Bank (EIB, 2022)[9], large companies are more likely to be both exporters and importers than SMEs (65% vs. 44%).  Red tape, high taxation and generally the business environment and regulatory constraints are a major obstacle for 54% of businesses compared to 28% in the EU[10];  The digitisation of SMEs is below the European average based on the OMEGA8I index, with 39% of SMEs compared to 55% in the EU having a basic level of digitalisation and 17% vs 34% in the EU using cloud computing services. According to a survey by the National Documentation Centre (EKT 2022)[11], large enterprises attach greater importance to digital transformation, in particular 54.4% of large enterprises compared to only 39.9% of SMEs consider digital transformation to be a very important strategy for developing their activities[12]. this is linked to the lack of digital skills of executives and employees of SMEs. At the same time, as a result of a lack of digital skills, they are very vulnerable to cyber threats. SMEs also face difficulties in protecting their investments in research and development due to lack of information on relevant national and European legislation.  The speed of transition to the green economy through decisions adopted at European level (e.g. on electromobility) limits the ability of many SMEs to adapt to the economy (e.g. car repair shops). The problem is exacerbated by the small size of Greek businesses and the lack of economies of scale to implement the required investments and the recruitment of appropriately qualified personnel. According to an EIB survey (2022), large companies are more likely than SMEs to have implemented investments or measures to address the risk of catastrophe due to climate change, limiting greenhouse gas emissions and energy efficiency. The proposed national and European solutions focus mainly on the utilization of European programs for the partial subsidization of green entrepreneurship actions. However, a prerequisite for the implementation of these actions is the existence of minimum own funds, information on the available European programmes, but also the existence of appropriate staff to manage these programmes[13].  Moreover, Greek businesses are characterized by low dynamism as the rate at which businesses open and close is low, especially in the housing and food service sectors, where the share of SMEs is particularly high. This is also related to the fact that the majority of start-ups are still set up for purely livelihood reasons in the context of a lack of alternatives and for reasons of continuing the economic tradition and not As a result, the share of SMEs that produce innovation themselves and adopt innovation-technologies from abroad to maintain their market position in Greek industry stands at 43% compared to 50.4% in the EU[]4].Lower dynamism usually reflects limited innovation, low productivity and sluggish employment growth. - Greek companies use internal capital to finance investments to a greater extent than European companies (75% vs. 65% - EIB, 2022). This phenomenon is more pronounced in SMEs (81%) than in large enterprises (70%). Also, according to the same survey, the share of enterprises facing financing constraints stands at 16% in Greece compared to 6.2% in the EU, while especially in SMEs this percentage rises to 19.1%. Despite the improvement in the availability of external financing in 2022 according to the 8GNI survey conducted by the EU and the ECB, Greek SMEs lag behind the European average in access to finance, while the problem is particularly acute in the categories of micro and small enterprises. The problem concerns both the volume of financing, given the difficulty of SMEs to access alternative financing other than banking, and the cost of financing, as the rise in monetary policy rates and the higher NPL ratio recorded in the loan portfolio of SMEs lead to increased borrowing costs[15]. both for the continuation of their operation and for the implementation of investments in areas such as research and development, innovation, skills development of human resources and green and digital transformation, as well as the undertaking of export activity. Given that the cost of undertaking these actions is too high for a small business, it is crucial that it has access to sources of external financing either from the banking system or from the capital market. However, at all stages of development, small businesses face greater financing difficulties than large companies.Indicatively, in the case of young entrepreneurs and start-ups, this can be due to several reasons: e.g. they do not have a proven track record of financial performance, they do not have collateral or investors do not have information to assess their credit risk or the value of intangibles their assets. As a result, they are trapped in small-scale operation and inefficient business practices, resulting in many of them operating in the informal economy, resulting in increased tax evasion. However, even in the case of small and medium-sized enterprises that have access to finance, their lending rates are particularly high in the Greek case, both in relation to the lending rates of large enterprises, and compared to other countries of the EU-27 and the euro area (EBA, 2022)[16],Typically, the difference between the average interest rate on bank loans above 1 million. Related to the financing difficulties is the significant lack of sufficient knowledge of SMEs on financial issues, due to a lack of qualified executives, which directly affect management decisions at company level, which directly affect management decisions at company level. in terms of financing, credit management, making use of available European programmes and implementing future investments[17].  Proposals for national and European policies to support SMEs Next, I will refer to interventions to support SMEs, which I believe should be implemented in four main areas.  Facilitating access to finance  Utilization of national and European financial instruments to enhance bank financing of SMEs According to Bank of Greece data[18], large corporations continue to outperform the amount of borrowing money they raise from the banking system, a trend that is also observed in many countries internationally[19]. Therefore, bank financing of SMEs could be enhanced by further utilizing national and European financial instruments. In recent years, the contribution of the financial instruments of domestic and international development agencies, such as the European Investment Bank (EIB), the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EIB) and the Hellenic Development Bank (EBA), to the credit expansion of SMEs has been significant. In particular, in the three-year period 2020-2022, about half of bank loans to SMEs were supported by European or state support programs, a proportion much higher than for all businesses. In the first half of 2023, disbursements of business loans to SMEs linked to financial instruments amounted to approximately 600 million. They accounted for almost a quarter of new fixed-term loans to SMEs compared to only 10% for all businesses. Finally, the importance of capital strengthening and more generally the resolution of so-called non-systemic banks, including cooperative banks, which could have a more active role in financing SMEs, should be stressed.  Diversification of funding sources The diversification of funding sources by exploiting capital markets, as well as equity schemes such as those in high-tech start-ups) and Rithith ecaig (investing in companies not listed on the stock exchange), crowdfunding, the operation of business angels (idipecece access to finance. However, as pointed out in the Pissarides Report (2020), an improvement in the quality of financial statements and overall corporate governance is needed to overcome asymmetric information problems that prevent potentially interested investors from entering. In addition, the expansion of funding supported by micro-credits must be accelerated. The microfinance sector in Greece is starting, as three institutions have already been licensed by the Bank of Greece, while the Hellenic Development Bank plays an active role in capital financing Investment by designing and offering programs, two of which supported by resources from the Recovery and Resilience Facility[20].  Use and better coordination of available European funds Given the rise in interest rates, entrepreneurs should also make use of the resources available from European programmes. In this context, domestic businesses are already supported by low-interest loans granted under the Recovery and Resilience Facility (JRC). It is recalled that the minimum interest rate for granting loans of the Recovery Fund and Resilience (RRF) for small and micro enterprises remains at 0.35%, while for the rest of the enterprises as of 24 October 2022 it stood at 1%[21], The particularly beneficial financing conditions are reflected in the demand of SMEs for these loans, as until the beginning of June out of the total number of investment projects submitted to the loan arm of the National Recovery and Resilience Plan Greece 2.0 61% (260 out of 425) was submitted by micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). In the same direction, the conclusions of a recent EIB survey indicate that half of SMEs with active investment plans target or already use UDF resources. In addition to the resources of the Recovery and Resilience Facility, use should be made of the resources of the European Structural Funds and the EINH, which aims to mobilise private resources to stimulate private investment. At the same time, however, additional actions to support SMEs should be considered through KERonnotei, the European Economic Fund and the Euratom Regulatory Proposal proposed by the Commission to strengthen industry. However, given that European resources directed to SMEs are often fragmented, the establishment of a National Strategy for SMEs and Entrepreneurship[22] (equivalent to the National Industrial Strategy) is required, within the framework of which the investment priorities of the NSRF and the National Recovery and Resilience Plan should be included. This will allow better coordination of co-funded actions at the policy design stage, maximising the impact of co-funded European programmes. It should be noted that assessing the impact of public support programmes is key to fine-tuning their design and evaluating their performance[23]. In addition to the above, given that Greek SMEs in many cases lack sufficient knowledge on important financial issues (due to lack of specialized staff), it is necessary to implement targeted actions upgrading financial education and facilitating accessibility to information on available sources of finance for SMEs[24]; 3.2. Improving the business environment, reducing administrative burdens, improving market access and ensuring a level playing field Compliance with regulations, standards and administrative formalities affects SMEs more than larger enterprises due to their limited financial and human resources. As the European Commission has shown[25], on average, a large company spends 1 per employee to comply with regulation, a medium-sized company spends around 4 and a small business spends up to 10. Therefore, emphasis should be placed on cutting red tape by reducing reporting and data obligations, evaluating legislative proposals in terms of potential impacts on SMEs and overall better regulation to reduce administrative burdens. In this context, innovative solutions through a 'protected regulatory environment' should also be considered. This provides up-to-date information to regulators and supervisors, as well as experience with new technologies, while enabling policy experimentation. It is noted that some Member States have already experimented with this method with regard to innovative financial services. Overall, a balanced, simplified and predictable regulatory and fiscal framework including tax relief measures, especially for cross-border activities, as well as simpler and predictable state aid rules will help strengthen SMEs' competitiveness and incentivise investment in green and digital projects, job creation as well as increased cooperation between large companies and SMEs. At the same time, facilitating SMEs' access to markets inside and outside the EU through a single set of tax rules, removing trade barriers and better information on trade and customs procedures and formalities in third countries and reducing administrative costs of exports as well as enhancing cooperation between businesses in creating export value chains or clusters will further strengthen expansion prospects and SME growth[26],  Facilitating the green and digital transitions, social entrepreneurship and access to qualified staff Many SMEs face significant difficulties in transitioning to more sustainable business models. One third of SMEs in the EU report that they need to carry out complex administrative and legal procedures to make their business more resource efficient[27]; In view of this, interventions are needed[28]:  Support SMEs with organized and systematic information and training in order to understand environmental risks and incorporate the logic and rules of corporate sustainability and transparency.  Improvement of the institutional and legal framework, aiming at promoting the green economy and green entrepreneurship.  Financial support, measures can include subsidies, tax breaks, credits for small businesses as well as improving the connection of SMEs to the financial system. The development of sustainable finance tools that will respond to the needs and specificities of SMEs is a prerequisite for a just green transition and sustainable and inclusive growth. Public funds should also be directed towards enhancing the use of digital technologies, such as intelligence and artificial intelligence, cloud computing and high-performance computing, as they can offer significant opportunities for SMEs to improve the efficiency of production processes and the capacity to innovate in products and business models and to enhance their competitiveness and contribute to their growth them[29]. In this context, emphasis should also be placed on R&D programmes between universities, public research bodies and private enterprises, as well as facilitating the diffusion of knowledge from academia to business. At the same time, measures are needed to protect SMEs' investments in research and development. This requires simplifying intellectual property registration procedures, facilitating access to strategic advice on intellectual property issues and simplifying the use of intellectual property as a lever to access finance. At the same time, actions are needed to strengthen the social entrepreneurship of SMEs, i.e. to support the social inclusion and economic advancement of people coming from vulnerable groups of the population, as well as new initiatives and incentives at national and European level to further help SMEs recruit, train and retain a skilled workforce and overall upgrade the skills of SMEs and entrepreneurs[30],  Combating late payment With the pandemic and the now rising cost of energy and raw materials, the number of tariffs paid late is increasing significantly. Despite the relevant EU Directive[31], less than 40% of payments in the EU  whether by public authorities or businesses  are made within the contractual deadline. Late payments jeopardise SMEs' liquidity and sometimes their existence[32]. In addition, late payments prevent SMEs from investing, promoting their green and digital transformation and hiring more employees. Therefore, a stronger framework, also making use of digital tools, is needed, which could potentially include capping late payments between businesses, such as for the public sector, introducing stronger enforcement and monitoring obligations, providing SMEs with effective dispute resolution tools and alternative mediation mechanisms, preventing abuses and unfair practices. In closing, I would like to point out that the growth of the Greek economy is directly intertwined with the growth and prosperity of SMEs. The effort for the green and digital transition to a new growth model with emphasis on entrepreneurship and extroversion requires the support of SMEs with new national and European initiatives, the outline of which I described earlier. The immediate priority is to make timely use of available European funds, especially those related to the Recovery and Resilience Facility, to boost investments in human capital, green energy and digital technologies. In the context of European actions, it is necessary to implement the European Commission's proposal for the creation of a "Relief Package" for SMEs (8ME Ethivi ArthoKasb). The EIB lends to financial intermediaries - banks, leasing companies or other financial institutions - on more favourable market terms, either directly or indirectly (through public institutions). Title: Speech by Bank of Greece Governor Yannis Stournaras on "The role of industry in Greece's economic development" at the Open Event of the SBSE Annual General Meeting
text: Address by the Governor of the Bank of Yannis Stournaras on the subject: "The Role of industry in economic development of Greece", at the Open Event within the framework of the Annual Ordinary General Assembly of SBSE 29/09/2023 - Speeches  The contribution of industry to the Greek economy  Resilience and dynamic recovery of Greek industry The Greek industry recorded a significant recovery in the period 2017-2022, after a period of severe recession, 2011-2015. In fact, this recovery was greater than that of the economy as a whole. Industrial production, and manufacturing production in particular, recorded high growth rates, even during the pandemic crisis, resulting in an increased share of industry in the total output of the economy. In particular, real gross value added (GVA) in manufacturing increased on average by 4% over the period 2017-2019 and recorded even higher growth in 2020 (7.5%) and 2021 (12.1%). In 2022, growth in the manufacturing sector continued, but at a slower pace (4.5%). The share of industry's GVA in the total GVA of the economy increased particularly in the period 2020-2022, reaching 17% in 2022, from 13.8% in 2019. However, the share of industrial GVA (17%) in the total GVA of the economy, and in particular that of manufacturing (10%), lags behind that of the euro area in 2022 (20% and 16.5%, respectively). The strong growth in manufacturing over the period 2017-2021 was accompanied by an increase in total factor productivity and an increase in labour productivity. The most dynamic sectors of manufacturing in terms of growth and productivity that emerged were "petroleum products", "computer manufacturing", "manufacture of motor vehicles", "manufacture of machinery and equipment", "manufacture of metal products" and "manufacture of basic pharmaceutical products".  Increasing investment and extroversion The recovery in manufacturing production is reflected in the increased investments made, especially in 2021 (16.5% compared to 2020 and 8.1% compared to 2019). As a result, the level of investment in manufacturing in 2021 accounted for 9.8% of total investment in the economy. The sectors that absorbed the highest investment were: "food-beverages-tobacco", "petroleum products", "base metals and manufacture of metal products", manufacture of basic pharmaceuticals, "manufacture of plastic products and production of non-metallic mineral products", "chemicals" and "wood and paper industry". Also, R&D investment in manufacturing accounted for 34.2% of total private R&D investment in 2021. The recovery of the manufacturing sector and the increase in its productivity are associated with a significant increase in its export performance. Specifically, export performance in manufacturing, defined as the ratio of exports in manufacturing to total gross product of manufacturing, increased from 55.3% on average in the period 2017-2020 to 61% in 2021. - Continue industrial production growth in 2023 and maintain positive expectations Industrial production, after increasing by 2.3% in 2022, continued to move marginally upwards (0.7%) also in the period January-July 2023, mainly due to the strong increase in manufacturing production (4.2%). Expectations in the industrial sector are improved (in the period January-August 2023) according to the Economic Sentiment Index (E8I) compiled by the European Commission. While the PMI index in August 2023 remained above 50 (as of February 2023), implying a strengthening of manufacturing activity, in contrast to the path of the PMI index for the euro area indicating a contraction in activity.  Weaknesses and challenges of Greek industry Greek companies have been smaller over time than their European counterparts.[1] Specifically, the average industrial enterprise in Greece employed about 5-6 workers in the period 2011-2018 compared to about 15 that was the European average. This is linked to the inability to develop economies of scale, the difficulty in finding financing, as well as the difficulty of expanding into new markets. These factors reduce the productivity and competitiveness of Greek enterprises. During the debt crisis, businesses made a significant reduction in investment, due to increased uncertainty and reduced demand. As a consequence, Industrial investment was limited to low levels, resulting in a low degree of renewal of production equipment and processes and methods of production, storage and distribution of products and services. [2] Although in the last decade in Greece the share of people with a tertiary education degree has increased by 11.5 percentage points, the skills of human resources are still at low levels compared to the EU.[3] Therefore, the education and training system does not match the degree desired by the needs of the labour market. At the same time, apart from the importance of developing human capital, its economically rational distribution is also extremely important, as Greece has the highest rate of overtraining in the OECD (28%, compared to 11% which is the average of OECD countries). The skills mismatch in the Greek labour market has multiple consequences. Overskilled workers feel less job satisfaction, They receive a lower salary than workers with similar skills, while businesses lack a talented workforce. Matching skills correctly is particularly important in an economy that has lost a significant part of its workforce due to migration and can help boost productivity. Greece has the lowest average score in the Global Management Survey in a sample of selected OECD economies, which undermines the productivity of Greek industrial enterprises. In particular, Greek companies have the lowest performance in terms of human resources management, planning, employee supervision, as well as the development of synergies, dialogue and cooperation. On the contrary, they tend to do better at taking decisions, possibly by just one person. The above clearly indicates the central role played by the family character of the majority of Greek businesses, where the corporate culture revolves around the founder, with little room for talent development, judgment and discretion by employees. Workers in Greek companies also show the lowest levels of autonomy in the OECD, a sign of low confidence. Greece ranks low in the European Innovation Index. In addition, a significant shortfall is also recorded in expenditure by enterprises for R&D, with Greek companies spending 0.59% of HEII for 2019 compared to European companies spending 1.42% of GDP for the same year. This undermines the innovation capacity of Greek industry, limiting its ability to compete with other European countries. The digital transformation of the economy and businesses in the country is moving faster than in the past, but not yet enough to close the gap with the EU. According to data from the 2018-2020 survey (018), in the Industry sector, the percentage of innovative enterprises stands at 72.1%, compared to 62.4% in the period 2016-2018, showing an increase of 9.7 percentage points. The rate of innovation and the degree of cooperation for the development of innovative activities increases with the increase in the size of the enterprise, as large companies can use internal capital, they have access to additional sources of finance and can take advantage of economies of scale to promote R&D. Despite progress in recent years, the digital intensity index for enterprises in the manufacturing sector with more than 10 employees (see Eu8l3l) was, in 2022, 12.6% in Greece, compared to 24.4% for the euro area. Important challenges remain both the adoption of an integrated strategy to improve the coordination of relevant public policies and the reversal of the reluctance of many businesses to adopt cutting-edge technologies and substitute obsolete ones administrative practices.[5] As a result, Greece continues to perform poorly in integrating digital technologies based on OMEGA8I (2021) data. In particular, it ranks 21st in the EU in terms of digital skills, with a low share of employed ICT specialists, 2%, compared to 4.3% in the EU; while only 12% of Greek companies offered digital skills training programs to their employees compared to the EU average of 20%. Greece is also characterised by poor ICT infrastructure and low connectivity performance, placing it 27th in the EU. Businesses show slow integration of digital technologies, resulting in Greece being in 22nd place in the EU, with low performance especially in e-commerce and the integration of advanced technologies (e.g. cloud computing, artificial intelligence, etc.) by businesses. Finally, despite the progress recorded in the digitalisation of public administration, Greece ranks 26th in the EU in terms of digital public services, lagging significantly behind digital public services to businesses, with a performance of 54 compared to the EU average of 84. Additional challenges for Greek industry are, among others, the lack of competitive energy costs with the domestic wholesale electricity price being higher compared to other European countries, which existed before the energy crisis, the loss of scientific personnel to foreign countries due to the "Land Administration", and the weaknesses in the licensing and siting framework of businesses due to the lack of defined land uses.  Policy recommendations Greece needs to move quickly with a realistic and coherent industrial policy, which will create conditions for a competitive industry that innovates, produces, exports, generates incomes and new high-paid jobs. Today, the challenge of moving from a low-skilled, low-tech-intensive economy to a medium- and high-tech-intensive economy is enormous, as is strengthening Greece's participation in global value chains. In this context, the development of Greek industry should be based on the following four axes:  Extroversion and internationalization  Green transformation  Innovation, Research and Development and specialization  Improving the business environment 3.1 Extroversion and internationalisation Strengthening the extrovert orientation of the sector through the development of internationally tradable products and the participation of Greek industries in international value chains must be at the heart of industrial policy. Emphasis should be placed on strengthening sectors and products that exploit comparative advantages and high added value. The Action Plan of the National Industry Strategy highlighted five major industrial ecosystems for the Greek economy: agri-food, building materials, health, digital technologies and applications, green technologies/circular economy. At the same time, seven specialized markets are identified in the Greek Industry: food n Iot Mohog, new generation materials, health technologies and applications, robotics applications, electromobility, defense industry, ship repair and construction. It is necessary to orient the productive fabric of manufacturing in the international market and within the framework of International Production Networks (BTIs) that are developed even at regional level (e.g. energy networks in the SE Mediterranean, innovation enclaves in Thessaloniki and B. Greece, etc.). The major changes observed in the global economy, namely digitalization and green transition, make it possible for the productive fabric of manufacturing to participate in International Production Networks and therefore its further internationalization. The participation of Greek manufacturing in BTIs, and especially in regional BTIs[6], requires horizontal interventions that will create, and even improve, structures and the environment, from public administration, supply chain and energy costs to financial tools and infrastructure, in order to enable Greek manufacturing to compete within regional BTIs. Finally, emphasis should also be placed on developing strategic partnerships and attracting foreign direct investment, which will add know-how and enable entry into new markets.  Green transformation The green transformation is promoted through the European Green Deal[G] and the National Energy and Climate Plan (NECP) which highlights as a primary objective for industry the reduction of fossil fuel consumption by increasing the use of alternative fuels and improving its energy efficiency. However, this requires the mobilization of significant investments and the reform of the institutional framework for the active production and storage of energy through RES, as well as the adoption of measures to improve the active and passive energy efficiency of industry. These actions, in addition to reducing the environmental footprint, can also have economic implications by reducing energy imports and contributing to the reduction of energy costs, a factor that is particularly important for industrial enterprises, as Greece has historically uncompetitive energy costs. This objective concerns the whole industry, but prioritises energy-intensive sectors. The industry's transition to clean energy, a greener production model and new growth models, notably through circular economy principles and with the help of innovation and digital technology[8], is now essential. The implementation of circular economy models creates significant business opportunities and scope for the development of new innovative and environmentally sustainable (green) products. The exploitation of these opportunities by businesses It requires strengthening industrial innovation in the field of green products, improving the institutional framework, as well as developing markets for green products.[9]  Innovation, R&D and specialisation The immediate and effective promotion of digital transformation, with emphasis on the utilization of Industry 4.0 technologies, can strengthen the growth prospects of the industry, creating new business opportunities and helping to address obstacles and limitations that businesses face today using previous technologies. The digital modernisation of manufacturing enterprises requires, in addition to physical capital investments, new business operating practices, as well as human capital with appropriate skills. It also requires a long-term strategy from the state, focusing mainly on the digitalisation of public services, the improvement of connectivity infrastructure, the creation of digital innovation hubs, but also the improvement of the regulatory framework. Improving human capital skills requires coordinated interventions to upgrade both higher and vocational education and training to meet market needs. This could include better links between the education system and business, facilitating cooperation between business and academia to fund research efforts. Also, assessing the needs of the manufacturing industry in the short and long term, and integrating them into the design for the education and training of human resources. As far as administrative practices are concerned, the State has an important role to play in promoting best practice, and it is particularly important to decouple the operation of the enterprise from its founders (modelled, for example, on the German Minimatic). In order to boost R&D and innovative activity, the following could be considered: tax deductions for the purchase or replacement of equipment as well as for the construction or renovation of a building to be used for R&D activities, offsetting of R&D costs against insurance contributions, as well as tax deductions on profits from R&D activities. In addition, increased funding for start-ups and emerging technologies and structures to support them at different stages of their life cycle could be considered. This is with a view to developing the domestic start-up ecosystem and providing services for stages of high technological maturity, enhancing efforts (especially of SMEs) to commercialization of new ideas and research results. Improved financing can contribute to the digital transformation of industrial enterprises through the installation and upgrade of key equipment and digital operations, as well as by boosting domestic production of digital systems and technologies.  Improving the business environment Improving the business environment can be achieved by cutting red tape, digitalising public services and simplifying those procedures with high administrative costs. Addressing tax disincentives is also key to improving the business environment. For example, the reform of the institutional framework by introducing accelerated tax depreciation on fixed assets (mainly machinery and machinery) in order to provide incentives for investments in industry. The possibility for companies to adjust or choose the depreciation method, as well as the depreciation rate, could make a positive contribution to the creation of new investments due to increased liquidity, as well as improve the prospects for dynamic growth of the industry. In the same context, additional actions are needed to reduce energy costs, which have a negative impact mainly on energy-intensive industrial sectors. Measures to strengthen energy interconnections with neighbouring countries, a more efficient functioning of the energy market, a review of regulated tariffs and high taxation as well as subsidies to implement the green transition are measures that could be considered. [10] Finally, improved permitting and siting procedures will reduce operating costs for Greek manufacturing enterprises, also contributing to better environmental protection. In this context, incentives for establishment within organised areas should be introduced for both new and existing enterprises.  Proposals for the European industrial policy framework The ThnEU-19 pandemic and the energy crisis, exacerbated by Russia's invasion of Ukraine, have highlighted the EU's excessive dependencies on third countries, which can undermine its policy objectives and sovereignty. As As a result, the European Commission first relaxed EU state aid rules to allow for significant national subsidies to industry, and then updated its new industrial strategy, building on the lessons learned from the pandemic. The Industrial Strategy for Europe focuses on the following key areas: strengthening the resilience of the single market; addressing the EU's strategic dependencies, accelerating the green and digital transitions. [11] In response to rising inflation, the U.S. has incentivized opt-ins and green technologies through the Ioihaop Kthayop Aoi (AI), raising concerns about unfair competition and violating World Trade Organization principles. The EU responded in February 2023 with the Green Deal industrial plan (Green DealIt will cover four main pillars: a predictable and simplified regulatory environment, faster access to finance, improved skills, and open trade for resilient supply chains.[12] As part of the Green Deal industrial plan, the Commission proposed the Net Zero Emissions Industry Act to accelerate the creation of green technologies in the EU and ensure its autonomy in clean fuels and technologies to ensure a rapid transition to clean energy. [13] A key element of the Green Deal plan is the relaxation of state aid rules to support environmentally friendly industrial projects.[14] To finance the Green Deal, the Commission proposed to build on existing resources such as KERonnotei and INBDII, as well as to set up a new common European Fund (Euphoric Fertility Eupa) to collectively finance projects in critical and emerging technologies, which would also support less prosperous and less technologically advanced countries. The proposal for a common European fund did not go ahead after some member states opposed a new initiative that would involve joint borrowing at EU level before the available funds of the NHS were exhausted. Therefore, what is missing from this plan is a comprehensive European approach. An excessive focus on national subsidies can lead to: First, to a an intra-European subsidy race, wasting considerable resources. Second, a two-speed Europe, where countries with high public debt cannot adequately support their industries, while countries with a stronger fiscal position can provide substantial support. This would exacerbate inequalities and undermine the future of the common currency. Thirdly, in national champions resulting in the undermining of the single market, a decline in competition and a consequent reduction in innovation. On the contrary, a well-designed industrial policy emphasising the European approach has the potential to accelerate the green and digital transitions, ensure improved living standards and the EU's strategic autonomy. In closing, I would like to point out that the course of the Greek economy is directly intertwined with the growth and prosperity of Greek industry. In this context, the implementation of the Action Plan of the National Industry Strategy will help increase the contribution of industry to GDP, increase exports of industrial products and create new and well-paid jobs. However, a basic prerequisite for the success of the Plan is the absorption and utilization of available European resources and financial tools. The utilization of these funds in combination with the mobilization of increased private investments can help the green and digital transformation and increase the competitiveness and extroversion of Greek industry. Title: Speech by Bank of Greece Governor Yannis Stournaras at the 19th Tax Forum on: "Fiscal developments  Combating tax evasion"
text: Address by the Governor of the Bank of Greece's Yannis Stournaras at the 19th Postal Meeting on "Fiscal Developments - Combating Tax Evasion" 31/10/2023-Speeches Ladies and gentlemen, I am very pleased to be here today and have the opportunity to share some thoughts on the role of fiscal policy, recent developments and the need to combat tax evasion. Import Over the past three years we have experienced an unprecedented series of exogenous shocks, mainly on the supply side. We faced a pandemic, resulting in a partial shutdown of the global economy. We are facing a war in Europe and wider geopolitical instability, the most recent example being the escalating turbulence in the Middle East region, leading to ever-increasing uncertainty and profound changes in energy markets and trade standards. At the same time, the effects of climate change are intensifying, forcing economies to prioritise both finding resources to repair the costs involved and taking initiatives to accelerate the green transition. All of these disorders have significant long-term effects. In other words We are entering an era of changes in established economic relations and upheavals in the balances of the recent normal. An immediate visible impact of these changes has been the return of high inflation worldwide. Central banks responded by tightening the monetary policy. While significant progress is being made, the battle to fight inflation has not yet been won. At the same time, for as long as the monetary policy tightening with a view to stabilising prices, the fiscal stance should be restrictive so as not to create excess demand that could be feed back current inflationary pressures. The aim of the new fiscal rules foreseen to be activated in 2024 is to change the medium-term fiscal planning, with restrictions on additional fiscal measures. Reducing public debt and mitigating risks Its sustainability in the medium to long term will be done by controlling the growth rate of public expenditure. By extension, any fiscal space will be used either to create a reserve or to reduce public debt, while any exceptional A budgetary measure on the expenditure side should be financed by a measure increasing revenue by an equal amount. In these uncertainties, maintaining economic stability and fiscal sustainability for policymakers is a significant challenge. In such an environment, credibility in conducting economic policy with a medium-term plan and creating fiscal space to find additional resources without disrupting fiscal stability become crucial. The problem of tax evasion In this light, the fight against tax evasion and a fairer distribution of the tax burden should be prioritised. The resulting increase in tax revenues will create additional fiscal space, facilitating a broader reform of the tax system while promoting tax fairness. It will therefore allow the financing of possible exceptional measures to support the economy in the event of macroeconomic shocks, without jeopardising fiscal sustainability. The problem of tax evasion is one of the most important facing economies internationally. In Greece, although it is difficult to estimate the exact extent of tax evasion, numerous studies show that the problem is much more acute than in other countries[1]. According to a recent survey[2] the size of the shadow economy[3] in Greece is estimated at 20.9% of GDP, higher than the EU average (17.8%) and despite the fact that the country recorded the third largest decrease among European countries in the last 20 years. The breadth of the tax base is directly linked to the problem of tax evasion and, at the same time, raises issues of tax justice. The income tax base in Greece remains limited, focused on wage labour, resulting in an asymmetrically large burden of high tax and contribution rates for a small part of the population. Greece's narrow tax base and widespread tax evasion They essentially violate the principle of horizontal equality - that is, people with the same ability to pay taxes do not enjoy the same tax treatment due to widespread tax evasion. The recent statistics of AADE and ELSTAT are indicative of the magnitude of the problem. For example: The total declared income of individuals to AADE[4] in 2021 was approximately 84 billion. (of which 66 billion or 79% from salaried services and maritime income). In the same year, household final consumption expenditure based on ELSTAT[5] was higher by around 40 billion[6]. About 70% of taxpayers declaring business income activity is classified in an income bracket below 10,000, with total taxable income from business activity amounting to 4.3 billion. Overall, the average income declared to AADE (from salaries, profits, miscellaneous earnings) is lower by about 25% than the expenditure made by households in 2021 according to the ELSTAT Family Budget Survey. of the same year, while at the same time household deposits (savings) increased by 7% compared to 2020[G]. 57% of households declare annual incomes below 10,000 to the tax office. 37% of individuals have incomes at risk of poverty (up to 5,000)[8]. Therefore, based on the above data, the categories that are relatively more prone to tax evasion are mainly the self-employed and micro-enterprises, which is more or less the case in all countries of the world. Almost everywhere, These categories taxpayers generally declare a smaller percentage of their income to the authorities than employees or large companies, because the probability of being detected is comparatively low. This phenomenon has very significant consequences for tax revenues, especially in the case of Greece, due to the higher percentage of small businesses and self-employed compared to most developed countries. Tax evasion is also observed in indirect taxation. Specifically, for 2021, Greece has the third highest VAT revenue gap or VAT gap (\/AT 9th) in the EU, equal to 17.8% of potential VAT revenues (or 3.2 billion) [9]. In Greece, in addition to system distortions, high VAT rates, which often act as an incentive for tax evasion, and the inability to pay tax obligations are an important factor for VAT revenue losses. However, it should be noted that the indicator has improved significantly compared to 2017[10], mainly as a result of the proliferation of electronic transactions and enhanced tax compliance. At the same time, citizens with very high incomes have at their disposal a series of tax avoidance tools, such as the establishment of private companies. In Greece, the most common tools used for this purpose are the transfer of real estate to offshore companies along with the change of tax residence. Legal entities evade taxes by a variety of methods, the most common of which is the issuance or receipt of fictitious invoices; a practice widespread mainly in small and medium-sized enterprises, aimed at simultaneously reducing income tax and VAT, and the occurrence of fictitious losses. Large-sized enterprises, as a rule, cannot resort to such solutions - as a result, they also appear to pay the largest percentage of corporate income tax. Policy recommendations I would like to continue my speech with a series of policy proposals aimed at addressing the problem in order to ensure the overperformance of tax revenues, paving the way for either a reduction in the tax burden or a further strengthening of fiscal reserves. Many of them have been published from time to time in the reports of the Bank of Greece, while many coincide with the recent initiatives of the Government.  Further expansion of electronic transactions by extending the use of portable trading machines (PO8) to more economic activities. The increased use of electronic transactions has been instrumental in improving the performance of VAT revenues. Electronic transactions, unlike cash transactions, are traceable, which facilitates the work of control mechanisms and limits the scope for tax evasion. The increase in electronic transactions has led over time to a spectacular increase in the elasticity of VAT revenues in relation to the tax base. Before imposition In 2015 and the consequent expansion of electronic transactions, an increase in the tax base of one percentage point is estimated to have led to an increase in VAT revenues of approximately 0.8 amount. Mon. (i.e. the elasticity of VAT revenue was 0.8). At the end of 2022, the elasticity of VAT revenues is estimated to have exceeded 1.7. Due to the increased elasticity, the projected expansion of the economy in the coming years and the consequent strengthening of the market share of durable goods in consumer expenditure should continue to have a positive impact on VAT revenues[11],  Incentives for payments through debit cards, but also through banks. The share of private consumption spent through payment cards increased from around 20% in 2019 to over 37% during 2022. Despite this spectacular increase, this share still lags significantly behind the euro area average, which stood at 46% in 2021. In fact, OECD data show that interventions lowering the cash payment ceiling for retail transactions have helped the reducing tax evasion by improving revenue collection.  Providing incentives in the form of tax exemptions for the disclosure of transactions in sectors of high tax evasion, which would correspondingly weaken incentives for tax evasion (e.g. effective tax incentives for electronic payments in specific professional categories).  Continuation of the upgrade of AADE's electronic tools that expands the possibilities of managing and utilizing the information collected through electronic transactions. The ongoing interconnection of cash registers with tax authorities will make a positive contribution in this direction. The role of the IAPR is important in improving tax collection as a series of actions have been launched to reorganise and modernise control and collection methods (e.g. use of risk analysis to select audits, cross-checking - third sources, etc.), giving priority to new tax cases, large debtors and strategic defaulters. This has been possible thanks to the exploitation of new technologies and the introduction of new electronic tools for the exchange of information in real time through the central information system I3XI8 of the AADE[12], (e.g. "ITIGOTA" application, electronic interconnection of PO8 devices with cash registers, etc.).  The stability and further simplification of the tax system will facilitate the functioning of the tax collection mechanism. Indicatively, the ratification of the updated and simplified Public Collection Code Revenue[13] enhanced the collection of public revenues by reducing compliance costs, as the new code combats pluralism, systematizes and clarifies scattered provisions of laws, while at the same time abolishing obsolete legislation.  Finally, the intensification of efforts to create tax consciousness and cultivate tax education. The issue of cultivating tax consciousness is crucial and is directly linked to actions to combat tax evasion. Tax evasion is considered an illegal act and is strongly anti-social behaviour. The concealment of income in order to pay lower tax and the appearance of false expenditures constitute theft of public wealth. The citizen who constantly complains about a more organized and fair state must understand that he himself possesses substantial role in completing this goal. On the other hand, public administration must be characterised by the principles of transparency and accountability in order to create a framework of trust in the management of public funds. The citizen with a tax culture in such an environment understands that the tax revenues of his country return to him, either improving his standard of living or imposing lower taxes in the future. Inference In the current context of heightened uncertainty, the need to find additional resources while safeguarding fiscal stability makes it imperative to combat the problem of tax evasion, which will also contribute to the gradual reform of the tax system. The Government's planned interventions to combat tax evasion are undoubtedly initiatives in the right direction. The aim of these measures is to further reduce the VAT gap to the European average of 9% by 2026, which translates into additional revenues of 2 billion. annually. The fight against tax evasion will also make it possible to change the fiscal policy mix by alleviating the tax burden on workers and businesses and distributing it more fairly, which is imperative and should be continued. Tax reductions have positive multiplier effects on the economy, both on the demand and supply sides. A further reduction in tax rates and Social security contributions will support employment, competitiveness and, ultimately, economic growth and act as an incentive to reduce tax evasion and undeclared work. In the long term, therefore, it will also have a positive impact on public revenues. Thank you very much for your attention.
