Title: Speech by Bank of Greece Governor Yannis Stournaras on "The importance of Financial Literacy" at the 4th Conference of the Institute of Financial Literacy
text: Address by the Governor of the Bank of Yannis Stournaras on "The importance of Financial Literacy" at the 4th Conference of the Institute of Financial Literacy 01/11/2023 - Speeches Import It is a great pleasure for me to participate in the Fourth Financial Literacy Conference organized by the Institute of Financial Literacy under the guidance of Professor Nikolaos Filippas. The Bank of Greece supports and cooperates closely with the Institute of Financial Literacy, as well as with other Organizations that consistently and reliably promote financial literacy in our country, since the Bank of Greece is a Regular Member of the OECD International Network for Financial Education and at the same time the National Financial Literacy Coordinator of the OOoth MohognothK action. which takes place every March. Definition of Financial Literacy According to the OECD, financial literacy is based on the combination of knowledge, skills, behaviour and mindset that an individual must possess in order to be able to make effective financial decisions to maintain their long-term financial well-being. The lack of this, i.e. financial illiteracy, can prevent individuals from managing their finances properly, with ultimately negative consequences such as excessive borrowing and financial exclusion. According to the literature, financially literate individuals are less vulnerable to exploitation or deception, less prone to over-borrowing, more effective at planning retirement, participating more frequently in financial markets, and using fintech more. Financial literacy is key to financial inclusion, which in turn can help reduce income inequality and enhance financial stability. However, several studies show that many people do not have sufficient basic financial knowledge in terms of e.g. calculating or understanding interest rates, understanding the concept of inflation and risk differentiation. The results of research by OECD show that less than half of the adult population in 320 countries are financially literate people, with the problem of finance illiteracy is much more pronounced in women and young people, as shown by other similar studies around the world. According to the 2014 Global Financial Literacy Survey in the European Union (EU), an average of 52% of adults were financially literate, with the highest rates recorded in Northern Europe and the lowest in the South. In Greece the corresponding figure was 45%. Why financial literacy is important for citizens: In today's complex financial reality, financial literacy skills are the most essential for citizens of all ages. Here are some key reasons why financial literacy is important to citizens:  Making informed financial decisions: Financial literacy equips individuals with the necessary knowledge and skills to make informed decisions about their personal finances. It helps them understand concepts such as budgeting, saving, investing and borrowing. With a high level of financial literacy, individuals can make more informed choices about their money, leading to improved financial well-being.  Personal finance management: Financial literacy enables individuals to effectively manage their personal finances. It equips them with the right skills to be able to create and maintain a budget, track their expenses, set financial goals, and prioritize their spending. This helps individuals to avoid unnecessary debts, reduce financial stress and work towards their financial goals.  Avoiding financial traps: Lack of financial literacy can make individuals vulnerable to financial fraud, predatory lending, or other financial traps. With a high level of financial literacy, individuals can better recognize and avoid fraud, understand the risks associated with certain financial products, and make wiser decisions about their money.  Planning for the future: Financial literacy helps individuals plan for the future by understanding concepts such as retirement planning, insurance, and real estate planning. It enables them to make appropriate long-term financial decisions, such as saving for retirement, building up emergency capital and protecting their assets. Having a proper understanding of Above concepts, individuals can then work towards achieving their long-term financial security and stability.  Financial stability: Financially literate citizens contribute to a nation's overall financial stability. When individuals have a good grasp of personal finance, they are less likely to default on their loan obligations, engage in risky financial behaviors, or rely heavily on benefit systems. This leads to a healthier financial system and a more stable economy. 6. Empowerment and independence: Financial literacy empowers individuals to take control of their financial lives and become more independent. It helps them build the confidence they need to manage their money, negotiate better loan terms, and navigate the complex financial system safely. This empowerment allows individuals to make choices that align with their financial objectives and ambitions. Overall, financial literacy is crucial for citizens as it enables them to make informed decisions, manage their personal finances effectively, avoid financial pitfalls, plan for the future, contribute to financial stability and become empowered and independent and inclusive. Therefore, enhancing citizens' economic and financial literacy is of particular importance and importance for modern societies, and has become an essential and long-term policy priority for many states, with Central Banks and other supervisory authorities playing an important role in this regard. Overall, rapid developments in all areas of social activity, unforeseen risks, as well as the complexity of the financial system make financial literacy a necessary civic skill for the 21st century. The actions of the European Central Bank (ECB) on Financial Literacy The European Central Bank (ECB) has recognised the importance of financial literacy in promoting financial stability and empowering citizens to make informed financial decisions. While the ECB focuses primarily on monetary policy and ensuring the stability of the euro, it also supports financial literacy initiatives in several ways: Research and data collection: The ECB surveys and collects data on financial literacy levels across the euro area. information helps to identify the geographical areas in which the Financial education is most necessary. Partnerships: The ECB works with a variety of stakeholders, including national central banks, governments and other bodies, to promote financial literacy initiatives. These partnerships They include, inter alia, the development of educational materials as well as the creation of awareness-raising campaigns. Education programmes: The ECB shall, where appropriate, support or even sponsor educational programmes aimed at improving financial literacy, in particular in schools and local communities. These programs typically cover topics such as budgeting, savings, investments, and understanding financial products. Publications and resources: The ECB provides information and resources on financial literacy on its website. These include publications, articles and online tools to help individuals better understand financial concepts and products. Consumer protection: ECB supports stronger consumer protection laws and regulations to ensure that Financial products and services are transparent and understandable. Through Its initiatives also attempt to help significantly in the protection of consumers from aggressive economic practices. Financial inclusion: Promoting financial inclusion is closely linked to financial literacy. The ECB works to ensure that all Citizens have access to basic financial services, while at the same time having the necessary knowledge to use them effectively. Financial stability: Through the promotion of finance literacy, the ECB contributes to overall financial stability. Informed consumers are less likely to adopt risky financial behaviours that could destabilise the economy. Regulation and supervision: The ECB plays an important role in the supervision of financial sector within the euro area. Part of this supervision is to ensure that financial institutions act responsibly and do not engage in practices that could harm consumers. Communication: The ECB communicates the importance of financial literacy to the general public and encourages citizens to take proactive measures to manage their personal finances prudently. Monitoring and evaluation: The ECB periodically assesses the effectiveness of financial literacy initiatives to ensure that they have a positive impact on citizens' financial literacy and behaviour. It is important to note that while the ECB supports financial literacy efforts, many financial education initiatives are carried out by national governments and other organisations within the euro area. The ECB's role is to coordinate and support these efforts on a broader scale to safeguard financial stability and promote financial prosperity among euro area citizens. The Bank of Greece's Financial Literacy Activities The Bank of Greece, in the context of its social responsibility, supports efforts to promote learning and financial literacy, and supports actions that enhance financial literacy in recognition of its positive effects on the economy as a whole and on financial stability. In particular, in the context of these actions, the Bank of Greece Museum, in view of its educational role and given that the vast majority of its visitors are high school students and students, offers guided tours tailored to the needs of these age groups and hosts educational events focusing on specific economic issues such as inflation, electronic payments and the euro. designed to promote financial literacy among the public. In particular, in June 2019, the temporary exhibition of the Bank's Museum "Payments: a road map" was inaugurated, in the context of which the museum pedagogical program "Cashless how?" was developed, which is approved by the Institute of Educational Policy of the Ministry of Education. This action aims at the financial education of students of the last year of gymnasium and high school students. Also, the Centre for Culture, Research and Documentation of the Bank of Greece has published an innovative book on financial education and empowerment of primary school children entitled "The ABC of the economy", an original dictionary of financial literacy, addressed to primary school students, presented at the Museum of the Bank of Greece. The author of the book is Professor of Finance at the University of Piraeus Nikolaos D. Filippas and illustrator Alexia Lougiaki. The book includes 124 basic entries in economics and finance, accompanied by nine short and comprehensive stories, which contribute to a fuller understanding of the concepts mentioned. A second dictionary-guide for financial education and empowerment of adolescents, who are called upon to face a constantly changing environment, is being completed. Improving individuals' financial literacy has become a long-term policy priority for many countries, with central banks and supervisors playing an important role in this regard. Financial literacy is becoming increasingly important for economic efficiency and the successful conduct of economic policy, and therefore for economic prosperity. First, citizens who understand the workings of the economic environment are better able to make optimal choices. Second, combined with the former, they are more likely to support "prudent policies", while strengthening financial literacy ensures the sustainability of public finances and enhances the efficiency and flexibility of markets. Overall, promoting digital financial literacy can empower individuals and equip them with the required financial knowledge and skills, including digital ones, encourage them to seek financial advice from responsible sources, prevent irrational behaviour and enhance the ability to assess economic conditions prudently. This is because, among other things, it is vital to understand the consequences of debt, especially for the most vulnerable groups, such as young families and low-income households. Moreover, the additional pressure that ageing puts on pension systems requires higher levels of financial literacy. People live longer but save proportionately less, with Greece ranking among the lowest in the EU in terms of savings for old age. The lack of proper retirement-savings planning means that individuals are potentially unprepared for the financial challenges of old age. Strengthening financial literacy plays an important role in the EU's strategy for growth and social prosperity. Therefore, actions and interventions are needed to strengthen financial literacy in schools. For example, the inclusion of a financial literacy course in primary and secondary school curricula will help students become familiar with key financial concepts that will help them make sound financial decisions later in life.

Title: Speech by Bank of Greece Governor Yannis Stournaras entitled: "The Contribution of Costas Simitis to the modernization of the Greek economy 1996-2004" at the event in honour of Former President of the Republic of Greece. Prime Minister Costas Simitis
text: Address by the Governor of the Bank of Greece Yannis Stournaras entitled: "The Contribution of Costas Simitis to Modernization of the Greek economy 1996-2004" at the event in his honor pr. Prime Minister Costas Simitis 06/11/2023 - Speeches The event is organized by the Network for Reform in Greece and Europe, the Jacques Delors Institute and the magazine Reform, supported by the Economic Forum of Delphi. The fundamental question of history "which forces mobilize nations?" has been answered many and varied from Herodotus and Thucydides to modern historical, social and political scientists, depending on the era and the prevailing conditions. Today, it seems that the answer to this fundamental question lies in the triptych: "quality of democracy and institutions, strong economy, effective foreign policy". Few prime ministers, from the National Independence in 1830 until today, have had the contribution of Costas Simitis to the decisive strengthening of this triptych, and therefore to the mobilization of the nation. Dear friends Aristides Agathoklis and Yiannis Voulgaris will speak at today's event about foreign policy and institutions. I will confine myself to Costas Simitis' contribution to the modernization of the economy. The crowning achievement of Costas Simitis' governments was Greece's entry into the euro area. But it wasn't the only one. During his premiership, emblematic public works were completed, such as the Airport El. Venizelos, the unification of archaeological sites, the Attiki Odos, the Rio-Antirrio bridge, Metra, the Tramway. "Twenty years of infrastructure were condensed into four", wrote the authoritative magazine "Teth Eoohaididi" at the time. The Olympic Games were carefully prepared and organized. Emblematic privatizations were carried out in the financial sector, with the Ionian Bank being the top one, strategic alliances with major foreign banks, such as Emporiki Bank and OGTHAI Arpoith, as well as equity swaps of Public Enterprises, with total privatization revenues of 13.5 billion. dollars in the period 1996-2001. The large systemic banking groups, as we know them today, were essentially formed then. The legislation on the Hellenic Capital Market Commission and the Stock exchange. The Public Debt Management Agency (PDMA) was created. The consolidation of Public Enterprises proceeded, before they were introduced into the Stock exchange. Income policy has been modernised, in consultation with the trade unions, thus helping to reduce inflation while raising real wages within the limits allowed by productivity growth. Social spending has increased. Reforms were made to modernize the State. An important example is the rationalization of the selection process of the administrations of Public Enterprises and organizations, by establishing meritocratic criteria. Many of these reforms, such as the changes in income policy that I have already mentioned, combined with fiscal, monetary and structural policies, as well as the inflow of Community funds, took place in the first four years, and contributed decisively to the achievement of the major objective, which was Greece's accession to the euro area. And all this, in a climate of social consensus and acceptance, where this difficult goal had, with the substantial contribution and inspiration of Costas Simitis, turned into a national vision that inspired most of society. Greece's accession to the euro area in 2001 is, in my view, the greatest achievement in the country's modern economic history, sealing its European orientation and placing it at the centre of European developments. It has also solved, once and for all, the problem of monetary and exchange rate instability that has plagued Greece for long periods of time since its national independence. The same, by the way, still happens with many small, open economies. European or non-European. The value of membership was shown a few years later, when the institutions and governments of euro area member states intervened to prevent Greece from defaulting, the result of an unduly expansionary fiscal policy. They intervened by refinancing almost all of the its public debt, on very favourable terms, ensuring its sustainability for many years. Joining the euro area is a historic achievement, if we consider: firstly, the negative initial economic conditions and the large - the greater than all other candidate Member States - their distance from the reference figures of the respective convergence criteria of the Maastricht Treaty: inflation, public sector deficit, public debt, interest rates and exchange rate (i.e. the inclusion of the drachma in the Mechanism Exchange Rates of the European Monetary System). Second, the distrust of Greece's partners in the European Union due to its negative economic policy performance from the late 1970s to the end of the 1980s, with only a short bright interlude in which, too, Costas Simitis starred. The Greek economy achieved its entry into the euro area by meeting all five convergence criteria. This happened after a successful but arduous course of six years, 1994-2000, but especially in the period 1996-2000, during which exceptional events occurred at great economic cost to the country, such as the Imia crisis in 1996, the international emerging markets crisis of 1997/98, the earthquake of September 1999 and the war in Kosovo in 1999. But how was this Herculean feat achieved and what useful conclusions can be drawn for the future? Firstly, there were specific objectives, the five convergence criteria, which were soon adopted as political and economic priorities. Although it was unpleasant for many to prioritize nominal over It soon became apparent that the achievement of the five criteria and early entry into the euro area was a prerequisite for sustainable real convergence, and therefore a matter of major political, social and economic importance. The Revised Convergence Programmes from 1994 onwards recognised the need for fiscal consolidation, and nominal convergence in general, which was not at all, if at all, self-evident at the time. Secondly, there was political leadership (S 3 ath G8ir), determination, coordination, continuity, consistency and perseverance. Since 1994, almost the same team, the Ministry of National Economy, Finance and the Bank of Greece, under the coordination of the Minister of National Economy, has been responsible until the end for the implementation of the project, both at political and technocratic level. But after 1996 and, good luck for Greece, the election of Costas Simitis as leader of PASOK after the death of Andreas Papandreou and the Taking over as Prime Minister, the goals became much more ambitious and coherent, their pursuit much more persistent and his political cover economic staff much stronger. The last element is very important, as the economic staff is the most sensitive pole of any government. The media and the general public do not usually judge on the basis of long-term prospects and goals, but on the basis of everyday life, where good economic news goes almost unnoticed, while unpleasant news often makes headlines. The absolute political coverage of the economic team by Prime Minister Costas Simitis became apparent as soon as tax measures with high political costs began to be taken (in order to make the "haves and have-nots" pay, according to the popular expression of that time) in order to accelerate the rapid reduction of the budget deficit. Thirdly, dogmatism and sterile approaches were avoided and realistic and flexible instruments (fiscal, monetary/exchange rate policy, income, structural) were adopted, as well as timetables that were updated in the context of rolling Convergence Programmes. The successful course of the economy and the parallel achievement of economic stabilization and economic growth also canceled certain dogmatic and ideologically charged perceptions that had hitherto found fertile ground in Greece. The widespread perceptions at the time, which had to be refuted ideologically, technocratically and politically, were of the type "in Greece inflation cannot be reduced below 10% because there are structural rigidities and a large agricultural sector", or, even more, of the type "there can be no growth along with economic stabilization", a very widespread doctrine of an obsolete era. Now that may sound strange, but back then they dominated. Fourthly, and with the most catalytic Budget of 1997, i.e. the first Budget of Costas Simitis as Prime Minister, the social and developmental dimension of economic policy has not been abandoned. On the contrary, high rates of economic growth were achieved, social protection expenditure as a percentage of GDP increased by at least three percentage points, tax evasion was significantly reduced, a large property tax was imposed on the "haves and haves", the ratio of direct to indirect taxes improved significantly, while real wages increased every year within the limits of productivity growth, thus improving the degree of social acceptance of productivity economic policy. It is, of course, true that the inputs of the Second Community Support Framework have played an important role in the development dimension of economic policy. However, the growth effort was mainly based on the strong increase in private investment, which was the result of the reduction in interest rates, the gradual stabilisation of the economy, and in particular the reduction of inflation and public deficits, as well as the improvement of the business climate. It is striking, and certainly not common based on international experience, that in a period of economic stabilization with a drastic reduction in budget deficits and inflation (around twelve percentage points each between 1993 and 1999), high rates of economic growth and rapid convergence of Greece's GDP per capita with that of the euro area average were achieved: GDP per capita went from 66% of the European average in 1996 to 72% in 2004. It had, in fact, restored what had been lacking for so many years: confidence in economic policy. For the first time, economic policy has not been reversed by the political electoral cycle, as it had been in 1981, 1985, 1989, 1990 and 1993. This is mainly due to Prime Minister Costas Simitis, who ignored the high political cost, especially of the 1997 Budget submitted by the economic staff, signaling his determination to move forward unwaveringly until the completion of the accession effort.

Title: Speech by Dimitris Malliaropulos, Chief Economist and Director of Economic Analysis and Research of the Bank of Greece, at ICAP 16th Conference on Credit Risk Management, titled: Have central banks won the battle against inflation?
text: Speech by Dimitris Malliaropulos, Chief Economist and Director of Economic Analysis and Research of the Bank of Greece, at ICAP 16th Conference on Credit Risk Management, titled: Have central banks won the battle against inflation? 15/11/2023-Speeches It is a great pleasure to participate in this years conference by ICAP and have the opportunity to share with you some thoughts on the macro challenges the world economy faces today. The times are indeed uncertain in many ways, compounding risks and policy dilemmas. Cyclical developments are interacting with profound structural changes, not least climate change and the digital transition, including transformative technologies like artificial intelligence. The continuum of unprecedented shocks that hit the global economy in the last few years has led to a long series of complex risks to manage. These risks, to name a few, relate to higher-for-longer interest rates, debt sustainability, financial stability, Chinas slowdown, commodity price volatility, as well as geo- economic fragmentation and socio-political polarisation. I decided to focus my remarks today on inflation, not only because I am a central banker, but also because I think that inflation well summarises the actual and expected outcomes of several underlying forces and distributions of risks. So far, historical regularities, the resilience of the economy and market sentiment would suggest that the fight against inflation has been won at a small cost for growth. The fact that inflation is in a declining path and a hard landing of the global economy has been avoided in the first two years of aggressive monetary policy tightening has tempted many to argue that we are out of the woods and converging back to trend. Let me explain, in the remainder of my speech, why we must stay cautious and vigilant. The first reason is looming risks of persistent inflation and, thus, higher-for-longer interest rates. As an ECB Executive Board member recently noted: in about 90% of unresolved inflation episodes, inflation declined materially within the first three years after the initial shock, but then either plateaued at an elevated level or accelerated again.[1] Inflation persistence in the short to medium term may be driven by mechanical dynamics, if base effects from volatile energy and food prices reverse from disinflationary to inflationary. Another important source of inflation persistence is indirect and second-round effects from price rigidities and the catch-up of wages to past inflation. As a result, inflation may be more persistent because downward adjustments of selling prices by firms will be smaller and less frequent and increasing unit labour costs will be only partially absorbed by shrinking profit margins. In addition, structural changes like the rising share of services in the economy that are generally labour-intensive and less sensitive to interest rates[2], as well as prolonged labour market tightness due to shortages of workers and skills could weaken monetary policy transmission and delay the disinflation process. Against this backdrop, it is obvious that the disinflation process critically depends on the strength and speed of monetary policy transmission to financial conditions and the real economy. Although bank lending rates and sovereign bond yields have responded strongly to policy rate hikes, notwithstanding the lags, risk premia in equity and corporate bond markets have remained rather compressed, implying looser-than-expected financial conditions overall. Historical regularities for advanced economies and the, unseen yet, effects of quantitative tightening suggest that further tightening of financial conditions is in the pipeline. A scenario of abrupt repricing of risk assets is more likely when private debt is high, inflationary pressures are more pronounced, interest rates are high and asset valuations are stretched, like today. Meanwhile, a set of factors have resulted in a muted transmission of monetary policy to growth. First, real interest rates are still low by historical standards, even after their recent sharp increases, and hence, aggregate expenditure remains relatively resilient. Moreover, there is still ample liquidity in the market following the low-interest-rates era and quantitative easing; the expansion of central banks balance sheet has been outsized and its unwinding remains very gradual. Second, structural changes, like the higher share of fixed rate mortgages during the low- for-long era has made indebted home owners less sensitive to interest rate hikes. Companies are also less sensitive to interest rate hikes to the extent that they have issued long-term debt at a low cost during the period of low interest rates. Moreover, the increased importance of intangible assets in firms capital may have also weakened the response of investment to increased cost of borrowing. Third, pandemic-related distortions, such as excess savings, and buoyant labour markets have helped keep private consumption robust. In the US, for example, excess savings of households are estimated at about three trillion US dollars, i.e. about 15% of US GDP. Finally, loose fiscal policy - particularly in the US -- has bolstered aggregate demand muting the transmission of monetary policy tightening to the real economy. The gradual dissipation of these factors should bolster monetary policy effectiveness. Looking farther out, megatrends such as deglobalisation and climate change could keep inflation elevated. The shift from offshoring to on-shoring and friend-shoring implies higher marginal costs for firms. In a recent corporate survey by the ECB, 60% of the respondent European multinationals confirmed that changes in their supply chains and production locations had pushed up prices over the past five years, while 45% expect such shifts to exert more inflationary pressures in the future. Meanwhile, extreme weather events and natural disasters are expected to become more frequent and disruptive, translating into negative supply shocks for the economy, while the green transition and climate adaptation policies will make conventional energy and critical inputs for producing clean energy more expensive. Carbon tax also needs to double or triple to achieve climate neutrality.[3] Needless to say that geo-economic fragmentation and trade restrictions amid strategic competition would only aggravate price pressures globally. The second set of risks we face is fiscal risks pertaining to a less favourable snowball effect, namely higher-for-longer interest rates coupled with weaker growth. The State has become more interventionist than in the past, underpinning economic resilience in times of compounding economic shocks. However, massive fiscal support packages during recent crises have soared public debt in advanced economies near historically record levels, contributing to high inflation. Recently, the credit rating of the US was downgraded owing to worsening fiscal prospects, which implies a steepening of the US yield curve, namely an increase in the term premium demanded by investors to hold US debt. Other countries, like the UK, with a high share of inflation-linked debt are confronted with a fast rise in debt-servicing costs and nominal debt levels in an era of more persistent inflation. Elevated debt levels coupled with higher-for-longer interest rates push government bond yields higher. Rising debt servicing costs for governments are therefore here to stay and have a lasting effect on governments ability to respond to crises: gross interest payments in 2024 for major advanced economies will be around 1 pp of GDP higher than in 2021. The cost of public borrowing is also set to remain high because investors may price in increased risk of debt distress ahead. Experience from past monetary tightening episodes suggests that long-term bond yields of highly indebted sovereigns tend to rise more strongly than those of less indebted ones. This reflects shifts in credit risk premia: sovereign CDS spreads tend to widen much more for high-debt sovereigns amid changes in global financial conditions, not least those that reflect a monetary tightening. Further upward pressure on government bond yields stems from the reversal of large-scale asset purchases by major central banks during the period of quantitative easing. These purchases have been one reason why changes in long-term yields have not been sensitive to policy rate hikes in the past. As these purchases are now being reversed, the sensitivity of yields is likely to increase. The yield increases could be amplified by illiquidity in government bond markets, in particular in longer duration instruments. High levels of public borrowing, including sizeable financing needs for the green transition and infrastructure investment to cope with climate change challenges, could keep interest rates up. Financial markets might struggle to absorb both the large supply of new debt and the debt withdrawal from central bank portfolios. In this set-up, a repricing of government bonds could lead to financial market tensions. Beyond the short run and conditional on the monetary policy reaction, dampened economic activity from renewed adverse supply shocks, also in light of the recent geopolitical turmoil, could outweigh the positive impact of higher inflation on debt ratios. Finally, we should not overlook stagflation risks. A new regime of higher inflation and lower growth remains a probability. Natural disasters due to climate change lead to destruction of physical capital stock. Companies more exposed to climate risk will see their capital depreciate at a faster pace. Climate change adaptation policies will only partially compensate for this loss of capital stock. Green investments will reduce the economic cost of climate change but there is so far no evidence that they will also boost long-term productivity growth. As a result, limited policy space, capital stock destruction and its slow replacement due to the green transition, and long periods of subdued productivity growth, among others, could depress economic potential. In sum, the battle against inflation is not won yet. It is going to be a long and bumpy road in times of structural shifts and breaks, as the ECB President Christine Lagarde noted at Jackson Hole earlier this year. The last mile of disinflation is the hardest, so there is no room for complacency. Policymakers might be called upon to take bold or even radical decisions regarding the monetary and fiscal policy frameworks and tools, while international cooperation seems more needed than ever to address global challenges and macro risks. If there is one thing characterising current times, this is uncertainty about the global growth prospects and the disinflation process, even in the absence of additional shocks. Yet, let us not forget that all times have been uncertain in history and good leadership involves understanding the risks, preparing contingency plans, hedging the bets and communicating uncertainty with confidence to steer expectations. Thank you! [1] Isabel Schnabel, The last mile (europa.eu). [2] Stedman, K.D., and E., Pollard (2023), Why has monetary policy tightening not cooled the labour market enough to quell inflation?, KcFed Economic Bulletin. [3] See, for example, IMF Fiscal Monitor Climate Crossroads: Fiscal Policies in a Warming World, October 2023 for estimates and references.

Title: Speech by Bank of Greece Governor Yannis Stournaras at "The Seventh Sustainability Summit for SE Europe and the Mediterranean"
text: Speech by Bank of Greece Governor Yannis Stournaras at the conference " 8 ibib 3      " 21/11/2023 - Speeches It is my pleasure to participate once again in this EOPOPTIDI conference, which has now been established as one of the most important conferences on sustainability in Greece and the Mediterranean region in general  two regions that are extremely exposed to the negative effects of climate change. I would therefore like to share with you some thoughts on the urgent need to move to more sustainable development. OR Humanity is currently facing multiple, often simultaneous, crises. These crises concern geopolitical, energy, social issues, and all, directly or indirectly, are related to sustainability. The global economy is fragile as the recovery from the pandemic and the war in Ukraine slows, while divergences between economies and countries widen.[11 In this challenging environment, the financial sector needs to remain resilient to potential macroeconomic and geopolitical shocks, supporting the economy while taking measures to address challenges related to digital transformation and climate change.[2] At the current juncture, nature is in unprecedented danger, as widely recognized by the scientific community. In particular, the United Nations Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPPOO) confirmed in its sixth assessment report that Global warming is causing a significant increase in risks to ecosystems and people.[3] Moreover, in his study of biodiversity, the distinguished scientist Rthy IItB DuthduriB states that the economic growth of recent decades has been achieved at considerable cost to nature  we now need 1.6 planets Earth to maintain the current standard of living, as our demands are far greater than the resources available to the planet. [4] Extreme weather events have become more frequent and more severe, with increasing losses in capital  human, natural and economic. Consider the devastating fires and floods in Greece during this summer and autumn, which disrupted services and caused significant damage to systems and infrastructure. All of the above leads us to the painful realization of how inextricably linked to nature is our well-being and, ultimately, our survival. Of course, these weather events, in addition to losses, have given impetus to the design of response policies, including strengthening adaptation actions and resilience mechanisms. [5] Similarly, the reactions of states, and especially of the European Union, to the crises of recent years have created new resources, such as the Recovery and Resilience Fund, which enabled countries to accelerate the energy transition. Despite progress in climate finance, both the transition to a low-emission economy and adaptation to climate change still need significant reinforcement. Investment is still insufficient[6] and there are critical challenges that need to be addressed at institutional level in order to mobilise the huge amount of financial resources needed. For example, there is a lack of common methodologies and sufficient transparency in assessments of companies' E8O performance, which does not contribute to creating a strong single market for sustainability financing. In addition, multiple voluntary sustainability reporting reporting frameworks and the absence of companies' transition plans make it difficult to allocate capital efficiently and make sound investment and risk management decisions. [G] Also, the pace and size of funding for climate change adaptation projects remains well below what is needed.[8] In today's challenging environment, these challenges and weaknesses should prompt stronger and more decisive action. Our efforts need to be accelerated and coordinated, both nationally, at European and international level. Aiming for sustainable development  as reflected in all 17 UN Goals[9]  can be a catalyst for a global solution to the successive crises facing humanity; with proper management of the increasing risks from climate change, creating opportunities for growth, benefiting society and the economy. In particular, the transition to a low-emission economy is expected to bring about structural changes, new jobs and new business activities  for example in process and product energy efficiency, development of networks and green infrastructure, renewable energy,[10] but also in actions and projects related to climate change adaptation. For the European economy, and especially for the euro area, there will be no definitive response to the new major challenges  whether the crises I mentioned earlier, such as climate change and the green transition with increased investment and financing needs  without greater and broader fiscal integration, completion of the banking union and creation of a genuine capital markets union.[11] But we should not wait for the political conditions in the euro area to mature before all this moves forward together. For example, the capital market union is already ready to be implemented immediately, as are the European Commission's proposals on bank crisis management and the European deposit insurance scheme.[12] At this point I would also like to refer to the role of central banks in tackling climate change, as it is clear that we all have a role to play, even if elected governments have the primary say. Central banks can and have already taken active action in managing climate and sustainability risks and supporting the transition to a more sustainable and socially responsible economy  always within our mandate and for the benefit of societies. This is because climate-related risks are a source of instability and vulnerability for the financial system, as they can affect the transmission of monetary policy and create price stability shocks. Thus, central banks take concrete measures to prevent risks to price stability and, together with supervisors, to ensure that the financial system is resilient to these risks. In 2021, at the Governing Council of the European Central Bank (ECB), we agreed on a comprehensive and ambitious action plan to further integrate climate considerations into our strategy and more systematically integrate sustainability considerations into our actions.[13] Since then, we have been making progress in implementing this plan  for example, the ECB has started to take climate change into account in its corporate bond markets, collateral framework, disclosure requirements and risk management.[ 14] These measures are consistent with the Eurosystem's primary objective of maintaining price stability, while supporting European transition policies. In addition, the measures incentivise companies and financial institutions to be more transparent about and reduce greenhouse gas emissions. At the Bank of Greece, climate change and sustainability have always been high on our agenda. We started working on these issues in 2009, when we set up a multidisciplinary committee, the Climate Change Impact Study Committee (CCISC). Since then, we have been working systematically on research, including contributing to policy-making, to limit the adverse effects of climate change and facilitate adaptation to climate change. In addition, in June 2021 we created the Centre for Climate Change and Sustainability of the Bank of Greece, with the main purpose of coordinating our relevant activities, while in November of the same year, in the context of the United Nations Climate Change Conference (POP26), we published our commitment to contribute, within our mandate, to the implementation of the Paris Agreement, with relevant actions in the fields in which we operate. [15] Over the past 15 years, the Bank of Greece has achieved several milestones related to climate change and sustainability, including: the publication of relevant reports and analyses; participation in the eight-year project IIEE-IP Aaariin Ogthoth for the implementation of the National Adaptation Strategy, contributing to international and European sustainability issues3  such as the Network Central Banks and Supervisors for a Green Financial System (NOV8), investing in green bonds and applying sustainable and responsible investment principles to non-monetary policy portfolios, as well as actions to enhance economic and climate literacy. We also systematically promote cooperation and ongoing dialogue with policymakers and stakeholders  for example, the Bank of Greece participates in the development of studies coordinated by the Ministry of Finance and the Ministry of Energy and Environment. In fact, in the coming period, in mid-December, we will publish the first results of the studies carried out in the framework of the work of the CCISC and the project I_ib Aarariin Ogthoth, on the impact of climate change on critical sectors, such as agriculture and transport. In closing, I would like to reiterate that the current conjuncture, that of multiple crises, should not slow down global efforts to achieve sustainable development. On the contrary, as I have already said, striving for sustainable development can be part of the solution. International cooperation, strong political commitment, coordinated actions with monitoring and evaluation, inclusive governance, active participation of society, and of course access to adequate financial resources, with an emphasis on the most vulnerable regions and social groups.[16] I hope that today's conference papers will also contribute in this direction. Thank you.  South African. 2023: N3nia3 Oi RitathioThd (requests). Title: Speech by Bank of Greece Governor Yannis Stournaras on the occasion of his award of an Honorary Doctorate from the Department of Economics of the University of Patras on "Monetary Policy and Climate Change"
text: Address by the Governor of the Bank of Greece's Yiannis Stournaras at the award of his Honorary Doctorate Department of Economics of University of Patras on "Monetary Policy and Climate Change" 08/12/2023-Speeches Dear Mr. Rector, Mr. Dean, Mr. President, Dear Ladies and Gentlemen, Dear Colleagues and Friends, It is a great honor and pleasure to be awarded today an Honorary Doctorate by the Department of Economics of the University of Patras, a department that during the years of its operation has made a significant and systematic effort to contribute to economic science, promote cooperation and extroversion and adapt the curriculum to international developments in the scientific field and educational practices. At the same time, I would like to praise the University of Patras as a whole, an Institution of Higher Education, distinguished and renowned thanks to its academic research in the fields of science, engineering, informatics, agriculture, health sciences and humanities, social and economic sciences. I would like to make special mention of the international orientation of the University and its participation in programs, joint ventures and agreements with other universities, research institutes and organizations abroad, which is an example of extroversion for the Universities of our country. My speech today will focus on the crucial issue of climate change, an issue that central banks have been increasingly concerned with in recent years, and, as I am pleased to see in the curricula of the Department of Economics, relevant courses are taught and prepared accordingly Postgraduate dissertations.!! Humanity today faces multiple, often simultaneous, crises and challenges. These crises and challenges concern geopolitical, energy, social issues, and all, directly or indirectly, to a greater or lesser extent, are related to climate change and sustainability in general. We are approaching critical turning points which, if and when they are overcome, will lead to even greater changes. In particular, nature lies , , X ,7 . [2] [3] at unprecedented risk, as recognized by the scientific community, And extreme weather events have become more frequent and more severe. All the above have as an impact the increasing losses in capital - human, natural and economic, something we are also experiencing in Greece, and lead us to the painful realization of how inextricably linked to nature is our prosperity and, ultimately, our survival.  The macroeconomic impacts of climate change Both extreme weather events linked to climate change and the green transition have significant macroeconomic impacts and are not a problem of any distant future. The objective of monetary policy is to maintain price stability over the medium term, but climate change affects both short- and long-term inflation and growth, making it increasingly difficult for central banks to properly assess the economic outlook and subsequently formulate an appropriate monetary policy. Overall, we expect volatility in macroeconomic fundamentals such as inflation and growth to increase, which creates further uncertainty in our forecasts over the medium term and ultimately in monetary policymaking. Understanding the macroeconomic implications of climate change is therefore essential to assess how the transmission mechanism of monetary policy and thus the achievement of our price stability objective will be affected. More specifically, the impact on economic activity of more frequent and severe extreme weather events is immediate and adverse. Growth suffers in the short term, as damage is caused to infrastructure, building equipment and natural capital Business. In addition, economic activities in the affected areas are interrupted or restricted for a long time and supply distortions occur [4] Chains. According to studies, GDP growth is reduced by more than 0.5 percentage points from extreme weather events in the year in which they occur. Even if output gradually recovers, heightened uncertainty affects consumer and investment choices, labour productivity and employment, with potential negative effects on economic activity. At the same time, unless immediate climate change mitigation measures are taken, chronic impacts will continue to escalate, causing additional damage to the economy, while even greater funds will be required for adaptation investments. Regarding [5] Recent studies show that excessive warming in the summer months is putting upward pressure on food prices, particularly in warmer countries. In such an environment, with heightened volatility and risks to price formation, keeping inflation expectations close to our target becomes more difficult. Additional effects on output and inflation are also expected from the green transition. Measures and policies towards net zero emissions include different combinations of taxation, subsidies, regulations, etc. For example, the price of carbon (whether set through tax or other means) may need to rise significantly. This may, Ovith Rvpoye, push inflation higher, requiring a more restrictive monetary policy stance to achieve the inflation target. The impact on inflation from investment in new, greener technologies and the downgrading of less energy-efficient capital is uncertain. As a result, there are different and ambiguous forces in the long-term equilibrium interest rate. Defining credible and effective transition and climate change adaptation policies is crucial to reduce relative uncertainty, but also to prepare economic actors appropriately and smoothly. Moreover, climate change is expected to disproportionately affect different regions and sectors of the economy, so that the impact on inflation will not be the same across all euro area countries, posing an additional challenge to the smooth transmission of monetary policy. The increase in macroeconomic volatility also leads to greater uncertainty in our forecasts over the medium term and subsequently in the formulation of monetary policy. Climate change affects the financial system, through the risk of natural disasters but also through the risk of transition. A direct impact comes from the compensation paid by insurance undertakings following natural disasters. For example, compensation for the recent floods in Thessaly is estimated to exceed EUR 350 million. Most of them are expected to be covered by reinsurance undertakings. Moreover, impairment of assets of companies affected by natural disasters can weigh on banks' balance sheets, due to the lower value of their assets (such as shares and bonds), the increase in non-performing exposures and the decrease in the value of collateral. This increases banks' liquidity risk and funding costs, affecting the terms and flows of bank lending to firms and households. But actions to tackle and adapt to climate change can also be an opportunity if they are seen as investments that bring new, more effective and more sustainable forms of growth towards a more resilient and green economy. Financing these investments is also an opportunity for the financial system and for European citizens' savings to be used more efficiently.  Actions of the European Central Bank and the Bank of Greece It is clear that we all have a role to play in tackling the climate crisis, even if elected governments have the primary say, through taxes, subsidies, regulation and public investment. Central banks can and have already taken active action - always within our mandate and for the benefit of societies. This is because climate-related risks are a source of instability and vulnerability for the financial system, as they can influence, as I have already mentioned, the transmission of monetary policy and create shocks to price stability. Thus, central banks take concrete measures for their own functioning, the conduct of monetary policy and, of course, their supervisory responsibilities. In 2021, at the Governing Council of the European Central Bank (ECB), we agreed on a comprehensive and ambitious action plan to further integrate climate change considerations into our monetary policy strategy and More systematic consideration of sustainability issues in our actions.'Since then, we have been making progress in implementing this plan  for example, the ECB has started to take climate change into account in corporate bond reinvestments, seeking their purchase by better climate-performing issuers, and in the collateral framework, while integrating climate change issues into its analyses; In [8] Macroeconomic forecasting models and risk management. In addition, the common stance by Eurosystem Central Banks  including the Bank of Greece  on the application of sustainable and responsible investment principles to the management of non-monetary policy portfolios and the disclosure of their climate footprint data is being implemented as of March 2023. In addition, the ECB is expected to introduce climate change disclosure as a new criterion eligibility for collateral in monetary policy operations. In this context, it also explores setting limits on the share of assets issued by entities with a high carbon footprint that banks can pledge as collateral for monetary operations . , [i] [10] policy._' In addition, central banks and supervisors have taken initiatives to assess and quantify climate change risks and integrate them into the risk management systems of banks, insurance companies and other financial sector companies at a micro- and macro-prudential level. For example, the ECB's Single Supervisory Mechanism has conducted stress tests to assess the financial impact of climate change on significant banks in the euro area, and encourages banks to integrate climate risk assessment into their credit processes and credit risk assessment in general. The European Systemic Risk Board also identifies climate risk as one of the systemic risks to the financial system and explores appropriate policy tools to address it at macroprudential level. All these measures are in line with the Eurosystem's primary objective of maintaining price stability, while at the same time supporting European policies for the green transition. At the Bank of Greece, climate change and sustainability have always been high on our agenda. We started working on these issues in 2009 when we set up a multidisciplinary committee, the Climate Change Impact Study Committee (CCISC). Since then, we have been working systematically on research, including contributing to policy-making, to limit the adverse effects of climate change and facilitate adaptation to climate change. In addition, in June 2021 we created the Centre for Climate Change and Sustainability of the Bank of Greece, with the main purpose of coordinating our relevant activities, while in November of the same year, in the context of the United Nations Climate Change Conference (POP26), we published our commitment to contribute, within our mandate, to the implementation of the Paris Agreement, with related actions and corresponding action plan for the fields , [11] [12] where we operate.  We also systematically promote cooperation and ongoing dialogue with policy makers and stakeholders  for example, the Bank of Greece participates in the development of relevant studies under the coordination of the Ministry of Finance and the Ministry of Energy and Environment. In fact, in the coming days we will publish the first - interim - results of the studies carried out in the framework of the work of the CCISC and the project I_iith aaiia Strategic Adaptation. In collaboration with the Academy of Athens, we will present updated data on climate change projections, while the first sectors for which we will announce results are agriculture and transport. Along with the impacts of climate change, we will also present data on vulnerability, a multidimensional concept that incorporates natural and socio-economic factors, as effective planning of a national climate change adaptation policy creates needs to assess it at regional and local level.  New challenges At the Eurosystem, we are committed to regularly reviewing the effectiveness of our actions to tackle climate change  and whether we need to adapt our actions accordingly. As climate and sustainability are relatively new, alongside the significant advances we have made, there are still new, important challenges ahead of us. One such challenge is the integration of climate considerations into sovereign asset markets in monetary policy portfolios, with a similar logic as for markets [13] corporate bonds. After the pandemic, the amount of transnational green bonds that issued by the European Union has increased significantly. Therefore, green bonds could potentially be the key elements of a Eurosystem bond portfolio in the future. In addition, other monetary policy tools that can potentially be considered, in the context of greener monetary policy, are targeted longer-term refinancing operations (see Iog- 877 ortho) to increase green financing or reduce risks from activities that do not contribute to the green transition.[14] Another major challenge is to integrate climate considerations into our economic analysis. Uncertainty combined with the non-linear impacts of climate change need improved macroeconomic analysis and integration into our macroeconomic models to make our inflation and growth projections more accurate. This will help to better assess the risks and opportunities posed by climate change and the green transition. Further analysis will provide a better understanding of the effects of these factors on the monetary policy transmission mechanism and enable informed policy decisions. And of course, apart from climate change, there are other critical factors related to the environment, such as biodiversity loss, which may gradually become new fields of analysis and inclusion in the scope of our actions. In closing this speech, I will quote the statement of UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres at the opening of the United Nations Climate Change Conference in Dubai: "the vital signs of the Earth are weakening [...] while to avoid its destruction [15] We need cooperation and political will." The current conjuncture, that of multiple crises, we need just that, international cooperation and strong political commitment, coordinated actions with monitoring and evaluation, inclusive governance, active participation of society, and of course access to adequate financial resources, with ,. , - I161 Focus on the most vulnerable regions and social groups. Thank you.  The undergraduate program of study includes Energy Economics, Natural Resources & Environmental Economics, Climate Change Economics. Title: Speech by Bank of Greece Governor Yannis Stournaras at SEV's honorary event for Theodoros Papalexopoulos
text: Address by the Governor of the Bank of Yannis Stournaras at SEV's honorary event for Theodoros Alexopolos 19/12/2023-Speeches Theodoros Papalexopoulos was an emblematic personality. A man with extensive education, values and vision, both for his country and for the business, Titan, that he managed. The words and phrases that spontaneously come to my mind when I talk about Theodore: Eupatrides. The man who wanted to give a moral dimension to capitalism. I would describe him in English: In the field of April. He belonged to the generation of industrialists who created values, business models and behaviors to emulate. He had an elaborated opinion, that even when you disagreed with him it was not easy to argue with him. He had square and simple thinking  he said that the crisis was created because for decades we spent much more than we produced, with the state, and not only, leading this imbalance. His favorite theory was that Greek society became addicted to the idea that it has rights but not obligations. He believed that Greece should have independent institutions of private initiative and civil society, and that the country's reconstruction plan should include everyone and not be confined to the narrow framework of an economic, social and political elite. He said: "What should never happen is to raise our hands and say: But what can I do for the country? That is out of the question! We must all, wherever we can, set an example of effort. Above all, we should not seek guarantees of success in taking the initiative. Does the farmer, when he ploughs his field and sows, have any guarantee that the seed will bear fruit? Well, we all have a debt of sowing in this place." A low-key man, he rarely gave interviews, but he was present through his works at many levels of Greek society: apart from his business activity, he was, among others, president of SEV, founding member and president of the Foundation for Economic and Industrial Research (IOBE), founding member and former president of the Citizens' Movement for an Open Society, founding member of AIoth Thoath Bydipthdd BoioI. His close collaborator and friend, his friend Raphael Moses, had said: "If there were 10 like him, the social and economic landscape of Greece would be greatly upgraded today." The phrase would certainly be considered, just in case, an extreme exaggerated figure of speech. However, when the characterization refers to Theodoros Papalexopoulos, the exaggeration becomes without difficulty, an objective evaluation of the person and his contribution to the prosperity of our country. I fully agree with this observation of Raphael Moses and add to it! According to Theodoros Papalexopoulos, it was imperative to create a center of scientific thought and reliable information, which would study and explain the great challenges and benefits for the country to the ruling classes and the media from the great challenge of the time, which was accession to the European Community. So, together with Dimitris Marinopoulos, they created the first free thought tank in the country, IOBE, from whose offices they passed in various capacities but were all marked by Papalexopoulos, ten Finance Ministers, five Governors and Deputy Governors of the Bank of Greece, several bank presidents, two PPC governors and many reputable businessmen and academics, including my humility. The late Odysseas Kyriakopoulos had said about Theodoros Papalexopoulos: "Eupatrides, leader of the industrial sector and private initiative in the Metapolitefsi. He took over the leadership of SEV during the difficult period of the first socialist government of the country and its accession to the EEC. He fought for the necessary preparation of Greek production to ensure the competitiveness of Greek companies. He was a model businessman. A visionary but also a source of inspiration for all of us who followed his example. Co-founder and great supporter of IOBE and AIBA". The respected journalist Margarita Pournara added another dimension: that of culture. He says specifically about Theodoros Papalexopoulos: "An authentic pro-European, with excellent cultivation and love for Greek culture, he helped Eleusis and its archaeological site a lot, while he also contributed to the restoration of the temple of Nemean Zeus in Nemea. He deeply believed that we modern Greeks should improve daily as a national debt to history. I knew him for many years, but I had the honor and pleasure to work with him when I was Director General of IOBE and he was a member of the Board of Directors. He had an inexhaustible inspiration in every science. He gave me ideas for research projects that resulted from his many years of experience as a real producer and his deep scientific knowledge. But above all, he stood out for his modesty, kindness, humor and social attitude. His absence is strongly felt all these years after his death from the Greek economy and society.

Title: Speech by Bank of Greece Governor Yannis Stournaras on: "The challenges of the labour market in Greece" at the 2nd MD Forum
text: Speech by Bank of Greece Governor Yannis Stournaras on: "The challenges of the labour market in the Greece" at the 2nd  typi 19/12/2023-Speeches The global economy, although slowed in 2023, is showing great resilience to the triple crises (health, energy and cost of living). The tightening of monetary policy to avoid inflation expectations becoming entrenched, the impact of the war in Ukraine, rising uncertainty due to geopolitical tensions in the Middle East, and persistent inflation due to the unprecedented rise in international energy prices, are weighing on economic activity. However, in the euro area, labour market conditions remain favourable, with unemployment low and employment on the rise.  Labour market: developments and prospects In Greece, the labour market has shown resilience over the past few years. Even during the health crisis, with the significant recession due to containment measures, the negative effects were limited. There are two main reasons for this. First, the support measures taken by the government in a timely manner to protect both employment and the income of employees, such as the suspension of employment contracts, the special purpose compensation, the possibility of teleworking and the extension of unemployment benefits, were particularly effective, as they significantly reduced redundancies, even in sectors that were significantly affected by the pandemic, such as catering and accommodation, and helped prevent workers from being cut off from the labour market and businesses. Second, thanks to reforms, which continue to be implemented since the past decade, the labour market has become more flexible and able to respond more effectively to adverse conditions. The significant economic growth that followed the post-health crisis period and reforms led to positive developments in labour market aggregates: the unemployment rate fell to 12.4% in 2022, while it continues to decline this year and stood at 10.8% in the third quarter of 2023. Total employment increased accordingly, as in the third quarter of 2023 total employees exceeded 4.25 million, and was increased by 1.3% compared to the nine months of 2022. Over the same period, the labour force participation rate for the 15-64 age group increased, mainly reflecting an increase in the labour force participation rate of women. Paid employment, according to the balance of flows of salaried employment of the ERGANI system, returned to pre-pandemic levels, while Employment prospects, although they have declined in the third quarter of the year, mainly due to uncertainty from the war situation in the Middle East and natural disasters in the country, remain positive. During the same period in Greece, but also in the euro area, employment growth was strongest in certain sectors, such as construction and tourism, which grew more dynamically than the rest. Labour demand is high in these sectors and, although the unemployment rate has remained relatively high, there is an increasing number of job vacancies. The increase in job vacancies and the difficulties faced by companies in finding staff have led to labour market mobility, increased employment and higher wages. Labour costs remained at relatively low levels until 2022, despite the fact that the Greek economy was growing rapidly, the unemployment rate was steadily declining and labour market tightness was increasing, making it more difficult for businesses to hire staff in line with their needs. Even in 2022, when, due to the war in Ukraine, energy costs skyrocketed dragging up inflation, compensation per employee increased by 2.8%. In real terms, they even decreased, as the wage increases given were relatively small and the coverage rate of workers by collective agreements remains limited. As a consequence, the international competitiveness of the Greek economy in terms of labour costs improved in 2022, as nominal unit labour costs in Greece declined, while in many of the country's key trading partners it increased. Significant wage increases were given to low-wage earners who are paid the minimum wage, as the minimum wage was successively increased by 2.0% on 1 January 2022, by 7.5% on 1 May 2022 and by 9.4% from 1 April 2023 and finally stood at 780 euros. These increases are significant as they concern more than 1/4 of employees with private law contracts and significantly boosted their disposable income, especially in conditions of high inflation. In 2023, there is a remarkable increase in labor costs, as in the nine months of 2023, wages per employee, according to ELSTAT data, increased by 4.8%. This development, in addition to the increase in the minimum wage, is also due to increased wage claims aimed at offsetting last year's inflation, which eroded real disposable income. In the medium term, further wage pressures are expected, as: a) increases are expected from 1 January 2024 in the salaries of civil servants who have been stuck for more than a decade, b) a further increase in the minimum wage and daily wage is expected in May 2024, according to the timetable that has been voted, c) as of 1 January 2024 the suspension of the seniority allowance for private sector employees is lifted without retroactivity and d) the increasing tightness In the labour market, it is expected to put pressure on higher pay for companies to hire or retain existing staff. It is important to continue improving the competitiveness of the domestic economy by ring-fencing wage increases in this context. Raising the minimum wage and labour wages more generally should support economic competitiveness and price stability, but also safeguard overall employment. Wage increases should take into account productivity developments over the medium term, as well as high uncertainty, otherwise they risk amplifying inflationary pressures, worsening the competitiveness of the Greek economy and ultimately reducing workers' real incomes. Labour market growth is expected to continue over the medium term. According to Bank of Greece forecasts, total employment is expected to keep pace with the rise in economic activity, while unemployment is expected to fall to single digits and approach pre-economic crisis levels. Labour costs are expected to remain high over the medium term, as a result of tight labour markets.  Labour market challenges Despite a significant improvement in the labour market in recent years, several distortions persist. The unemployment rate, although declining steadily and significantly in recent years, remains above the euro area average, while the unemployment rate among vulnerable groups (young people, women), despite decreasing, remains high. It should be noted that the natural unemployment rate, although decreasing, remains high, which is a sign of structural problems. The long-term unemployment rate continues to fall, but remains the highest in the EU both in terms of total unemployed and by gender, with the majority of the long-term unemployed being women. As unemployment persists, people's skills become devalued and they are more likely to withdraw from the labour market, which increases the risk of social exclusion, poverty and rising inequalities. The composition of unemployment, and in particular long-term unemployment, highlights the need to focus on lifelong learning, better matching workers' skills with labour market needs and continuing to implement active policies employment for their integration and retention in the labour market. The reduction in unemployment is linked to an increase in labour market tightness and the difficulty for businesses to find qualified personnel according to their needs. The tightness in the labour market, which reflects whether job vacancies exceed the number of job seekers, has increased since the pandemic, with tourism, agriculture, manufacturing and construction the most tight. In addition, the problem of the mismatch between jobs sought and offered remains significant, as some enterprises find it difficult to find suitable workers because they either do not have the required qualifications or have turned to other sectors with better employment prospects or even to other countries (0C3PP). The employment rate for the 20-64 age group has been increasing since the pandemic with the recovery of economic activity, but remains low compared to the EU average. The participation of men and women, especially young people, in the labour market is of particular importance, as population ageing is likely to slow down growth and, in many cases, undermine the sustainability of social security systems. The increase of youth employment and the return of highly skilled workers from abroad (Gaip Gothaip) require strengthening their demand in sectors and jobs with high added value, attracting foreign investment and enhancing the extroversion of the Greek economy. In this context, the action of the Ministry of Labour and Social Insurance under the name "Etho   " concerning the mechanism for connecting talented employees residing in Greece and abroad with highly qualified positions from companies operating in Greece, acquires particular importance. According to the latest forecasts by the European Commission, the accelerated demographic ageing of the population in the coming decades will increase the participation of older people in the total population and adversely affect the labour market, constituting a major factor of uncertainty.By 2050, the share of people aged 65 and over in the total population of the European Union is expected to increase from 21.1% to 29.0% (7.9 percentage points), The share of the economically active population (15-64 years) is projected to fall to 57.4% (-6.5 percentage points) and the share of young people aged 0-14 is estimated to fall to 13.6% (-1.4 percentage points). In addition, the old-age dependency ratio (Article 390) will increase, putting pressure on social security and health systems and pension expenditure. This unfavourable demographic change is mainly attributable to increased life expectancy and a persistently low fertility rate. Even more ominous are the forecasts for Greece, as it is projected that by 2050 the percentage of the economically active population (15-64 years) will fall further by 11.4 percentage points (from 63.6% to 52.2%).  Policy recommendations These distortions are some of the biggest challenges in the labour market, which require: First, implementation of the reforms included in the National Recovery and Resilience Plan to enhance overall productivity, potential output growth and structural competitiveness. This will increase the economy's ability to spend more, with an emphasis on investment, without worsening the external balance. Emphasis should be placed mainly on sectors that can affect the potential growth rate; such as the rapid implementation of private sector investment actions, the increase of productive investments with an inflow of foreign direct investments of high added value, the strengthening of extroversion and entrepreneurship. Increased capital investment boosts labour productivity as well as the overall productivity of the economy, making it more competitive, and leads to the creation of new and better-paid jobs. In this way, the benefits of improving the labour market will be disseminated to as many of the population as possible. Second, investing in human capital and fostering entrepreneurship are key strategies for successful labour market adaptation. Higher education is a key driver of employment growth that can help create and fill skilled jobs with high pay, strengthening the so-called 'knowledge triangle' (education-research-innovation). It is important to have greater links between universities and private sector enterprises, which will allow university research to be disseminated and exploited, and curricula need to be adapted to the development of skills sought by the market to facilitate graduates' transition to the labour market. In an environment of rapid technological development, where knowledge is depreciated much faster than in previous times, and with humanity potentially facing very great discoveries in the field of quantum computers and artificial intelligence, investment in research and innovation is the most basic prerequisite for business development, and universities can be a valuable helper in this direction. Finally, encouraging student mobility to foreign universities enhances the exchange of learning, teaching, training and work skills and provides additional tools for students to enter the labour market. Thirdly, the continued implementation of active employment policies that encourage not only the participation of young people in the labour force, but also the retention of older people in the labour market. Such policies are linked to increasing labour mobility and flexibility, as well as to acquiring and upgrading skills that meet the modern requirements of the economy. The continuation of the implementation of effective training programs of the The upgrading of technical education will contribute to job retention and the integration of vulnerable groups into the labour market. Fourthly , interventions to strengthen the network of reconciliation of family and professional life, facilitating the integration and retention in the labour market of the non-economically active population, with an emphasis on women and young people. Such interventions include incentives to start a family and have children, as well as strengthening early childhood education and care structures. Fifthly, institutional interventions to reduce social security contributions or subsidise them, which will reduce non-wage costs and will contribute, in conjunction with increased controls, especially in sectors with increased delinquency, to reducing undeclared and declared work. Sixth, the integration of migrants, to fill the key labour and skills gap in the domestic labour market. At the current juncture, there are significant labour shortages in key sectors of the economy, such as tourism, agriculture, industry and construction, and many jobs remain unfilled. Amid demographic challenges and an ageing population, The debate on the overall positive impact of migration on the Greek economy is more relevant than ever. After all, migration due to the climate crisis is likely to be unprecedented, as the ever-increasing incidence of extreme weather It will drastically enhance global mobility.
